chapters.title: Chapter I
paragraphs: On imitating Christ, and despising the world's vanities

"He who follows me shall not walk in darkness," says the Lord. These are the words of Christ, and they teach us how closely we must imitate his life and character if we seek true enlightenment and freedom from all blindness of heart. Let our deepest effort, then, be to reflect on the life of Jesus Christ.

2. His teaching surpasses all the teaching of holy men, and those who have his Spirit find hidden nourishment within it. But many people hear the Gospel often yet feel little desire for it, because they do not have the mind of Christ. Whoever wants to fully and truly understand Christ's words must strive to shape his whole life according to Christ's example.

3. What good does it do you to discuss the Holy Trinity in learned terms, if you lack humility and so displease the Trinity? Truly, it is not clever words that make a person holy and righteous—it is a good life that makes someone dear to God. I would rather feel genuine sorrow for my sins than be able to define it perfectly. Even if you knew the entire Bible and all the sayings of every philosopher, what would any of it profit you without God's love and grace? "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity," except to love God and serve him alone. This is the highest wisdom: to let go of the world and reach toward the heavenly kingdom.

4. It is vanity to chase after riches that will perish, and to put your trust in them. It is vanity to crave honors and to elevate yourself. It is vanity to follow the desires of the flesh and be led by them, for this will only bring misery in the end. It is vanity to wish for a long life while caring little about living a good one. It is vanity to focus only on the present life and give no thought to what comes after. It is vanity to love what quickly passes away, rather than hurrying toward where eternal joy awaits.

5. Keep in mind the saying: "The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing." Strive, then, to turn your heart away from love of visible things and fix it on what is unseen. For those who follow their own bodily desires stain their conscience and lose the grace of God.
(1) John viii. 12. (2) Revelations ii. 17. (3) Ecclesiastes i. 8.

chapters.title: Chapter II
paragraphs: On thinking humbly of yourself

Every person naturally desires to know things, but what good is knowledge without the fear of God? A humble peasant who serves God is surely better off than a proud philosopher who studies the stars but neglects self-knowledge. Whoever truly knows himself sees his own unworthiness and takes no pleasure in human praise. If I knew everything in the world but lacked love, what good would it do me before God, who will judge me by my actions?

2. Let go of the excessive desire for knowledge, for it brings much distraction and self-deception. Those who have knowledge want to appear learned and be called wise. But many things we can learn profit the soul little or nothing. And it is foolish beyond measure to pursue anything other than what serves your soul's well-being. Many words do not satisfy the soul, but a good life refreshes the mind, and a clean conscience gives great confidence before God.

3. The greater and more complete your knowledge, the more severely you will be judged—unless you have lived a holy life. So do not be puffed up by any skill or knowledge you possess; instead, be humbled by the responsibility it carries. If you think you know many things and understand them well, remember that there is far more you do not know. Do not be proud, but rather admit your ignorance. Why do you want to place yourself above others, when many people are more learned and more skilled in Scripture than you? If you want to learn anything of real value, learn to be unknown and counted as nothing.

4. This is the highest and most valuable lesson: to truly know yourself and think little of yourself. To think nothing of yourself and always think well of others—this is great and perfect wisdom. Even if you saw your neighbor sin openly and seriously, you should not consider yourself better, because you do not know how long you will remain upright. We are all weak and fragile. Consider no one more fragile than yourself.

chapters.title: Chapter III
paragraphs: On knowing the truth

Happy is the person whom Truth itself teaches—not through passing words and symbols, but directly. Our own judgment and feelings often deceive us, and we see very little of the truth. What good is it to argue about hidden and obscure matters that will not even be held against us in the judgment, since we did not know them? It is foolish to neglect what is useful and necessary and give our minds to things that are merely curious or even harmful. We have eyes, but we do not see.

2. Why should we concern ourselves with debates about categories and classifications? The person to whom the Eternal Word speaks is set free from endless questions. From this one Word all things come, and all things point to him; he is the Beginning who also speaks to us. Without him, no one truly understands or judges rightly. The person for whom all things are one—who traces all things back to one source and sees all things in that unity—can remain steady in spirit and at rest in God. O God, you who are the Truth, make me one with you in everlasting love. I grow weary of reading and listening to so many things. In you alone is everything I wish for and desire. Let all the scholars be silent. Let all creation be still before you. Speak to me, you alone.

3. The more unity and simplicity a person has within, the more things—and deeper things—he understands, and without strain, because he receives the light of understanding from above. A spirit that is pure, sincere, and steady is not scattered even when it has many tasks, because it does everything for God's honor and tries to be free from self-seeking. What hinders and troubles you more than your own undisciplined heart? A person who is good and devout plans inwardly before acting outwardly, and so is not pulled astray by selfish desires but brings everything under the judgment of right reason. Who has a harder battle than the one who strives to master himself? This should be our constant effort: to master ourselves, to grow stronger each day, and to keep pressing toward perfection.

4. Every form of perfection in this life has some imperfection attached to it, and all our insight carries some darkness. A humble knowledge of yourself is a surer path to God than deep scholarly research. Learning itself is not to blame, nor is any good knowledge; but a good conscience and a holy life are worth more than all of it. Because many people pursue knowledge instead of good living, they go astray and bear little or no fruit.

5. If only people gave the same effort to uprooting vice and planting virtue that they give to pointless debates, there would not be so much wrongdoing among ordinary people, nor such lax living in religious communities. On the Day of Judgment, we will not be asked what we have read, but what we have done—not how well we spoke, but how faithfully we lived. Tell me: where are all those scholars and teachers you once knew, who flourished in learning while they were alive? Others now fill their positions and perhaps never give them a thought. While they lived, they seemed important; now no one speaks of them.

6. How quickly the glory of this world fades away! If only their lives had matched their learning—then all that study would have served a real purpose. How many people are ruined by empty learning in this world, caring little about serving God. Because they prefer to be great rather than humble, they "become vain in their own thinking." Only the person with great love is truly great. Only the person who considers himself small and counts every worldly honor as nothing is truly great. Only the person who regards all earthly things as worthless compared to gaining Christ is truly wise. And only the person who does God's will and abandons his own will is truly learned.
(1) Psalm xciv. 12; Numbers xii. 8. (2) John viii. 25 (Vulg.).

chapters.title: Chapter IV
paragraphs: On being careful in our actions

We must not trust every word we hear or every feeling within ourselves, but carefully and patiently test whether something is from God. Sadly, we are so weak that we find it easier to believe and speak evil about others than good. But those who are mature do not give quick attention to every piece of news, for they know that human nature is inclined toward evil and unreliable in speech.

2. It is great wisdom not to be hasty in action or stubborn about our own opinions. Part of this wisdom is also not to believe everything we hear, and not to repeat everything to others, even if we believe it. Seek advice from someone who is wise and has a good conscience. Let yourself be taught by someone better than you, rather than following your own ideas. A good life makes a person wise in the things of God and gives experience in many matters. The more humble and obedient a person is toward God, the wiser and more at peace he will be in everything.

chapters.title: Chapter V
paragraphs: On reading the Holy Scriptures

What we must look for in Holy Scripture is truth, not clever wordplay. All Scripture should be read in the same spirit in which it was written. We should seek what is beneficial in Scripture rather than what feeds subtle arguments. So we ought to read simple and devotional books as readily as deep and challenging ones. Do not let the reputation of the writer be a stumbling block to you, whether he has little learning or much. Let the love of pure truth draw you to read. Do not ask who said this or that; pay attention to what is said.

2. People pass away, but the truth of the Lord endures forever. God speaks to us in many ways, without favoritism. Our own curiosity often gets in the way of reading Scripture well, when we try to analyze and debate passages that we should simply receive and move past. If you want to benefit from your reading, read with humility, simplicity, and honesty—without trying to gain a reputation for learning. Ask questions freely, and listen in silence to the words of holy people. Do not be bothered by the hard sayings of those older than you, for they are not spoken without good reason.

chapters.title: Chapter VI
paragraphs: On excessive desires

Whenever a person wants anything beyond what is reasonable, he immediately becomes restless. The proud and the greedy are never at rest, while the poor and humble in heart enjoy deep peace. A person who has not fully died to self is quickly tempted and overcome by small and trivial things. It is hard for someone who is weak in spirit, still partly ruled by the body and drawn to physical pleasures, to pull away completely from earthly desires. When he does pull back from them, he often feels sad, and he gets easily angry if anyone opposes his will.

2. On the other hand, if he gives in to his desires, he is immediately weighed down by a guilty conscience—because he followed his own cravings and still did not find the peace he was hoping for. True peace of heart comes from resisting our passions, not from giving in to them. There is no peace in the heart of someone who lives for the flesh, or in someone who is absorbed in outward things—only in the person who is devoted to God and living in the Spirit.

chapters.title: Chapter VII
paragraphs: On avoiding empty hope and pride

The life of anyone who puts trust in people or in any created thing is empty. Do not be ashamed to serve others for the love of Jesus Christ, or to be considered poor in this life. Do not rely on yourself, but place your hope in God. Do what you can, and God will bless your good intentions. Do not trust in your own learning or in anyone's cleverness, but rather in the favor of God, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.

2. Do not boast about your riches if you have them, nor about your powerful friends, but in God, who gives all things and who, beyond all his gifts, desires to give you himself. Do not be proud of your physical strength or beauty, for a slight illness can ruin and wither it. Do not be vain about your skills or talents, or you may displease God, from whom every good gift comes.

3. Do not consider yourself better than others, or you may appear worse in the sight of God, who knows what is in every heart. Do not be proud of your good deeds, for God judges differently than we do, and what pleases people often displeases him. If you have any good quality, believe that others have more, and you will preserve your humility. It does you no harm to place yourself below everyone else, but it does great harm to place yourself above even one person. Peace is always with the humble, but in the heart of the proud there is envy and constant anger.

chapters.title: Chapter VIII
paragraphs: On the danger of too much familiarity

Do not open your heart to everyone, but share your concerns with someone who is wise and fears God. Spend less time with young people and strangers. Do not flatter the rich or eagerly seek the company of the powerful. Let your companions be humble and simple, devout and gentle, and let your conversations be about things that build up the soul. Do not be overly familiar with any woman, but commend all good women to God. Choose God and his angels alone as your companions, and avoid drawing attention to yourself.

2. We should love all people, but not make close companions of everyone. It sometimes happens that a person is highly regarded by reputation, but in person disappoints those who meet him. We sometimes think our closeness will please others, but instead we displease them all the more when they see our faults.

chapters.title: Chapter IX
paragraphs: On obedience and submission

It is truly a great thing to live under obedience, to be under authority, and not to be our own master. It is far safer to live in submission than in a position of power. Many obey out of necessity rather than love, and they resent it, complaining over the smallest things. They will never gain freedom of spirit unless they submit with their whole heart for the love of God. Run wherever you like—you will find no peace except in humble submission to those placed over you. Dreaming about other places and changing your situation has deceived many.

2. It is true that everyone naturally follows his own preferences and is drawn to those who think like him. But if Christ is among us, it is sometimes necessary to give up our own opinion for the sake of peace. Who is so wise that he knows everything perfectly? So do not trust too much in your own opinion, but be willing to listen to others. Even if your opinion is good, giving it up for God's sake and following another's judgment will benefit you more.

3. I have often heard that it is safer to listen and receive advice than to give it. It can happen that both opinions are good, but refusing to listen to others when reason or circumstances call for it is a sign of pride or stubbornness.

chapters.title: Chapter X
paragraphs: On the danger of too many words

Avoid the noise and bustle of people as much as you can, for talk about worldly things—even when begun innocently—quickly captures us and stains us with vanity. Many times I wish I had kept silent and not gone out among people. But why do we talk and gossip so often, when we rarely return to silence without some wound to our conscience? We love to talk because we hope to gain comfort from conversation and to refresh our tired minds with a variety of ideas. And we eagerly talk and think about the things we love or want—or else about the things we most dislike.

2. But sadly, this is often pointless and empty. This outward comfort is a real obstacle to the inner comfort that comes from God. So we must watch and pray, that our time does not slip away unused. If it is right and fitting for you to speak, speak about things that build people up. Bad habits and neglect of our spiritual growth make us careless about what we say. Still, devout conversation about spiritual things helps spiritual progress greatly—especially when people of like mind and spirit come together in God.

chapters.title: Chapter XI
paragraphs: On seeking peace and making spiritual progress

We could enjoy great peace if we stopped busying ourselves with what other people say and do—things that are none of our concern. How can anyone stay at peace who meddles in other people's affairs, who looks outward constantly, and who rarely turns inward to examine himself? Blessed are the single-hearted, for they will enjoy deep peace.

2. How did so many of the saints become so perfect and so contemplative? Because they devoted themselves to rooting out all worldly desires, and so they could cling with their whole heart to God and be free to think of him. We are too caught up in our own emotions and too worried about passing things. Rarely do we fully conquer even a single fault, and we have little zeal for daily growth in grace. So we stay lukewarm and half-hearted.

3. If we were fully attentive to ourselves and not entangled in outward things, we could grow wise in the ways of salvation and make real progress in prayer and contemplation. Our greatest obstacle is this: we have not freed ourselves from our cravings and desires, and so we do not even try to walk the path the saints walked. When even a small trouble comes our way, we are too quickly cast down and turn to the world for comfort.

4. If we would stand firm like courageous people and hold our ground in the battle, we would see the Lord helping us from heaven. For he is always ready to help those who trust in him and fight the good fight. He even provides us with opportunities to struggle, so that we can win the victory. If we think spiritual progress means only outward observances and routines, our devotion will quickly fade. Instead, let us lay the axe at the very root of our life, so that once freed from our disordered desires, we may possess our souls in peace.

5. If we rooted out just one fault each year, we would soon reach perfection. But instead, we often feel that we were better and holier at the beginning of our conversion than after many years. Our zeal and progress ought to grow each day, yet now it seems remarkable if someone can even hold on to a portion of their early fervor. If we pressed ourselves a little harder at the start, we would later find that we could do everything with ease and joy.

6. It is hard to break a habit, and even harder to go against your own will. But if you cannot overcome small and easy obstacles, how will you overcome greater ones? Resist your will at the very beginning, and unlearn bad habits before they lead you step by step into worse trouble. If only you knew what peace a holy life would bring to you, and what joy it would bring to others—you would surely be more eager for spiritual growth.

chapters.title: Chapter XII
paragraphs: On the value of adversity

It is good for us to have sorrows and hardships at times, because they often remind us that we are merely strangers and pilgrims on this earth who should not place our trust in anything worldly. It is good that we sometimes face opposition and are judged harshly and unfairly, even when we do and intend what is right. Such experiences help keep us humble and protect us from vanity. When others speak ill of us unfairly and give us no credit for the good we do, we are driven to seek God's approval more earnestly as our inner witness.

2. A person should rely wholly on God, so that he does not need to seek much comfort from other people. When someone who fears God is troubled, tested, or plagued by evil thoughts, he recognizes how much he needs God—since without God he can do nothing good. Then he is heavy-hearted, he groans, he cries out from the anguish in his heart. He grows weary of life and longs to depart and be with Christ. All this teaches him that in this world there can be no perfect security or complete peace.

chapters.title: Chapter XIII
paragraphs: On resisting temptation

As long as we live in this world, we cannot be free from trouble and trial. As it is written in the book of Job, "The life of man on earth is a trial." So each of us should be on guard against temptation and stay watchful in prayer, so the devil finds no opportunity to deceive us—for he never sleeps but prowls around seeking someone to devour. No one is so perfect in holiness that he never faces temptation, and we can never be entirely free from it.

2. Yet temptations, even when they are heavy and hard to bear, can greatly benefit us. Through them we are humbled, purified, and taught. All the saints passed through great suffering and temptation, and they grew through it. Those who could not endure temptation fell away and were lost. There is no position so sacred, no place so hidden, that it is free from temptation and trouble.

3. No one is completely free from temptation as long as he lives, because we carry the root of temptation within ourselves—we were born with disordered desires. One temptation or sorrow passes, and another arrives. We will always have something to suffer, because we have fallen from our original happiness. Many who try to escape temptation fall even deeper into it. We cannot overcome by running away alone—only through patient endurance and true humility do we become stronger than all our enemies.

4. The person who merely resists temptation on the surface but does not pull it up by the root will make little progress. Instead, temptation will return more quickly and hit harder. Little by little, through patience and perseverance, you will conquer with God's help—more effectively than through force of will or frantic effort. When you are tempted, seek advice often. Do not be harsh with someone who is struggling, but comfort and strengthen him as you would want others to do for you.

5. The root of all temptation is an unstable spirit and a lack of trust in God. Just as a ship without a rudder is tossed by the waves, so a person who is careless and unsettled is tempted from every direction. As fire tests iron, so temptation tests an upright person. Often we do not know our own strength, but temptation reveals who we truly are. Still, we must be especially watchful at the beginning of temptation, for the enemy is most easily defeated when he is not allowed to enter the mind but is stopped at the door the moment he knocks. As one writer put it:
Resist at the start; the cure comes too late when the illness has taken deep root through long delay.

First, a bare thought enters the mind; then a vivid picture forms; then comes pleasure, then the pull of desire, and finally consent. Step by step, the enemy takes over completely—because he was not resisted at the beginning. The longer you delay your resistance, the weaker you become and the stronger the enemy grows.

6. Some people face their worst temptations at the beginning of their conversion, others near the end. Some are tested severely throughout their entire lives. Others are tempted only lightly, according to God's wisdom and justice—for he knows every person's character and circumstances, and he orders everything for the good of his chosen ones.

7. So we must not despair when we are tempted, but cry out to God all the more fervently, asking him to help us in every trial. As St. Paul says, God will, with the temptation, also provide a way of escape so that we can bear it. Let us humble ourselves under God's mighty hand in every temptation and trouble, for he will save and lift up the humble in spirit.

8. In temptation and trial, a person's true progress is revealed, and the reward is all the greater. It is no great thing to be devout and zealous when everything is going well. But if you remain patient in times of adversity, then there is hope for real growth. Some are kept safe from serious temptations but stumble in small, everyday ones—so that the humbling experience teaches them not to trust themselves in big things when they are weak in small ones.
(1) Job vii. 1 (Vulg.). (2) 1 Corinthians x. 13.

chapters.title: Chapter XIV
paragraphs: On avoiding rash judgment

Look carefully at yourself, and be careful not to judge the actions of others. When we judge others, we labor uselessly; we often make mistakes and easily fall into sin. But when we judge and examine ourselves, the effort is always worthwhile. We often judge things according to our own biases and preferences, and personal feelings easily lead us away from true judgment. If God were always the sole object of our desire, we would be far less troubled by the distortions of our own thinking.

2. But often some hidden motive within us, or some outward event, pulls us off course. Many people secretly pursue their own interests in what they do without even realizing it. They seem to be at peace as long as things go their way, but the moment their wishes are frustrated, they are shaken and unhappy. Differences in feelings and opinions frequently cause conflict—between friends, between fellow citizens, between religious and devout people.

3. An established habit is not easily given up, and no one is easily led to see things from another's perspective. If you rely more on your own reasoning or experience than on the power of Jesus Christ, your understanding will come slowly and with difficulty. For God wants us to be completely surrendered to him, and all our reasoning to be lifted up by a burning love for him.

chapters.title: Chapter XV
paragraphs: On works of love

No evil should ever be done for any worldly advantage or for the love of any person. Yet for the sake of someone in need, a good work may sometimes be set aside or replaced with a better one. In this way, the good work is not destroyed but improved. Without love, no work has any value. But whatever is done in love—however small or unremarkable—bears good fruit. For God looks at what a person is able to do, more than at the size of what he does.

2. The person who loves much does much. The person who does his work well does much. The one who serves the common good rather than his own interests does well. What often seems like love is really just natural desire—because it springs from self-interest, personal preference, the hope of getting something back, or the desire for gain.

3. The person with true and perfect love never seeks his own advantage, but only desires that God be glorified in all things. He envies no one, because he longs for no selfish pleasure. He does not wish to rejoice in himself, but longs to find his highest joy in God. He credits no one with goodness except God alone—the Source from whom all good flows, and the End, the Peace, the Joy of all the saints. If only we had even a spark of true love, we would clearly see that all worldly things are filled with emptiness.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI
paragraphs: On bearing the faults of others

Whatever you cannot change in yourself or in others, you should bear patiently until God arranges things differently. Consider that perhaps this trial is better for testing your patience—without which our merits count for very little. Still, when you encounter such difficulties, pray to God that he would give you the strength to bear them willingly.

2. If someone refuses to listen after being warned once or twice, do not argue with him, but leave everything to God—that his will may be done and his glory shown in all his servants, for he knows well how to bring good out of evil. Try to be patient with the faults and weaknesses of others, whatever they may be, for you yourself have many things that others must put up with. If you cannot make yourself into the person you want to be, how can you expect to shape someone else to your liking? We are quick to demand perfection in others, yet slow to correct our own faults.

3. We want others to be strictly corrected, but we resist correction ourselves. Other people's freedom bothers us, yet we insist on having our own way. We want rules to restrain others, but we refuse to accept any restrictions on ourselves. It becomes painfully clear how rarely we measure our neighbor by the same standard we use for ourselves. If everyone were perfect, what would we have left to endure from others for the sake of God?

4. God has arranged things so that we learn to bear one another's burdens, because no one is without fault, no one is without a burden, no one is self-sufficient, and no one is wise enough on his own. We must bear with each other, comfort each other, help, teach, and encourage one another. How much strength a person truly has is best revealed in times of hardship. Such times do not make a person weak—they reveal what kind of person he truly is.

chapters.title: Chapter XVII
paragraphs: On the religious life

You must learn to deny yourself in many things if you want to live in harmony and peace with others. It is no small thing to live in a religious community, to dwell there without complaint, and to remain faithful to the end. Blessed is the one who has lived well in such a community and brought his life to a good conclusion. If you want to stand firm and make real progress, consider yourself an exile and a pilgrim on this earth. To live a truly religious life, you must be willing to be thought a fool for Christ.

2. Outward clothing and appearance matter little. What makes a truly religious person is a change of character and the complete mastery of disordered desires. Whoever seeks anything other than God and the good of his soul will find only trouble and sorrow. And no one can remain at peace for long unless he strives to be the least of all and the servant of all.

3. You are called to endure and to work—not to a life of ease and idle talk. Here, people are tested like gold in the furnace. No one can stand firm unless he humbles himself with all his heart for the sake of God.

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: On the example of the holy fathers

Consider the inspiring example of the holy fathers, in whom true holiness and devotion shone brightly, and you will see how little—how nearly nothing—all our efforts amount to. What is our life compared to theirs? They were saints and friends of Christ, yet they served the Lord in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in hard work and weariness, in long prayers and holy meditations, in persecution and much reproach.

2. How many and how severe were the trials endured by the Apostles, the Martyrs, the Confessors, the Virgins, and all who chose to follow in Christ's footsteps! They gave up their lives in this world so they might keep them for eternity. How strict and simple was the life of the holy fathers who lived in the desert! What long and painful temptations they suffered! How often were they attacked by the enemy! What frequent and fervent prayers they offered to God! What rigorous fasts they kept! What burning desire for spiritual growth they showed! How bravely they fought to overcome their vices! How completely and steadily they reached toward God! By day they worked, and at night they devoted themselves to prayer. Even while working, they never stopped praying in their hearts.

3. They spent all their time fruitfully. Every hour with God seemed too short. The sweetness of contemplation was so great that they even forgot about their need for food. They gave up all wealth, honors, positions, friends, and family. They wanted nothing from the world. They ate only what was absolutely necessary. They were unwilling to serve the body even in its basic needs. So they were poor in earthly things, but rich beyond measure in grace and virtue. Outwardly they seemed to have nothing; inwardly they were filled with God's grace and heavenly blessings.

4. They were strangers to the world, but close friends of God. They considered themselves worthless, and the world looked down on them—but in God's eyes they were precious and beloved. They stood firm in true humility. They lived in simple obedience. They walked in love and patience. And so they grew strong in spirit and gained great favor with God. They were given as an example for all who seek to live faithfully, and they should inspire us far more than the masses of the lukewarm tempt us toward complacency.

5. How great was the devotion of those early religious communities! What fervent prayer! What noble competition in holiness! What strict discipline was kept! What reverence and obedience they showed to their leaders in everything! The traces they left behind even now bear witness that they were truly holy and perfect people, who fought bravely and trampled the world underfoot. Today, a person is considered great simply for not being a clear sinner, and for managing to endure with some patience whatever they have taken on.

6. How cold and negligent we have become in our time! We so quickly fall away from our early love that life itself becomes a burden because of our laziness and indifference. May the desire for holiness never fall asleep in you—you who have seen so many examples of devoted lives!

chapters.title: Chapter XIX
paragraphs: On the practices of a devout life

The life of a Christian should be adorned with every virtue, so that the inner person matches the outward appearance. In fact, the interior should be even better than the exterior, for God sees the heart. We must honor him with all our being, wherever we are, and walk in his presence as purely as angels do. Each day we should renew our commitment and stir up our zeal, as if it were the very first day of our conversion, saying: "Help me, O God, in my good resolutions and in your holy service. Grant that today I may make a true beginning, for until now I have done nothing!"

2. Our progress depends on our resolve, and great effort is needed by anyone who wants to advance. If the person who makes a firm resolution often falls short, what will happen to the one who resolves only half-heartedly or not at all? We abandon our resolutions in many ways, and even a small neglect of our spiritual practices rarely goes without some cost. The resolutions of the righteous depend more on God's grace than on their own wisdom, for they place their trust in him whatever they undertake. For we make our plans, but God directs the outcome, and our way is not in our own hands.

3. If a regular spiritual practice is sometimes set aside for an act of kindness or to help someone, it can easily be resumed afterward. But if it is dropped out of boredom or laziness, that is sinful, and the damage will be felt. Try as hard as we may, we will still fall short in many things. We should always make clear and specific resolutions, especially against the faults that trouble us most. Both our outer and inner life need to be carefully examined and ordered, because both matter for our progress.

4. If you cannot examine yourself constantly, do so at set times—at least twice a day, in the morning and in the evening. In the morning, make your resolutions. In the evening, review your day: how you spoke, what you did, what you thought—for in all these ways you may have offended God and your neighbor. Prepare yourself like a warrior against the devil's attacks. Control your appetite, and you will soon be able to control every other desire. Never be without something to do—be reading, writing, praying, meditating, or doing something useful for the community. Physical exercises, however, must be undertaken wisely, and they are not suited to everyone in the same way.

5. Practices that are not required of everyone should not be done publicly, but are safest kept private. Yet be careful not to neglect common duties while being more devoted to personal ones. Faithfully and honestly carry out the responsibilities placed on you first; then, if you still have time, follow your own devotion. Not everyone can do the same exercises. Different practices suit different people, and even for the same person, different seasons call for different exercises. Some are better for feast days, others for ordinary days. Some are needed in times of temptation, others in times of peace. Some fit our times of sadness, and others our times of joy in the Lord.

6. As the great feasts approach, we should renew our good practices and pray more earnestly for the intercession of the saints. We should make our resolutions from one feast to the next, as if each one were the time of our departure from this world and entry into the eternal celebration. So we ought to prepare ourselves with great seriousness during sacred seasons, to live more devoutly, and to observe each practice more carefully—as though we were about to receive the reward of our labors from God's own hand.

7. And if that reward is delayed, let us believe that we are not yet ready—not yet worthy of the glory that will be revealed to us at the appointed time. Let us prepare ourselves more carefully for our end. As the Evangelist Luke says: "Blessed is that servant whom the master finds watching when he comes. Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all that he has."
(1) Jeremiah x. 23. (2) Luke xii. 43, 44.

chapters.title: Chapter XX
paragraphs: On the love of solitude and silence

Find a suitable time for reflection, and think often about God's mercies toward you. Set aside curious distractions. Focus on things that bring you genuine sorrow for sin rather than mere entertainment. If you withdraw from pointless conversations, idle wandering, and the latest news and gossip, you will find plenty of time for fruitful meditation. The greatest saints avoided human company as much as they could and chose to live in quiet communion with God.

2. One writer said: "As often as I have been among people, I have returned less of a person." We often experience this after long conversations. It is easier to remain completely silent than to avoid saying too much. It is easier to stay hidden at home than to keep proper guard over yourself when out in public. So anyone who seeks the hidden, spiritual life must go with Jesus "apart from the crowd." No one ventures out safely who does not love staying in. No one speaks safely who does not love silence. No one leads safely who does not love being led. No one commands safely who does not love obeying.

3. No one rejoices safely who does not have a clear conscience within. The confidence of the saints was always rooted in the fear of God. They were no less humble and watchful within themselves for shining with great virtue and grace outwardly. But the confidence of the wicked springs from pride and presumption, and it ends in their own ruin. Never promise yourself security in this life, no matter how good a monk or how devoted a hermit you may seem.

4. Often those held in the highest esteem fall the hardest, precisely because of their overconfidence. For many people, it is actually beneficial to face inner temptation regularly, so they do not become overconfident or proud, and do not rely too heavily on worldly comforts. What a clear conscience a person would keep if he never chased fleeting pleasures and never became entangled with the world! What great peace and calm he would have if he cut off all empty concerns, thought only of what is wholesome and divine, and built his whole hope on God!

5. No one deserves heavenly comfort who has not first practiced sincere repentance. If you want to feel true sorrow in your heart, go to your room and shut out the noise of the world. As it is written: "Reflect in your own heart, in the quiet of your room, and be still." In solitude you will find what you often lose when you go out. Solitude, if you keep at it, grows sweet; but if you neglect it, it breeds restlessness. If you embrace it from the beginning of your spiritual journey and practice it faithfully, it will become a dear friend and your greatest comfort.

6. In silence and stillness, the devout soul makes progress and learns the hidden truths of Scripture. There the soul finds a fountain of tears to wash and purify itself each night, growing closer to its Maker the further it withdraws from worldly noise. God draws near with his holy angels to anyone who withdraws from friends and acquaintances. It is better to be unknown and care for your own soul than to neglect yourself while performing wonders. It is praiseworthy for a devoted person to go out rarely, to avoid being seen, and to have no desire to see others.

7. Why would you want to see what you may not have? The world and its desires are passing away. Physical cravings draw you out, but when the hour is over, what do you bring home except a heavy conscience and a scattered heart? A cheerful outing often leads to a sad return, and a merry evening leads to a gloomy morning. All bodily pleasure begins delightfully but in the end gnaws away at you and destroys. What can you see out there that you cannot see at home? Look at the sky, the earth, and the elements—for all things are made from these.

8. What can you see anywhere that will last under the sun? Perhaps you think you will be satisfied—but you never will. Even if you could see everything at once, it would still be an empty spectacle. Lift your eyes to God on high, and pray for forgiveness of your sins and failings. Leave empty pursuits to empty people, and focus on what God has commanded you. Close your door, and call upon Jesus, your Beloved. Stay with him in your room, for nowhere else will you find such peace. If you had not gone out and listened to idle talk, you would have kept yourself in greater peace. But since hearing new things sometimes delights you, you must bear the restlessness that follows.
(1) Psalm iv. 4.

chapters.title: Chapter XXI
paragraphs: On heartfelt sorrow for sin

If you want to make any progress, keep yourself in the fear of God. Do not long for too much freedom, but keep all your senses under discipline and do not give yourself over to empty amusement. Give yourself to heartfelt sorrow for sin, and you will find true devotion. This kind of sorrow opens the way for many good things that careless living quickly destroys. It is remarkable that anyone can truly rejoice in this life who considers how far from home he is, and how many dangers surround his soul.

2. Because we take our faults lightly and neglect to examine our hearts, we do not feel the sorrows of our soul. Instead, we often laugh foolishly when we have good reason to weep. There is no real freedom or genuine joy except in the fear of God with a clear conscience. Happy is the person who can cast away every distraction and focus on sincere sorrow for sin. Happy is the person who puts aside whatever might stain or burden his conscience. Fight with courage—one habit is overcome by another. If you know how to leave others alone, they will gladly leave you alone to do your own work.

3. Do not meddle in other people's affairs, and do not get tangled up in the business of important people. Keep your eye on yourself first of all, and give yourself advice before offering it to your closest friends. If you lack the approval of others, do not be discouraged by that, but be concerned that you are not living as carefully as a servant of God and a devout person should. It is often better and safer not to have many comforts in this life, especially physical ones. But if we lack divine comfort or experience it rarely, it is our own fault—because we do not seek genuine sorrow for sin, and we refuse to let go of empty and worldly pleasures.

4. Recognize that you are unworthy of divine comfort and more deserving of hardship. When a person has deep sorrow for sin, the whole world becomes heavy and bitter to him. A good person will always find reason for grief and tears, for whether he considers himself or thinks about his neighbor, he knows that no one lives here without suffering. The more honestly he examines himself, the deeper his grief becomes. The grounds for honest grief and heartfelt sorrow lie in our sins and vices, which entangle us so thoroughly that we can rarely lift our minds to heavenly things.

5. If you thought about your death more often than about how long you might live, you would surely strive harder to improve. And if you seriously considered the future pains of hell, I believe you would willingly endure hardship and discipline without complaint. But because these things do not reach the heart, and we still cling to pleasant things, we remain cold and miserably indifferent.

6. It is often spiritual poverty that makes the body so quick to complain. So pray humbly to the Lord that he would give you the spirit of true sorrow, and say with the prophet: "Feed me, O Lord, with the bread of tears, and give me tears to drink in full measure."
(1) Psalm lxxx. 5.

chapters.title: Chapter XXII
paragraphs: On reflecting on human misery

You are miserable wherever you are and wherever you turn, unless you turn to God. Why are you troubled because things do not go the way you wish? Who has everything according to his will? Neither I, nor you, nor anyone on earth. No one in the world is free from trouble or anguish—not even a king or a pope. Who has the happiest lot? The person who is able to suffer something for God.

2. Many foolish and unstable people say, "Look at that man's prosperous life—how rich, how great, how powerful, how honored he is!" But lift your eyes to the good things of heaven, and you will see that all these worldly things are nothing. They are utterly uncertain—even burdensome, because they are never possessed without worry and fear. Human happiness does not lie in having an abundance of material things; a modest portion is enough. Life on earth is truly wretched. The more a person desires to be spiritual, the more bitter this present life becomes, because he more clearly sees the defects of human nature. To eat, drink, stay awake, sleep, rest, work, and be subject to all the other necessities of the body—this is a real burden and affliction to a devout person who longs to be free from all sin.

3. The inner person is heavily burdened by the body's demands in this world. That is why the prophet prays devoutly to be freed from them, saying: "Deliver me from my necessities, O Lord." But woe to those who do not recognize their own misery, and even greater woe to those who love this miserable, decaying life! Some cling to it so desperately—even though they can barely scrape together what they need by working or begging—that if they could live here forever, they would give no thought at all to the Kingdom of God.

4. How foolish and faithless are those who are so buried in worldly things that they enjoy nothing but the pleasures of the flesh! In the end, they will sadly discover how worthless the things they loved really were. The saints of God and all true friends of Christ counted as nothing whatever pleased the flesh or flourished in this life. Their whole hope and desire reached upward to eternal and invisible things, so that the love of visible things would not drag them down.

5. Do not lose your desire for spiritual progress, brother. There is still time—the hour has not passed. Why do you keep putting off your resolution? Get up! Begin this very moment and say: "Now is the time to act, now is the time to fight, now is the right time for change." When you are troubled and uneasy, that is when you are closest to blessing. You must pass through fire and water before God brings you to a place of abundance. Unless you push yourself, you will not conquer your faults. As long as we carry this fragile body, we cannot be free from sin or live without weariness and trouble. We would gladly be free from all suffering, but since through sin we lost our innocence, we also lost our true happiness. So we must be patient and wait for God's mercy, until this tyranny passes and death is swallowed up by life.

6. How great is human frailty, always inclined toward evil! Today you confess your sins, and tomorrow you commit them again. Now you resolve to avoid a fault, and within an hour you act as if you had never resolved at all. We have every reason to humble ourselves and never think highly of ourselves, since we are so fragile and unstable. What was gained with great effort through grace can be quickly lost through carelessness.

7. What will become of us in the end, if we are already lukewarm and lazy at the beginning? It would be a disaster if we settled into comfort as though all were peaceful and secure, while our lives still show no sign of true holiness. We would do better to start over again, like eager beginners, and be trained in good living—in the hope that there may still be real growth and deeper spiritual progress ahead.
(1) Psalm xxv. 17.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIII
paragraphs: On meditating on death

Very soon your life here will end. Consider, then, how things will stand with you in the next world. A person is here today and gone tomorrow. Once out of sight, he is quickly out of mind. How dull and hard is the human heart, thinking only of the present and giving no thought to the future! In every action and thought, you should live as though you were going to die today. If you had a clear conscience, you would not greatly fear death. It would be better to guard against sin than to run from death. If you are not ready today, how will you be ready tomorrow? Tomorrow is uncertain—how do you know you will even have a tomorrow?

2. What good is a long life if we improve so little? A long life does not always bring improvement—it often only increases guilt. If only we could spend a single day in this world as it ought to be spent! Many people count the years since their conversion, yet how little fruit they have to show for it. If dying is fearful, living long may be even more fearful. Happy is the person who keeps the hour of death always before his eyes and prepares himself daily to die. If you have ever watched someone die, remember that you too will pass along the same road.

3. In the morning, consider that you may not live to see the evening. At evening, do not dare to promise yourself the morning. Always be ready, and live so that death never finds you unprepared. Many die suddenly and unexpectedly, for "at an hour you do not expect, the Son of Man comes." When that final hour arrives, you will see your whole past life in a very different light, and you will grieve bitterly over your negligence and laziness.

4. Happy and wise is the person who strives now to be the kind of person he would want to be at the moment of death! A thorough contempt for the world, a burning desire to grow in virtue, a love of discipline, the effort of repentance, willingness to obey, self-denial, and patient acceptance of any hardship for love of Christ—these are what give a person great confidence at the hour of death. While you are healthy, you have many opportunities for good works. But when you are sick, I do not know how much you will be able to do. Few people are made better by illness, just as those who travel constantly rarely become holy.

5. Do not trust in friends and relatives, and do not put off the work of your salvation until later, for people will forget you sooner than you think. It is better to provide for yourself now and send some good ahead of you than to depend on others' help. If you are not looking after your own soul now, who will care about it later? Now is the most precious time. Now is the accepted time; now is the day of salvation. But how sad that you do not use this time well, when you could be storing up treasure that would benefit you forever. The hour will come when you long for just one day—even one hour—to make things right, and I do not know whether you will be given it.

6. Dear friend, from what danger you could free yourself, from what great fear, if only you lived in constant awareness of death! Strive now to live in such a way that at the hour of death you may rejoice rather than be afraid. Learn now to die to the world, and then you will begin to live with Christ. Learn now to let go of all earthly things, and then you will be free to go to Christ. Discipline your body through repentance now, and then you will be able to face death with sure confidence.

7. Foolish one! Why do you assume you will live a long time, when you cannot be sure of a single day? How many have been deceived and suddenly snatched from life! How often have you heard of someone killed by violence, another drowned, another who fell and broke his neck, another who died at the table, another while playing! One died by fire, another by the sword, another by disease, another by a robber's hand. Death comes to all, and human life passes away swiftly like a shadow.

8. Who will remember you after your death? And who will pray for you? Work now, beloved—work all that you can. You do not know when you will die, or what will happen to you afterward. While you have time, lay up imperishable riches. Think of nothing but your salvation. Care only for the things of God. Make friends for yourself by honoring God's saints and following in their footsteps, so that when you depart, they may welcome you into everlasting dwellings.

9. Keep yourself as a stranger and pilgrim on this earth, someone to whom the affairs of this world do not belong. Keep your heart free and lifted up toward God, for here we have no lasting city. Direct your daily prayers toward him with tears and longing, that your spirit may be found worthy to pass in peace after death to its Lord. Amen.
(1) Matthew xxiv. 44. (2) Luke xvi. 9. (3) Hebrews xiii. 14.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIV
paragraphs: On the judgment and punishment of sinners

In everything you do, remember the end, and how you will stand before a strict Judge from whom nothing is hidden, who cannot be bribed, who accepts no excuses, and who judges with perfect justice. Miserable and foolish sinner—you who sometimes tremble before the face of an angry person—what will you answer to God, who knows all your wrongdoing? Why do you not prepare yourself for the day of judgment, when no one can be excused or defended by another, and each person must bear his own burden alone? Now your labor bears fruit. Now your tears are accepted, your groaning is heard, your sorrow is pleasing to God and purifying to your soul.

2. Even here on earth, the patient person finds great opportunity to purify his soul: when he grieves more for the other's malice than for his own injury; when he prays sincerely for those who wrong him and forgives them from the heart; when he does not hesitate to ask forgiveness from others; when he is quicker to show mercy than anger; when he frequently denies himself and strives to bring the flesh under the rule of the spirit. It is better to purify your soul from sin now than to cling to sins that must be purged later. We truly deceive ourselves through our excessive love of the flesh.

3. What will that fire consume but your sins? The more you spare yourself now and indulge the flesh, the heavier your punishment will be later, and the more fuel you are storing up for the burning. Where a person has sinned, there he will be punished most severely. The lazy will be driven forward with burning goads. The greedy will be tormented with unbearable hunger and thirst. The self-indulgent and pleasure-seekers will be plunged into burning pitch and foul sulfur. The envious will howl like wild dogs from sheer anguish.

4. Every sin will receive its own punishment. The proud will be filled with utter shame. The greedy will be crushed by miserable poverty. A single hour of suffering there will be more painful than a hundred years of the harshest penance here. There will be no rest, no comfort for the lost—though here we sometimes find a break from pain and the consolation of friends. Be troubled now, be sorrowful for your sins, so that on the day of judgment you may stand boldly among the blessed. For then the righteous will stand with great confidence before those who oppressed them and dismissed their struggles. Then the one who now humbly submits to human judgment will rise up to judge. Then the poor and humble will have great assurance, while the proud will be gripped by fear on every side.

5. Then it will become clear who was truly wise in this world—the one who learned to be a fool and to be despised for Christ's sake. Then every trial patiently borne will bring delight, and the mouths of the ungodly will be silenced. Then every faithful person will rejoice, and every irreverent person will mourn. Then the body that was afflicted will rejoice more than if it had always been pampered with luxuries. Then the plain garment will shine with beauty, and the expensive robe will seem worthless. Then the humble cottage will be praised more than the gilded palace. Then steady patience will prove mightier than all the power of the world. Then simple obedience will be valued above all worldly wisdom.

6. Then a pure and good conscience will bring more joy than all learned philosophy. Then contempt for riches will carry more weight than all the world's treasure. Then you will take more comfort from having prayed faithfully than from having eaten well. Then you will rejoice more in having kept silence than in having spoken at length. Then holy deeds will be far stronger than many fine words. Then a disciplined life and genuine repentance will bring deeper pleasure than all earthly delight. Learn now to suffer a little, so that then you may escape heavier suffering. Test here what you can endure, to prepare for what lies ahead. If you can barely endure a little now, how will you endure eternal torment? If a small suffering makes you so impatient now, what will the fires of hell do then? You cannot have two paradises—you cannot take your fill of pleasure here and also reign with Christ hereafter.

7. If until this very day you had lived in honors and pleasures, what would it all profit you if death came to you this instant? Everything is vanity, then, except loving God and serving him alone. For the person who loves God with all his heart does not fear death, punishment, judgment, or hell—because perfect love gives sure access to God. But the person who still delights in sin—no wonder he fears death and judgment. Still, it is a good thing if love cannot yet keep you from evil that at least the fear of hell holds you back. But whoever sets aside the fear of God will not remain in goodness for long and will quickly fall into the devil's traps.
(1) Wisd. v. 1.

chapters.title: Chapter XXV
paragraphs: On the eager improvement of our whole life

Be watchful and diligent in God's service, and remind yourself often why you left the world behind. Was it not so that you could live for God and become a spiritual person? Be eager, then, for your spiritual growth, for you will soon receive the reward of your labors, and neither fear nor sorrow will come near you again. Now you labor a little, and you will find great rest—indeed, everlasting joy. If you remain faithful and diligent, God will surely be faithful and generous in rewarding you. Hold on to a confident hope that you will reach the victory, but do not fall into complacency, or you will become lazy or proud.

2. A certain man, anxiously torn between hope and fear, once threw himself down in prayer before an altar in a church, overwhelmed with grief. He reflected within himself: "Oh, if only I knew that I would persevere to the end!" And immediately he heard a voice within him from God: "And if you did know—what would you do? Do now what you would do then, and you will be perfectly secure." At once he was comforted and strengthened. He surrendered himself to God's will, and his anxious turmoil ceased. He no longer had any desire to search curiously into what the future held, but focused instead on discovering God's good and acceptable will—the starting point and goal of every good work.

3. "Hope in the Lord and do good," says the prophet; "dwell in the land and you will be fed." One thing holds many people back from progress and earnest change: the dread of difficulty and the effort required for the struggle. But those who advance furthest in virtue are the ones who fight hardest to overcome whatever is most difficult and most opposed to their nature. A person gains the most and earns the greatest grace precisely where he most overcomes and masters himself.

4. Not everyone has the same passions to overcome, but the person who works diligently will make more progress—even if his struggles are harder—than someone with a milder temperament who is less committed to pursuing virtue. Two things are especially helpful for spiritual growth: firmly turning away from the sin you are most naturally drawn to, and eagerly pursuing the virtue you most lack. Also strive hard to guard against and overcome the faults in yourself that bother you most when you see them in others.

5. Wherever you are, seek to gain something for your soul. When you see or hear good examples, let them stir you to follow them. When you see something blameworthy, take care not to do the same—or if you have done it, correct yourself quickly. Just as your eyes observe others, so others' eyes are on you. How sweet and encouraging it is to see devoted people living with self-discipline and good order! And how sad and painful it is to see them living carelessly, failing to practice what they were called to do! How harmful it is to neglect the purpose of your calling and turn your attention to things that are none of your business!

6. Remember the commitment you have made, and keep the image of the Crucified always before your eyes. You should truly be ashamed when you look at the life of Jesus Christ, that you have not yet tried harder to conform yourself to him—though you have been on this path for a long time. A devout person who studies the life and passion of our Lord with serious attention will find there, in abundance, everything profitable and necessary. There is no need to look for anything beyond Jesus. If only Jesus crucified would come into our hearts—how quickly and completely we would learn everything we need to know!

7. The person who is earnest accepts and bears well everything that comes his way. The person who is careless and lukewarm has trouble upon trouble and suffers on every side, because he has no inner comfort and is not allowed to seek it in outward things. The person who lives without discipline is heading for serious ruin. The person who looks for an easier, lighter path will always be dissatisfied, because one thing or another will always displease him.

8. If only we had no other task than to praise the Lord our God with our whole heart and voice! If only you never needed to eat, drink, or sleep, but could always praise God and devote yourself entirely to spiritual things—then you would be far happier than now, when you must serve the body for so many needs. If only these physical necessities did not exist, and there were only the spiritual nourishment of the soul—which, sadly, we taste too rarely.

9. When a person reaches the point where he seeks comfort from no created thing, then he truly begins to enjoy God. Then he will be content with whatever happens to him. He will neither rejoice too much over abundance nor grieve too much over scarcity, but will commit himself entirely and with full trust to God—who is all in all to him, in whom nothing perishes or dies, but all things live and serve his word without delay.

10. Always remember your end, and that lost time never returns. Without effort and discipline, you will never gain virtue. If you begin to grow cold, things will start to go badly for you. But if you give yourself to zeal, you will find great peace, and your work will feel lighter because of God's grace and the love of virtue. A zealous and diligent person is ready for anything. It is harder work to resist sin and passion than to toil at physical labor. Whoever does not avoid small faults gradually slips into greater ones. You will always be glad at the end of the day if you have spent it well. Watch over yourself, stir yourself up, challenge yourself—and however things go with others, do not neglect yourself. The more firmly you push yourself, the more you will grow. Amen.
(1) Psalm xxxvii. 3.
ADMONITIONS CONCERNING THE INNER LIFE

chapters.title: Chapter I
paragraphs: On the inner life

"The kingdom of God is within you," says the Lord. Turn with all your heart to the Lord and leave this miserable world behind, and your soul will find rest. Learn to let go of outward things and give yourself to the inner life, and you will see the kingdom of God growing within you. For the kingdom of God is peace and joy in the Holy Spirit, and it is not given to the wicked. Christ will come to you and show you his comfort, if you prepare a worthy home for him within. All his glory and beauty come from within, and that is where he delights to dwell. He often visits the inner person, holding sweet conversation, giving soothing comfort, deep peace, and friendship beyond anything you could imagine.

2. Come, faithful soul—prepare your heart for this bridegroom, that he may come to you and dwell within you. For he says: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him." Give Christ his place, then, and refuse entry to everything else. When you have Christ, you are rich and have all you need. He will be your provider and faithful guardian in all things, so that you do not need to depend on people—for people change quickly and pass away, but Christ remains forever and stands by you faithfully to the end.

3. You should not place great trust in any fragile, mortal person, even if he is helpful and dear to you. And you should not be deeply troubled if someone sometimes opposes or contradicts you. Those who are on your side today may turn against you tomorrow—people shift like the wind. Place all your trust in God. Let him be your reverence and your love. He will answer for you himself, and will do for you whatever is best. Here you have no permanent home. Wherever you are, you are a stranger and pilgrim, and you will never find rest unless you are closely united to Christ within.

4. Why do you look here and there, when this is not the place of your rest? Your true home should be in heaven, and all earthly things should be seen as passing scenery. Everything passes away, and you along with it. Be careful not to cling to these things, or you will be caught and destroyed with them. Let your contemplation be on the Most High, and let your prayers be directed to Christ without ceasing. If you cannot yet grasp high and heavenly things, rest in the passion of Christ and dwell willingly in his sacred wounds. For if you devoutly take refuge in the wounds of Jesus and the precious marks of the nails and spear, you will find great comfort in trouble, and the slights of others will not bother you much. You will easily bear their unkind words.

5. Christ too, when he was in the world, was despised and rejected by people. In his greatest need, he was abandoned by friends and acquaintances to bear reproach. Christ was willing to suffer and be despised—and do you dare complain about anything? Christ had enemies and critics—and do you expect everyone to be your friend and supporter? How will your patience ever be crowned if you never face adversity? If you are unwilling to suffer anything, how can you be a friend of Christ? Endure with Christ and for Christ, if you wish to reign with Christ.

6. If you had once truly entered into the mind of Jesus and tasted even a little of his tender love, you would care nothing about your own comfort or discomfort. You would actually rejoice in hardship, because the love of Jesus makes a person willing to disregard himself. The person who loves Jesus, who is inwardly true and free from disordered desires, can turn readily to God, rise above himself in spirit, and enjoy fruitful peace.

7. The person who sees things as they truly are—not as they are said to be or seem to be—is truly wise, taught by God more than by any teacher. The person who knows how to live from within and set little value on outward things does not need special places or occasions for communion with God. The inner person quickly gathers himself, because he never gives himself entirely to outward things. No external work or necessary task stands in his way; he simply adjusts to events as they come. The person who is rightly ordered within is not bothered by the strange or perverse behavior of others. You are hindered and distracted only to the degree that you are caught up in outward things.

8. If things were right within you—if you were purified from evil—everything would work together for your good. This is exactly why so many things bother and trouble you: you are not yet perfectly dead to yourself, not yet separated from all earthly attachments. Nothing defiles and entangles the human heart like impure love for created things. If you reject outward comfort, you will be able to contemplate heavenly things and often experience inward joy.
(1) Luke xvii. 21. (2) John xiv. 23. (3) Hebrews xiii. 14.

chapters.title: Chapter II
paragraphs: On humble submission

Do not worry much about who is for you or against you. Simply focus on the present task and make sure that God is with you in everything you do. Keep a good conscience, and God will defend you. No one's hostility can truly harm the person God chooses to help. If you know how to be silent and to endure, you will undoubtedly see the Lord's help. He knows the right time and way to deliver you, so surrender yourself to him. It is God's part to help and to rescue us from all confusion. Often it is very good for our humility that others know about our faults and correct them.

2. When a person humbles himself over his shortcomings, he easily calms others and quickly satisfies those who are angry with him. God protects and delivers the humble. He loves and comforts the humble. He bends down to the humble and pours out great grace upon them. After they are brought low, he raises them to glory. To the humble he reveals his secrets, and gently draws and invites them to himself. Even after being criticized, the humble person remains at peace, because he rests on God, not on the world. Do not consider yourself to have made any progress unless you feel yourself to be less than everyone else.

chapters.title: Chapter III
paragraphs: On the good, peaceful person

First keep yourself at peace, and then you will be able to bring peace to others. A peaceful person does more good than a learned one. A hot-tempered person turns even good things into evil and is quick to believe the worst. A good, peaceful person turns everything into good. The person who lives in peace is suspicious of no one. But the person who is restless and discontented is tossed about by many suspicions—he is neither at rest himself nor does he let others be at rest. He often says what he should not, and leaves undone what would be most helpful. He watches what others are supposed to do, and neglects his own duties. So be zealous about yourself first, and then you may rightly be zealous about your neighbor.

2. You know very well how to excuse and justify your own actions, but you refuse to accept the excuses of others. It would be more just to accuse yourself and excuse your brother. If you want others to bear with you, bear with them. See how far you still are from true love and humility, which knows how to be angry with no one but itself. It is no great thing to get along with the good and the gentle—that comes naturally to everyone, and we all enjoy peace among those who think as we do. But to live peacefully with the difficult, the stubborn, the undisciplined, and those who oppose us—that is a great grace, a most admirable and courageous thing.

3. Some people keep themselves at peace and also maintain peace with others. Some have no peace themselves and do not allow others to have it either—they are troublesome to others, but always more troublesome to themselves. And some hold themselves in peace and work to bring others into peace as well. Yet in this sorrowful life, all our peace lies in humble endurance rather than in the absence of hardship. The person who knows best how to suffer will possess the most peace. He is the conqueror of himself, the master of the world, a friend of Christ, and an heir of heaven.

chapters.title: Chapter IV
paragraphs: On a pure mind and simple intention

A person is lifted above earthly things by two wings: simplicity and purity. Simplicity should be in the intention; purity should be in the desire. Simplicity reaches toward God; purity takes hold of him and savors his presence. No good action will trouble you if you are free within from disordered desire. If you aim at nothing but God's will and your neighbor's benefit, you will enjoy complete inner freedom. If your heart were right, then every creature would be a mirror of life and a book of sacred teaching. There is no creature so small or insignificant that it does not reflect the goodness of God.

2. If you were good and pure within, you would see all things clearly and understand them rightly. A pure heart sees the very depths of heaven and hell. As each person is inwardly, so he judges outwardly. If there is any joy in this world, the person with a pure heart surely possesses it. And if there is trouble and anguish anywhere, a guilty conscience knows it best. Just as iron cast into fire loses its rust and becomes entirely glowing, so the person who turns himself completely to God is freed from sluggishness and transformed into a new person.

3. When a person begins to grow lukewarm, he dreads even small efforts and eagerly accepts outward distractions. But when he begins to truly master himself and walk boldly on God's path, he considers as nothing those things that once seemed so burdensome.

chapters.title: Chapter V
paragraphs: On self-knowledge

We cannot place too little confidence in ourselves, because we often lack grace and good judgment. There is little light within us, and what we have we quickly lose through carelessness. Often we do not even realize how blind we are on the inside. We frequently do wrong and make even worse excuses for it. Sometimes we are driven by emotion and call it zeal. We criticize small faults in others and overlook serious ones in ourselves. We are quick to notice and tally up what we endure from others, but we do not consider what others endure from us. Anyone who honestly weighed his own behavior would not judge others so harshly.

2. The spiritually minded person puts care for his own soul above all other concerns. The person who attends to himself diligently finds it easy to stay silent about others. You will never be truly spiritual and devout unless you stop talking about others and pay full attention to yourself. If you focus entirely on yourself and on God, what happens outside will move you very little. Where are you when you are not present to yourself? And when you have run through everything else, what has it profited you if you have neglected yourself? If you want peace and true inner unity, you must set aside everything else and keep your gaze fixed on yourself alone.

3. You will make great progress if you keep yourself free from all worldly concerns. You will fall back terribly if you place value on anything in this world. Let nothing seem great, nothing noble, nothing attractive, nothing worth having—except God himself and the things of God. Consider as completely worthless any comfort that comes from created things. The soul that loves God looks down on everything that is less than God. God alone is eternal and beyond all measure, filling all things—the soul's comfort and the heart's true joy.

chapters.title: Chapter VI
paragraphs: On the joy of a good conscience

The testimony of a good conscience is the glory of a good person. Keep a good conscience, and you will always have joy. A good conscience can bear a tremendous amount and remains joyful even in the midst of hardship. A guilty conscience is always fearful and uneasy. You will rest peacefully if your heart does not condemn you. Never rejoice unless you have done well. The wicked never have true joy or inner peace, for "there is no peace, says my God, for the wicked." Even if they say, "We are at peace; no harm will come to us; who would dare to hurt us?"—do not believe them, for the wrath of God will suddenly rise against them, their deeds will come to nothing, and their plans will perish.

2. To glory in suffering is not difficult for the person who loves, for this kind of boasting is boasting in the cross of Christ. The glory that comes from other people is brief. Sadness always accompanies worldly honor. The glory of the good is in their conscience, not in the opinion of others. The joy of the upright comes from God and is in God—their joy is in the truth. Whoever desires true and eternal glory cares nothing for what is temporary. And whoever chases after temporal glory—or claims to despise it while still loving it—shows how little he truly cares for heavenly things. The person who is indifferent to both praise and criticism has great peace of heart.

3. A person with a pure conscience is easily content and at peace. You are no holier for being praised, and no worse for being criticized. You are what you are, and you cannot be judged better than God sees you. If you look honestly at what you are inside, you will not care what people say about you. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart. People look at the action, but God considers the intention. Always doing good and thinking little of yourself—that is a sign of a humble spirit. Refusing to seek comfort from any created thing is a sign of great purity and deep faith.

4. The person who seeks no outside approval for himself shows clearly that he has committed himself entirely to God. For as St. Paul says, it is not the person who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends. To walk inwardly with God, free from attachment to any outward thing—that is the state of a truly spiritual person.
(1) Isaiah lvii. 21. (2) 1 Samuel xvi. 7. (3) 2 Corinthians x. 18.

chapters.title: Chapter VII
paragraphs: On loving Jesus above all things

Blessed is the person who understands what it means to love Jesus and to let go of himself for Jesus' sake. You must give up everything you love for the sake of your Beloved, because Jesus wants to be loved alone, above all things. Love for created things is deceptive and unstable, but the love of Jesus is faithful and enduring. Whoever clings to created things will fall when they slip away; but whoever holds fast to Jesus will stand forever. Love him and keep him as your friend, for he will not abandon you when everyone else leaves, and he will not let you be lost in the end. One day, whether you want it or not, you will be separated from everything else.

2. Hold on to Jesus in life and in death, and trust in his faithfulness—for when everyone else fails you, he alone can help. Your Beloved is the kind who will not tolerate any rival; he alone wants to possess your heart and to sit on it like a king upon his throne. If you learned to strip away every created attachment, Jesus would gladly make his home with you. You will find that nearly all the trust you place in people, rather than in Jesus, is wasted. Do not rely on or lean upon a reed shaken by the wind, because "all flesh is grass, and its beauty fades like the flower of the field."
