3. You will be quickly disappointed if you look only at people's outward appearance. If you seek your comfort and advantage in others, you will often suffer loss. But if you seek Jesus in all things, you will truly find Jesus. And if you seek only yourself, you will also find yourself—but to your own ruin. The person who does not seek Jesus does himself more harm than the whole world and all his enemies could ever do.
(1) Isaiah xl. 6.

chapters.title: Chapter VIII
paragraphs: On the intimate love of Jesus

When Jesus is present, all is well and nothing seems hard. But when Jesus is absent, everything is difficult. When Jesus does not speak within, our comfort is worthless. But if Jesus speaks even a single word, the comfort we feel is overwhelming. Did not Mary Magdalene rise at once from the place where she was weeping when Martha said to her, "The Master is here and is calling for you"? Happy hour, when Jesus calls you from tears to the joy of the spirit! How dry and hard you are without Jesus! How foolish and empty if you desire anything apart from Jesus! Is this not a greater loss than if you lost the whole world?

2. What can the world give you without Jesus? To be without Jesus is the deepest hell; to be with Jesus is sweet paradise. If Jesus is with you, no enemy can harm you. Whoever finds Jesus finds a great treasure—indeed, a treasure above all treasures. And whoever loses Jesus loses an enormous amount—more than the whole world. The person who lives without Jesus is utterly poor; the person who is close to Jesus is immeasurably rich.

3. It takes great skill to know how to live with Jesus, and great wisdom to know how to keep him. Be humble and peaceful, and Jesus will stay with you. Be devout and calm, and Jesus will remain with you. But you can quickly drive Jesus away and lose his favor if you turn to outward things. And if you chase him away and lose him, to whom will you flee? Who will you look for as a friend then? Without a friend you cannot live well, and if Jesus is not your dearest friend, you will be deeply sad and alone. So it is foolish to trust or take delight in anyone else. It would be better to have the whole world against you than to have Jesus displeased with you. Of all who are dear to you, let Jesus be loved above all.

4. Let everyone be loved for Jesus' sake, but Jesus for his own sake. Jesus Christ alone deserves to be loved supremely, for he alone is found good and faithful beyond all friends. For his sake and in him, let both enemies and friends be dear to you, and pray for all of them that they may come to know and love him. Never desire special praise or affection for yourself, for that belongs to God alone, who has no equal. Do not wish for anyone to set his heart on you, and do not become absorbed in love for anyone else. Let Jesus be in you and in every good person.

5. Be pure and free within, unentangled by any created thing. You ought to bring a bare and clean heart to God if you want to experience how gracious the Lord is. And truly, unless you are drawn and led by his grace, you will never reach the point of casting aside everything else to be united with God alone. For when God's grace comes to a person, he can do all things; and when it departs, he becomes poor, weak, and given over to troubles. Even then, do not despair or lose heart, but calmly rest in God's will and bear whatever comes as praise to Jesus Christ. For after winter comes summer, after night returns day, and after the storm comes a great calm.
(1) John xi. 28.

chapters.title: Chapter IX
paragraphs: On the absence of all comfort

It is no great thing to despise human comfort when divine comfort is present. But it is a great thing—a very great thing—to be able to bear the loss of both human and divine comfort, and for the love of God to willingly endure the exile of the heart, seeking nothing for yourself and not looking to your own merit. What is so remarkable about being cheerful and devout when things go your way? That is an hour when everyone rejoices. The person rides easily enough who is carried by the grace of God. And what wonder is it if he feels no burden, when he is borne along by the Almighty and led by the supreme Guide?

2. We are willing to accept anything for comfort, and it is difficult for a person to be truly free from self-interest. The holy martyr Laurence overcame his attachment to the world—and even to his beloved priestly master—because he despised everything in the world that seemed pleasant. For the love of Christ, he calmly accepted the loss of God's chief priest Sixtus, whom he dearly loved. In this way, love for the Creator triumphed over love for a human being, and instead of human comfort he chose God's good pleasure. So learn from this: give up even a near and beloved friend for the love of God. And do not take it badly when a friend deserts you, knowing that in the end we must all be parted from one another.

3. A person must struggle long and hard within himself before he learns to fully overcome himself and draw his whole heart toward God. When a person relies on himself, he easily slips into seeking human comfort. But a true lover of Christ—someone who genuinely pursues virtue—does not fall back on such comforts and does not seek pleasant feelings that can be tasted and handled. Instead, he prefers demanding exercises and welcomes hard work for Christ.

4. When spiritual comfort is given by God, receive it with thanksgiving, recognizing it as God's gift—not something you earned. Do not become proud, do not rejoice recklessly, and do not presume foolishly. Rather, be more humble because of the gift, and more careful and watchful in everything you do—for that hour will pass, and temptation will follow. When comfort is taken from you, do not despair immediately, but wait for God's heavenly visit with humility and patience. God is able to give you back even greater favor and consolation. This is nothing new or strange to those who know God's ways, for among the great saints and ancient prophets this pattern of change was common.

5. That is why one psalmist, when God's favor was present, said: "In my prosperity I said, I shall never be shaken." But then he goes on to describe what he felt when the favor left: "You hid your face from me, and I was troubled." Yet he did not despair. Instead, he prayed all the more urgently, saying: "To you, O Lord, I will cry; I will pray to my God." And he received the fruit of his prayer, testifying: "The Lord heard me and had mercy on me; the Lord was my helper." And in what way? "You turned my mourning into joy; you took off my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness." If this happened even to the great saints, we who are poor and weak should not despair when we are sometimes warm with devotion and sometimes cold. The Spirit comes and goes according to his own good pleasure. That is why holy Job said: "You visit him in the morning, and suddenly you test him."

6. In what, then, can I hope? In what can I trust? Only in the great mercy of God, and in the hope of heavenly grace. For whether good people are near me, devout friends, holy books, beautiful writings, sweet hymns and songs—all these help little and have little flavor when God's favor has withdrawn and I am left to my own poverty. At such times, there is no better remedy than patience, self-denial, and resting in the will of God.

7. I have never found anyone so devout that he did not sometimes experience a withdrawal of God's favor and a loss of fervor. No saint was ever so filled with ecstasy or so enlightened that he was not tested sooner or later. For the person who has not been exercised by some temptation for God's sake is not worthy of the great vision of God. Temptation usually comes as a sign that comfort will follow, and heavenly consolation is promised to those who have been proved through trial. As it is written: "To the one who overcomes, I will give the right to eat from the tree of life."

8. Divine comfort is given so that a person may be stronger in bearing hardship. And temptation follows, so that he does not become proud because of the gift. The devil never sleeps; your flesh is not yet dead. So never stop preparing for battle—for enemies stand on your right and on your left, and they are never at rest.
(1) Psalm xxx. 6. (2) Job vii. 18. (3) Revelation ii. 7.

chapters.title: Chapter X
paragraphs: On gratitude for God's grace

Why do you seek rest when you were born to work? Prepare yourself for patience rather than comfort, and for carrying the cross rather than for joy. Who in this world would not gladly receive spiritual consolation and joy, if he could always have it? For spiritual comforts surpass all the pleasures of the world and all the delights of the flesh. Every worldly pleasure is either hollow or impure, while spiritual delights alone are truly pleasant and honorable—born from virtue and poured by God into pure hearts. But no one can enjoy these divine comforts whenever he wishes, because seasons of temptation are never far away.

2. There is a great difference between a genuine visit from God and a false sense of spiritual freedom rooted in self-confidence. God does well in giving us the grace of comfort, but we do wrong by not immediately giving God thanks for it. And so the gifts of grace cannot flow freely to us, because we are ungrateful to the Giver and do not return them to the Source from which they come. Grace always goes to the grateful, and what is usually given to the humble is taken from the proud.

3. I want no consolation that strips me of genuine sorrow for sin. I want no contemplation that leads to pride. Not everything lofty is holy; not everything sweet is good; not every desire is pure; not everything we hold dear pleases God. I gladly accept the kind of grace that makes me humbler, more cautious, and more ready to let go of myself. The person who has been taught by the gift of grace—and made wiser by having it withdrawn—will not dare to claim any good for himself. Instead, he will confess that he is poor and needy. Give to God what belongs to God, and take for yourself what is yours. That means: thank God for his grace, but recognize that the fault—and the punishment it deserves—is yours alone.

4. Always take the lowest seat, and the highest place will be given to you. For the highest cannot exist without the lowest. The greatest saints are the smallest in their own eyes. The more glorious they are, the more humble they are within—full of grace and heavenly glory yet having no desire for empty praise. Resting in God and strong in his power, they cannot be puffed up in any way. They attribute to God all the good they have received, and they "seek not glory from one another, but the glory that comes from God alone." Their one desire is that God be praised in himself and in all his saints, and they are always working toward this end.

5. Be thankful, then, for the smallest blessing, and you will deserve to receive greater ones. Let the least gift seem as great to you as the greatest, and let what seems ordinary be received as a special gift. If you consider the greatness of the Giver, no gift will seem small or worthless, for nothing given by the Most High God is insignificant. Even if he sends suffering and discipline, we should be grateful, because everything he allows to happen is for our good. Whoever wants to keep God's favor should be thankful when it is given, and patient when it is taken away. Pray for it to return. Be humble and watchful, so you do not lose it.
(1) Matthew xxii. 21. (2) Luke xiv. 10.

chapters.title: Chapter XI
paragraphs: On how few love the cross of Jesus

Jesus has many lovers of his heavenly kingdom, but few who are willing to carry his cross. He has many who seek comfort, but few who welcome hardship. He finds many companions for his table, but few for his fasting. Everyone wants to rejoice with him; few are willing to suffer anything for his sake. Many follow Jesus to eat his bread, but few will drink from the cup of his suffering. Many marvel at his miracles; few embrace the shame of his cross. Many love Jesus when nothing goes wrong. Many praise and bless him when they receive comfort from him. But if Jesus hides himself and withdraws for even a short time, they fall either into complaining or into deep despair.

2. But those who love Jesus for his own sake—not for any comfort of their own—bless him in every trial and heartache just as much as in the greatest consolation. Even if he never gave them a single comfort, they would still praise him and always give him thanks.

3. How powerful is the pure love of Jesus, unmixed with any self-interest or self-love! Should not those who are always seeking consolation be called self-serving? Do they not prove themselves lovers of self rather than of Christ—always looking for their own comfort and advantage? Where will you find someone willing to serve God for nothing in return?

4. Rarely is anyone found so spiritual as to be completely stripped of self-interest. Who can find a person truly poor in spirit and free from attachment to every created thing? "His worth is beyond measure—like treasure from the ends of the earth." A person may give away all his possessions, yet that is nothing. He may do great acts of penance, yet that is small. He may master all knowledge, yet that falls short. He may have great virtue and burning devotion, yet much is still missing—one thing, the most necessary of all. What is it? That having given up everything else, he gives up himself completely and goes out from himself entirely, retaining nothing of self-love. And having done everything he knows to be his duty, let him feel that he has done nothing. Let him not consider great what others might esteem, but honestly declare himself an unprofitable servant—just as Truth himself said: "When you have done all that is commanded you, say, 'We are unprofitable servants.'" Then he may be truly poor and naked in spirit, and say with the prophet: "I am poor and needy." Yet no one is richer than this person, no one stronger, no one freer—for he knows how to give up himself and all things, and how to see himself as the least of all.
(1) Luke xvii. 10. (2) Psalm xxv. 16.

chapters.title: Chapter XII
paragraphs: On the royal way of the Holy Cross

These words seem hard to many: "If anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." But far harder will it be to hear that final sentence: "Depart from me, you wicked, into eternal fire." Those who now willingly hear the word of the cross and follow it will not fear hearing the sentence of eternal condemnation. The sign of the cross will appear in heaven when the Lord comes to judge. Then all who served the cross—who shaped their lives after the Crucified—will approach Christ the Judge with great confidence.

2. Why, then, are you afraid to take up the cross that leads to a kingdom? In the cross is healing; in the cross is life; in the cross is protection from enemies. In the cross is heavenly sweetness and strength of mind. In the cross is joy of spirit, the height of virtue, the fullness of holiness. There is no salvation for the soul, no hope of eternal life, except in the cross. Take up your cross, then, and follow Jesus, and you will enter eternal life. He went before you bearing his cross, and he died for you on the cross—so that you too would carry your cross and learn to love being crucified upon it. For if you die with him, you will also live with him. If you share in his sufferings, you will share in his glory.

3. Everything depends on the cross, and everything lies in dying to yourself. There is no other way to life and true inner peace except the way of the holy cross and daily self-denial. Go where you will, seek whatever you want—you will find no higher way above or safer way below than the way of the holy cross. Arrange and plan everything according to your own wishes, and you will always find something to suffer, willingly or not. You will always find your cross—either pain in the body or trouble in the soul.

4. Sometimes God will seem distant. Sometimes your neighbor will test you. And what is worse, you will often be a burden to yourself. Yet you cannot be freed from this or find relief through any remedy or comfort. You must bear it as long as God wills. For God wants you to learn to endure suffering without consolation and to submit to it fully, so that through it you become more humble. No one understands the passion of Christ from the heart like the person who has experienced something similar. The cross is always ready and waiting for you everywhere. You cannot escape it wherever you go, because wherever you go, you carry yourself—and you will always find yourself. Turn above, turn below, turn outward, turn inward—in all directions you will find the cross. And patience is essential everywhere if you want inner peace and the everlasting crown.

5. If you carry the cross willingly, it will carry you and lead you to your destination—to the place where suffering ends, though that place is not here. If you carry it unwillingly, you make it a heavier burden and load yourself down even more—and still you must bear it. If you throw off one cross, you will certainly find another, and probably a heavier one.

6. Do you think you can escape what no mortal has ever avoided? Which of the saints was without the cross and suffering? Even Jesus Christ our Lord was never, in all his life, without the pain of his passion. "It was necessary," he said, "for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead, and so enter his glory." How can you look for a different path than this royal road—the way of the holy cross?

7. The entire life of Christ was a cross and a martyrdom—and do you seek rest and pleasure for yourself? You are wrong, deeply wrong, if you seek anything other than suffering. This whole mortal life is full of misery and marked with crosses everywhere. The higher a person rises in the spiritual life, the heavier his crosses often become, because the pain of his exile from heaven grows stronger with the depth of his love.

8. Yet the person afflicted in so many ways is not without refreshing consolation. He feels abundant fruit growing within him from bearing his cross. For when he willingly submits to it, every burden of suffering is transformed into assurance of divine comfort. The more the flesh is worn down by hardship, the more the spirit is strengthened by grace. Sometimes the desire to suffer—out of love for conformity with Christ's cross—becomes so strong that the person would not want to be without pain and trouble. He believes that the more and heavier the burdens he can bear for God's sake, the more pleasing he will be to God. This is not human strength but the grace of Christ, which can do such powerful things in weak flesh—making a person love and embrace what he naturally hates and flees from.

9. It is not natural for us to carry the cross, to love the cross, to discipline the body, to run from honors, to bear insults patiently, to think little of ourselves and want to be thought little of, to endure hardship and loss, and to desire no worldly success. If you look to yourself, you cannot do any of this on your own. But if you trust in the Lord, strength will be given you from heaven, and the world and the flesh will be brought under your control. You will not even fear your enemy the devil, if you are armed with faith and marked with the cross of Christ.

10. Set yourself, then, like a good and faithful servant of Christ, to carry bravely the cross of your Lord, who out of love was crucified for you. Prepare yourself to bear many troubles and all kinds of hardship in this wretched life, because that is how it will be for you wherever you are—and that is what you will find wherever you try to hide. This is how it must be; there is no way to escape suffering and sorrow except to bear them patiently. Drink your Lord's cup with love if you want to be his friend and share his life. Leave consolation to God; let him do as he sees best. But set yourself to endure hardship, and count it the greatest comfort. For "the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed in us"—even if you could endure every suffering alone.

11. When you reach the point where suffering becomes sweet and pleasant for Christ's sake, then know that things are going well with you—you have found paradise on earth. As long as suffering is hard for you and you try to escape it, things will not go well, and trouble will follow you everywhere.

12. If you set your mind to what you ought—namely, to suffer and to die—things will soon go better for you, and you will find peace. Even if you were caught up to the third heaven with Paul, you would still not be safe from suffering. "I will show him," said Jesus, "how much he must suffer for my name's sake." Suffering remains your portion, then, if you want to love Jesus and serve him always.

13. If only you were worthy to suffer something for the name of Jesus! What great glory would await you, what joy among all the saints, what a bright example to your neighbor! Everyone praises patience, yet few are willing to practice it. You should be ready to suffer a little for Christ, when so many suffer far more for the world.

14. Know this for certain: you must live the life of a dying person. The more a person dies to himself, the more he begins to live for God. No one is fit to understand heavenly things unless he has accepted suffering for Christ's sake. Nothing is more pleasing to God and more beneficial for you in this world than to suffer willingly for Christ. If you had the choice, you should prefer to suffer for Christ rather than to be filled with comforts—for then you would be more like Christ and more in step with all the saints. Our worthiness and growth in grace come not from many pleasures and comforts, but from bearing many trials and hardships.

15. If there had been anything better and more beneficial for human beings than suffering, Christ would surely have shown it by his word and example. He clearly urged both his disciples and all who wish to follow him to carry their cross, saying: "If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." So now that we have read and studied everything, let us hear the final conclusion: "We must through many trials enter the kingdom of God."
(1) Matthew xvi. 24. (2) Matthew xxv. 41. (3) Luke xxiv. 46. (4) Romans viii. 18. (5) 2 Corinthians xii. 2. (6) Acts ix. 16. (7) Luke ix. 23. (8) Acts xiv. 21.
ON INWARD CONSOLATION

chapters.title: Chapter I
paragraphs: On the inner voice of Christ to the faithful soul

"I will listen to what the Lord God will say within me." Blessed is the soul that hears the Lord speaking within and receives words of comfort from his mouth. Blessed are the ears that catch the gentle whisper of God and pay no attention to the whisperings of this world. Blessed indeed are the ears that listen not to the voice sounding outside, but to the truth teaching within. Blessed are the eyes that are closed to outward things but fixed on what is within. Blessed are those who search inward things and prepare themselves through daily practice to receive heavenly mysteries. Blessed are those who long to give their time to God and free themselves from every worldly distraction. Consider these things, my soul, and close the doors of your earthly desires, so that you may hear what the Lord God says within you.

2. This is what your Beloved says: "I am your salvation, I am your peace and your life. Stay close to me, and you will find peace." Let go of everything that passes away; seek what is eternal. For what are all temporary things but traps? And what help are any created things if the Creator abandons you? Put everything else aside, then, and give yourself to the Creator, to be faithful and pleasing to him, so that you may find true happiness.
(1) Psalm lxxxv. 8.

chapters.title: Chapter II
paragraphs: On what truth says inwardly, without the noise of words

"Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening." I am your servant. Give me understanding, that I may know your ways. Incline my heart to the words of your mouth. Let your speech fall gently like dew. The Israelites once said to Moses: "You speak to us and we will listen, but do not let the Lord speak to us, or we will die." No, Lord—that is not my prayer. Rather, with the prophet Samuel I humbly and earnestly ask: "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening." Let Moses not speak to me, nor any prophet. Rather, speak yourself, O Lord—you who inspired and enlightened all the prophets. For you alone, without them, can fill me with understanding, while they without you can accomplish nothing.

2. They can indeed speak words, but they cannot give the Spirit. They speak beautifully, but when you are silent they cannot set the heart on fire. They give us the Scriptures, but you reveal their meaning. They present mysteries, but you unlock what lies behind them. They proclaim commandments, but you help us obey them. They show the way, but you give the strength for the journey. They work only on the outside, but you instruct and enlighten the heart. They water the ground, but you make things grow. They cry out with words, but you give the listener understanding.

3. So let not Moses speak to me, but you, O Lord my God, eternal Truth—lest I die and bear no fruit, having been instructed outwardly but not set ablaze within. Let not the word heard but not followed, known but not loved, believed but not obeyed, rise up against me in judgment. Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening. You have the words of eternal life. Speak to me for my soul's comfort, for the improvement of my whole life, and for the praise and glory and eternal honor of your name.
(1) 1 Samuel iii. 9. (2) Psalm cxix. 125. (3) Exodus xx. 19. (4) John vi. 68.

chapters.title: Chapter III
paragraphs: On how all God's words should be heard with humility, and how many ignore them

"My Son, hear my words, for they are very sweet—surpassing all the knowledge of the philosophers and wise men of this world. My words are spirit and life, and they are not to be weighed by human understanding. They are not to be dragged out for empty approval, but to be heard in silence and received with deep humility and great love."
2. And I said: "Blessed is the man you teach, O Lord, and instruct in your law, that you may give him rest in times of trouble and keep him from being desolate on the earth."

3. "I," says the Lord, "taught the prophets from the beginning, and even now I do not stop speaking to all people. But many are deaf and hardened against my voice. Many prefer to listen to the world rather than to God. They follow the desires of the flesh more readily than God's good pleasure. The world promises things that are small and temporary, and it is served with great eagerness. I promise things that are great and eternal, and the hearts of mortals are slow to respond. Who serves and obeys me in all things with the same care he gives to serving the world and its rulers?
"Be ashamed, O Sidon," says the sea. And if you want to know why, listen to me.

For a small reward, people will travel long distances. For eternal life, many will hardly lift a foot from the ground. A worthless payment is eagerly pursued. For a single coin, people sometimes fight shamefully. For something meaningless and a trivial promise, they do not shrink from working day and night."

4. "But, to their shame, for a good that never changes, for a priceless reward, for the highest honor and a glory that never fades, people find it too much trouble to make even a small effort. Be ashamed, then, lazy and complaining servant—for others are found more eager for destruction than you are for life. They rejoice in emptiness more than you do in truth. Sometimes, of course, they are disappointed in their hopes. But my promise never fails anyone, and I never send away empty the person who trusts in me. What I have promised, I will give. What I have said, I will fulfill—if only a person remains faithful in my love to the end. I am the one who rewards all who are good and who powerfully confirms all who are faithful.

5. "Write my words in your heart and consider them carefully, for they will be very helpful to you in times of temptation. What you do not understand when you read it, you will understand in the hour of God's visit. I usually visit my chosen ones in two ways: through temptation and through comfort. And I teach them two lessons every day—one by showing them their faults, the other by urging them to grow in grace. Whoever has my words and rejects them has one who will judge him on the last day."
A PRAYER FOR THE SPIRIT OF DEVOTION

6. O Lord my God, you are all my good. And who am I to dare to speak to you? I am the poorest of your servants, a lowly nothing—far poorer and more worthless than I know or dare to say. Yet remember, Lord, that I am nothing, I have nothing, and I can do nothing. You alone are good, just, and holy. You can do all things. You are over all things. You fill all things, leaving empty only the sinner. Call to mind your tender mercies, and fill my heart with your grace—you who do not want your work to be empty and fruitless.

7. How can I bear this difficult life unless your mercy and grace strengthen me? Do not turn your face from me. Do not delay your visit. Do not withdraw your comfort, or my soul will become like parched, thirsty ground. Lord, teach me to do your will. Teach me to walk humbly and uprightly before you, for you are my wisdom. You knew me truly before the world was made and before I was born.
(1) John vi. 63. (2) Psalm xciv. 13. (3) Isaiah xxiii. 4.

chapters.title: Chapter IV
paragraphs: On walking in truth and humility before God

"My Son, walk before me in truth, and seek me always with a simple heart. The one who walks before me in truth will be safe from evil attacks, and the truth will deliver him from the tricks and slanders of the wicked. If the truth sets you free, you will be truly free, and you will not worry about the empty words of others."

2. Lord, this is true, just as you say. Let it be so with me. Let your truth teach me, guard me, and keep me safe to the end. Let it free me from every evil and disordered desire, and I will walk before you in great freedom of heart.

3. "I will teach you," says the Truth, "the things that are right and pleasing before me. Reflect on your sins with deep displeasure and sorrow, and never consider yourself anything because of your good works. In truth, you are a sinner, prone to many passions—bound and chained by them. Of yourself, you always tend toward nothing. You will quickly fall, be quickly overcome, quickly disturbed, quickly undone. You have nothing to boast about, but many reasons to see yourself as worthless, for you are far weaker than you can possibly understand.

4. "Let nothing you do seem great in your own eyes. Let nothing be grand, nothing precious, nothing admirable, nothing worthy of honor, nothing lofty, nothing praiseworthy or desirable—except what is eternal. Let the eternal truth please you above all things, and let your own deep unworthiness displease you continually. Fear nothing, reject nothing, flee from nothing as much as your own sins and faults, which should trouble you more than any material loss. Some do not walk sincerely before me; driven by curiosity and pride, they want to know my secrets and understand the deep things of God, while they neglect themselves and their own salvation. These often fall into great temptation and sin because of their pride and curiosity, for I oppose them.

5. "Fear the judgments of God; tremble before the wrath of the Almighty. Do not presume to debate the works of the Most High, but examine your own wrongs carefully—how greatly you have sinned and how many good things you have neglected. Some carry their devotion only in books, some in images, some in outward signs and symbols. Some have me on their lips, but little in their hearts. But others, enlightened in understanding and purified in their desires, constantly long for eternal things. They hear about earthly matters with reluctance. They meet the demands of nature with sorrow. These people understand what the Spirit of truth speaks within them, for he teaches them to look down on earthly things and to love heavenly things—to disregard the world and to desire heaven day and night."

chapters.title: Chapter V
paragraphs: On the wonderful power of divine love

I bless you, O heavenly Father, Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, for you have been pleased to think of me in my poverty. O Father of mercies and God of all comfort, I thank you for refreshing me from time to time with your own consolation, even though I am unworthy of any comfort. I bless and glorify you always, together with your only Son and the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, forever and ever. O Lord God, holy Lover of my soul—when you enter my heart, all my inward being will rejoice. You are my glory and the joy of my heart. You are my hope and my refuge in the day of my trouble.

2. But because I am still weak in love and imperfect in virtue, I need to be strengthened and comforted by you. Visit me often, then, and teach me through your holy discipline. Free me from evil passions and cleanse my heart from every disordered desire, so that—healed and thoroughly purified within—I may be made ready to love, strong to suffer, and steadfast to endure.

3. Love is a great thing, a good above all others. It alone makes every heavy burden light and every uneven path smooth. It carries the load and makes it no load at all. It makes every bitter thing sweet and good. The surpassing love of Jesus drives us to great deeds and stirs up a constant desire for even greater perfection. Love wants to rise up and not be held back by anything beneath it. Love wants to be free and detached from all worldly affection, so that its inner vision is not clouded, so that it is not entangled by prosperity or overcome by adversity. Nothing is sweeter than love, nothing stronger, nothing higher, nothing wider, nothing more pleasant, nothing richer or better in heaven or on earth—for love is born of God and cannot rest except in God, above all created things.

4. The one who loves flies, runs, and rejoices. He is free and nothing holds him back. He gives everything for everything and possesses everything in everything, because he rests in the One who is high above all, from whom every good thing flows. He does not look at the gifts but turns his heart to the Giver who stands above all gifts. Love often knows no limit but overflows beyond all measure. Love feels no burden, thinks nothing of effort, and reaches beyond what it can do—never pleading impossibility, because it considers all things lawful for love to be possible. Love is therefore strong for all things, and it accomplishes many things successfully, where the one who does not love fails and falls.

5. Love is watchful; even while sleeping, it keeps watch. Though weary, it is not tired. Though pressed, it is not crushed. Though alarmed, it is not terrified—but like a living flame and a burning torch, it leaps upward and passes through every obstacle in triumph. If someone truly loves, he knows what this voice cries out. For the burning desire of the soul is a great cry in the ears of God: "My God, my Beloved! You are all mine, and I am all yours."

6. Expand my love, that I may learn to taste with the deepest part of my heart how sweet it is to love, to be dissolved in love, and to be immersed in love. Let me be lifted up by love, rising above myself in overwhelming wonder and devotion. Let me sing the song of love. Let me follow you, my Beloved, into the heights. Let my soul pour itself out in your praise, exulting in love. Let me love you more than myself—loving myself only for your sake—and let me love all people in you who truly love you, as the law of love commands, which shines out from you.

7. Love is swift, sincere, devoted, pleasant, gentle, strong, patient, faithful, wise, long-suffering, courageous, and never self-seeking—for whenever someone seeks his own interest, he falls away from love. Love is careful, humble, and honest. It is not weak, not fickle, and not chasing after empty things. It is disciplined, pure, steady, calm, and guarded in all the senses. Love is obedient and submissive to all who are in authority. It considers itself worthless and lowly. It is grateful and devoted toward God, faithful and always trusting in him—even when God hides his face—for we cannot live in love without sorrow.

8. Whoever is not ready to suffer anything and to surrender to the will of the Beloved is not worthy to be called a lover of God. The one who truly loves must willingly embrace everything hard and bitter for the Beloved's sake, and must not be drawn away from him by anything that happens.
(1) 2 Corinthians i. 3.

chapters.title: Chapter VI
paragraphs: On the testing of a true lover
"My Son, you are not yet strong and wise in your love."
2. Why do you say that, my Lord?

3. "Because at the first sign of opposition, you abandon what you have started and eagerly look for comfort. A strong lover stands firm in temptation and does not believe the enemy's lies. Just as I please him in good times, so I do not displease him in hard times.

4. "A wise lover values the love of the giver more than the gift itself. He looks at the heart behind it more than its worth, and he places every gift below the Beloved. A noble lover does not rest in the gift, but in me, above every gift.

5. "All is not lost just because you sometimes think of me or my saints less than you would like. That good and sweet feeling you sometimes experience is the effect of grace at work and a foretaste of heaven. But you must not depend on it too much, for it comes and goes. To struggle against the evil impulses of the mind and to resist the devil's suggestions—that is a sign of real virtue and great merit.

6. "So do not let strange thoughts disturb you, wherever they come from. Hold bravely to your purpose and your sincere intentions toward God. It is not an illusion when you are sometimes suddenly lifted into a moment of spiritual joy and then brought back to the usual wandering thoughts of your heart. You endure them unwillingly rather than cause them, and as long as they displease you and you fight against them, it counts as merit and not as failure.

7. "Know this: your old enemy works hard to block your pursuit of good and to pull you away from every devout practice—from meditating on the saints, from reflecting on my passion, from the honest examination of your sins, from guarding your heart, and from your firm intention to grow in virtue. He fills your mind with evil thoughts so that he can wear you out with weariness and fear and drag you away from prayer and holy reading. Humble confession displeases him, and if he could, he would stop you from receiving Communion altogether. Do not believe him or pay attention to him, even though he has often set traps for you. When he brings evil and impure thoughts, blame him for it. Say to him: 'Get away, unclean spirit! Shame on you, wretched creature, for bringing such filth to my ears. Leave me, you hateful deceiver—you will have no part in me. Jesus will stand with me like a mighty warrior, and you will be put to shame. I would rather die and endure any suffering than give in to you. Be silent! I will not listen to you anymore, no matter how many snares you set. The Lord is my light and my salvation—whom shall I fear? Though an army rises against me, my heart will not be afraid. The Lord is my strength and my redeemer.'"

8. "Fight like a good soldier. And if you sometimes fail through weakness, rise with greater strength than before, trusting in my abundant grace. But be very careful of empty self-confidence and pride, for these lead many into error and sometimes into blindness that is almost impossible to cure. Let the ruin of the proud, who foolishly lift themselves up, serve as a constant warning and call to humility."
(1) Psalms xxvii. 1-3; xix. 14.

chapters.title: Chapter VII
paragraphs: On guarding grace through humility

"My Son, it is better and safer for you to hide the gift of devotion than to display it. Do not elevate yourself, do not talk much about it, and do not value it too highly. Instead, think less of yourself and recognize that this grace was given to someone who does not deserve it. Do not cling to this feeling, for it can very quickly turn into its opposite. When you are in a state of grace, remember how miserable and helpless you usually are without it. Progress in the spiritual life does not depend only on having the grace of comfort, but on bearing its withdrawal with humility, selflessness, and patience. When it is absent, do not stop praying or let your other duties slip. Instead, do your work even more willingly, as though you had gained more strength and understanding. And do not entirely neglect yourself because of the spiritual dryness and anxiety you feel.

2. "Many people, when things go badly for them, become impatient or lazy at once. The way of a person is not in his own hands—it is God's to give and to comfort, when, how much, and whom he wills, and no more. Some who were overconfident because of their devotion have destroyed themselves, because they tried to do more than they were able. They did not consider their own smallness but followed the impulse of the heart rather than the judgment of reason. Because they presumed beyond what was pleasing to God, they quickly lost grace. They became poor and worthless—people who had built their nest in heaven—so that, humbled and reduced to poverty, they would learn not to fly with their own wings but to take shelter under mine. Those who are still new and inexperienced on the Lord's path can easily be misled if they do not follow the counsel of the wise.

3. "But if they prefer to follow their own ideas rather than trust the experience of others, the results will be very dangerous—especially if they still refuse to be corrected. Those who are wise in their own eyes rarely accept being guided by others with patience. It is better to have a small amount of wisdom with humility and a modest understanding than great stores of knowledge with empty self-importance. It is better to have less than to have much that makes you proud. The person who gives himself entirely to joy acts foolishly, forgetting his former helplessness and the reverent fear of the Lord that guards against losing the grace that was given. And the person who, in times of trouble, gives way to despair and feels less trust in me than he should is not acting wisely either.

4. "The person who wants to feel too safe in peacetime will often be found too discouraged and full of fear in wartime. If you always knew how to remain humble and balanced, guiding your own spirit well, you would not so quickly fall into danger and trouble. It is good advice, when the fire of devotion is burning, to consider what will happen when the light is taken away. And when that does happen, remember that the light can return again. I have taken it away for a time as a warning to you and for my own glory. Such a trial is often more useful than having everything go the way you want.

5. "A person's merit is not measured by the number of his visions or consolations, or by his knowledge of Scripture, or by his high position. What matters is that he is grounded in true humility and filled with divine love—that he purely and sincerely seeks God's honor in all things, that he thinks nothing of himself, that he genuinely considers himself worthless, and that he actually rejoices in being looked down upon and humbled by others rather than honored."
(1) Jeremiah x. 23.

chapters.title: Chapter VIII
paragraphs: On having a low opinion of yourself before God

I will speak to my Lord, though I am only dust and ashes. If I think of myself as anything more, you stand against me, and my sins bear true witness—I cannot deny it. But if I humble myself and reduce myself to nothing, if I shrink from all self-importance and grind myself to the dust that I am, your grace will favor me and your light will draw near to my heart. Every last trace of self-regard, however small, will be swallowed up in the depths of my nothingness and will vanish forever. There you show me what I am, what I was, and how far I have fallen—"so foolish was I, and ignorant." If I am left to myself, I am nothing—all weakness. But if you suddenly look upon me, I am instantly made strong and filled with new joy. It is astonishing that I am so quickly lifted up and so graciously embraced by you, when my own weight constantly pulls me downward.

2. This is the work of your love, which goes ahead of me freely and helps me in so many ways. It guards me in great dangers and saves me—I can truly say—from countless evils. By loving myself wrongly, I lost myself. By seeking and sincerely loving you alone, I found both myself and you. Through love, I have been brought to an even deeper awareness of my own nothingness, because you, most gracious Lord, deal with me far beyond what I deserve and beyond anything I dare to ask or imagine.

3. Blessed be you, my God, for though I am unworthy of all your gifts, your generous and infinite goodness never stops doing good—even to the ungrateful and to those who have turned far from you. Turn us back to yourself, that we may be grateful, humble, and devout, for you are our salvation, our courage, and our strength.
(1) Psalm lxxiii. 22.

chapters.title: Chapter IX
paragraphs: On referring all things to God as the final goal

"My Son, I must be your supreme and final goal, if you truly want to be happy. With this aim, your desires will be purified—for they are too often selfishly bent toward yourself and toward created things. If you seek yourself in anything, you will immediately become empty and dry within. So refer everything to me first of all, for I am the one who gave you everything. See each blessing as flowing from the highest Good, and trace all things back to me as their source.

2. "From me, the humble and the great, the poor and the rich, draw water as from a living spring. Those who serve me with a free and faithful spirit will receive grace upon grace. But whoever wants to boast apart from me, or takes pleasure in some goodness he thinks is his own, will not be established in true joy and will not grow but will be greatly hindered and thrown into distress. So do not credit any good to yourself, and do not regard virtue as belonging to any person—attribute it all to God, without whom we have nothing. I gave everything; I will receive it all back again, and I require thanks with great seriousness.

3. "This is the truth, and by it all empty boasting is silenced. And if heavenly grace and true love enter you, there will be no envy, no constriction of heart, no self-love taking hold of you. Divine love conquers everything and expands all the powers of the soul. If you are truly wise, you will rejoice in me alone and hope in me alone. For no one is good but God alone—who is to be praised above all things and blessed in everything."
(1) Luke xviii. 19.

chapters.title: Chapter X
paragraphs: On the sweetness of despising the world and serving God

Now I will speak again, my Lord, and not keep silent. I will say to my God, my Lord, and my King, who is exalted above all: "How great is the goodness you have stored up for those who fear you!" But what are you to those who love you? What to those who serve you with their whole heart? Truly, the sweetness of contemplating you is beyond words—the sweetness you give to those who love you. In this above all you have shown me your love: that when I did not exist, you made me; when I wandered far from you, you brought me back to serve you and commanded me to love you.

2. O fountain of unending love, what can I say about you? How could I ever forget you, when you chose to remember me—even after I had wasted away and was lost? You have shown mercy beyond all hope to your servant, and you have given grace and friendship far beyond anything I deserved. What can I give you in return for this grace? It is not given to everyone to leave this world and enter a life of devotion. Is it really such a great thing for me to serve you, when every creature ought to serve you? It should not seem remarkable to me. Rather, this strikes me as the truly great and wonderful thing: that you would accept as your servant someone so poor and unworthy, and count him among your chosen ones.

3. Everything I have is yours, and with it I serve you. Yet in truth, it is you who serve me rather than I who serve you. Look—the heavens and the earth, which you created for humanity's sake, are at your command and carry out whatever you order daily. And even this is little, for you have even appointed angels to serve humankind. But surpassing all of this, you yourself chose to minister to us and promised to give yourself to us.

4. What can I give you in return for all your countless mercies? If only I could serve you every day of my life! If only I could, even for a single day, offer you a service worthy of you! For truly you are worthy of all service, all honor, and unending praise. You are truly my God, and I am your poor servant, bound to serve you with all my strength and never to grow weary of praising you. This is my wish, this is my deepest desire—and whatever is lacking in me, may you supply it.

5. It is great honor and great glory to serve you and to despise everything for your sake. Those who willingly submit to your most holy service will receive great grace. Those who cast aside every earthly pleasure for your love will find the sweetest comfort of the Holy Spirit. Those who enter the narrow way for your name's sake and let go of all worldly concerns will gain great freedom of spirit.

6. O joyful and delightful service of God, which makes a person truly free and holy! O sacred state of devoted service, which makes us equal to the angels, pleasing to God, fearful to evil spirits, and honored by all the faithful! O service to be embraced and always desired—in which the highest good is promised and a joy is won that will last forever!
(1) Psalm xxxi. 19.

chapters.title: Chapter XI
paragraphs: On examining and governing the desires of the heart
"My Son, you still have many things to learn that you have not yet mastered."
2. What are they, Lord?

3. "To bring your desires fully under my good pleasure, and to stop being a lover of yourself and instead become an earnest seeker of my will. Your desires often stir you up and push you forward, but consider honestly whether you are moved more by your own interests than by my honor. If it is truly me you seek, you will be content with whatever I decide. But if some hidden self-interest lies within you, that is exactly what weighs you down and holds you back.

4. "Be careful, then, not to chase too eagerly after any desire without first consulting me—or you may later regret it, and what once pleased you may turn to displeasure. Not every feeling that seems good should be immediately followed, and not every uncomfortable feeling should be immediately avoided. Sometimes it is wise to hold back even good desires and intentions, so that through impatience you do not fall into distraction, so that through lack of discipline you do not become a stumbling block to others, or so that the resistance of others does not suddenly throw you into confusion.

5. "Sometimes, indeed, you must use force and fight vigorously against your physical appetites, not caring what the body wants or doesn't want. Instead, strive to make the body obey the spirit, however unwillingly. It must be disciplined and brought into submission until it is ready for anything, learns to be content with little, finds pleasure in simple things, and never complains about any inconvenience."

chapters.title: Chapter XII
paragraphs: On growing in patience and struggling against evil desires

O Lord God, I see that patience is absolutely necessary for me, because so many things in this life go wrong. No matter how carefully I plan for peace, my life cannot proceed without struggle and trouble.

2. "You speak the truth, my Son. I do not want you to look for a peace that is free from trials and knows no hardship. Instead, consider yourself to have found peace when you are tested by many troubles and proved by many difficulties. If you say you cannot bear much, how will you endure the fire hereafter? Of two evils, always choose the lesser. To escape eternal torment in the future, strive to endure present suffering bravely for God's sake. Do you think the children of this world suffer nothing, or only a little? You will not find it so, even among the most successful of them.
3. "'But,' you will say, 'they have many pleasures and they follow their own wishes, so they bear their troubles lightly.'"

4. "Suppose that is true—suppose they have everything they want. But how long will it last? Like smoke, the rich of this world will vanish, and no trace will remain of their past joys. Even while they are alive, they do not rest without bitterness, weariness, and fear. The very things that give them pleasure often bring the punishment of sorrow. It serves them right: because they pursue pleasures without limit, they cannot enjoy them without confusion and bitterness. How short, how false, how disordered and degrading all these pleasures are! Yet in their blindness and dullness, people do not understand. Like mindless animals, for the sake of a little pleasure in this passing life, they bring death upon their souls. So, my son, do not chase after your lusts, but turn away from your appetites. Delight in the Lord, and he will give you your heart's desire.

5. "For if you truly want to find delight and be richly comforted by me, your blessing will be found in looking down on all worldly things and in cutting off every worthless pleasure. Abundant consolation will be given to you. The more you withdraw from the comfort of created things, the sweeter and more powerful the consolations you will find. But at first, you will not reach them without some sorrow and hard effort. Old habits will resist you, but they will be overcome by better ones. The flesh will complain again and again, but it will be held in check by fervor of spirit. The old serpent will provoke and embitter you, but he will be driven off by prayer. And by keeping busy with useful work, you will block his way in."
(1) Ecclesiastes xviii. 30. (2) Psalm xxxvii. 4.

chapters.title: Chapter XIII
paragraphs: On humble obedience, following the example of Jesus Christ

"My Son, whoever tries to withdraw from obedience also withdraws from grace. Whoever seeks private advantage loses what belongs to everyone. If a person does not submit freely and willingly to the one placed over him, it is a sign that his body is not yet fully under his own control—it still resists and grumbles. Learn, then, to submit quickly to your superior if you want to bring your own body into obedience. The outward enemy is easily overcome when the inner person has not been brought low. There is no more dangerous and deadly enemy of the soul than you are to yourself—when you are not led by the Spirit. You must truly learn to think less of yourself if you want to prevail over flesh and blood. Because you still love yourself too much, you shrink from surrendering your will to others.

2. "But what is so remarkable about you—dust and nothingness—submitting to another person for God's sake, when I, the Almighty and Most High, who created everything from nothing, humbly submitted myself to humanity for your sake? I became the most humble and despised of all people, so that you might overcome your pride through my humility. Learn to obey, O dust! Learn to humble yourself, O earth and clay, and to bow beneath the feet of all. Learn to crush your passions and to yield in complete submission.

3. "Be fierce against yourself, and do not allow pride to survive within you. Show yourself so lowly and small that anyone can walk over you and tread you down like mud in the street. What do you have to complain about, foolish creature? What can you answer to those who accuse you, worthless sinner, when you have offended God so many times and deserved hell more than once? But my eye has spared you, because your soul was precious in my sight—so that you might know my love, be grateful for my kindness, and give yourself completely to true submission and humility, patiently bearing the contempt you deserve."

chapters.title: Chapter XIV
paragraphs: On reflecting on God's hidden judgments, so we are not proud of our good deeds

You send your judgments against me, O Lord, and you shake all my bones with fear and trembling. My soul is deeply shaken. I stand astonished and remember that even the heavens are not pure in your sight. If you charged your angels with error and did not spare even them, what will become of me? Stars have fallen from heaven—what dare I expect, who am only dust? Those whose works seemed praiseworthy fell to the lowest depths, and those who once ate angels' food I have seen feeding on scraps fit for pigs.

2. There is no holiness at all if you, O Lord, withdraw your hand. No wisdom helps if you stop guiding the course. No strength avails if you cease to protect. No purity is safe without your watch. No self-discipline works if your holy care is not there. When we are left alone, we sink and perish. But when you visit us, we are raised up and we live. We are unstable, but you make us strong. We grow cold, but you rekindle us.

3. How humbly I must think of myself! How I must regard it as nothing, even if I seem to have some good! How deeply I ought to submit to your unfathomable judgments, O Lord, when I discover that I am nothing—nothing at all! O immeasurable weight, O ocean that cannot be crossed, where I find nothing of myself except utter nothing! Where, then, can I hide any claim to glory? Where is the confidence that comes from virtue? All vanity is swallowed up in the depths of your judgments against me.

4. What is all flesh in your sight? "How can the clay boast against the one who shaped it?" How can the person whose heart is truly subject to God be puffed up by empty talk? The whole world will not lift up the person whom Truth has humbled. No amount of human praise will move the person who has placed all his hope in God. For those who speak—they are nothing. They will cease with the sound of their words, but the truth of the Lord endures forever.
(1) Job xv. 15. (2) Isaiah xxix. 16. (3) Psalm cxvii. 2.

chapters.title: Chapter XV
paragraphs: On how we should speak about everything we desire

"My Son, in every matter, speak like this: 'Lord, if it pleases you, let this come to pass. Lord, if this will bring you honor, let it be done in your name. Lord, if you see that this is good for me and judge it to be useful, then let me use it for your glory. But if you know it will harm me and not benefit the health of my soul, take this desire away from me.' For not every desire comes from the Holy Spirit, even when it seems right and good. It is hard to judge with certainty whether a good or an evil spirit moves you to want this or that, or whether you are simply driven by your own impulses. Many have been deceived in the end who seemed at first to be moved by a good spirit.

2. "Whatever seems desirable to you, always seek it with the fear of God and humility of heart. Above all, surrender yourself completely and leave everything to me, saying: 'Lord, you know what is best. Let this or that be done, as you will. Give what you will, as much as you will, when you will. Do with me as you know best, as most pleases you, and as brings you the most honor. Place me where you will and deal with me freely in all things. I am in your hands—turn me whichever way you choose. I am your servant, ready for anything. I want to live not for myself but for you. If only I could live worthily and perfectly!'"
A PRAYER TO DO GOD'S WILL PERFECTLY

3. Grant me your grace, most merciful Jesus, that it may be with me, work in me, and remain with me to the very end. Grant that I may always desire and choose what is most pleasing and dear to you. Let your will be my will, and let my will always follow yours in perfect agreement. May I choose and reject only what you choose and reject. Let it be impossible for me to want anything apart from your will.

4. Grant that I may die to all worldly things and, for your sake, welcome being overlooked and unknown in this world. Grant me, above all that I could wish for, to rest in you, and let my heart find peace in you. You are the true peace of the heart; you alone are its rest. Without you, everything is hard and restless. In you alone, the supreme and eternal God, I will lie down in peace and rest. Amen.
(1) Psalm iv. 8.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI
paragraphs: On seeking true comfort in God alone

Whatever I desire or imagine for my comfort, I look for it not here but in the life to come. Even if I had all the pleasures this world could offer and could enjoy every delight, it is certain they could not last. So, my soul, you can be fully comforted and perfectly refreshed only in God—the Comforter of the poor and the One who lifts up the humble. Wait just a little while, my soul. Wait for God's promise, and you will have an abundance of every good thing in heaven. If you crave too eagerly the things of the present, you will lose the things that are eternal and heavenly. Use temporal things, but desire eternal ones. No earthly good can satisfy you, because you were not created for their enjoyment.

2. Even if you possessed every good thing ever created, you could not be happy and blessed. All your true happiness lies in God, who created all things—not the kind of happiness that the foolish lovers of this world pursue, but the kind that Christ's good and faithful servants wait for, and that the spiritual and pure in heart sometimes taste, whose true home is in heaven. All human comfort is empty and short-lived. True and blessed comfort springs from within, from the truth itself. The devout person carries his own Comforter—Jesus—with him everywhere, and says to him: "Be with me always and everywhere, Lord Jesus. Let it be my comfort to be able to give up all human consolation willingly. And if your comfort is absent, let your will and righteous purpose be my highest consolation. For you will not always be rebuking, nor will you hold your anger forever."
(1) Philippians iii. 20. (2) Psalm ciii. 9.

chapters.title: Chapter XVII
paragraphs: On casting all your cares on God
"My Son, let me do with you what I will. I know what is best for you. You think as a human being does; in many things you judge as human feeling leads you."

2. Lord, what you say is true. Your care for me is greater than all the care I could ever take for myself. The person who does not cast all his care on you stands on very shaky ground. Lord, as long as my will remains upright and firmly set on you, do with me whatever you please. Whatever you do with me can only be good. If you leave me in darkness, blessed be you. If you leave me in light, blessed be you. If you comfort me, blessed be you. And if you send me suffering, blessed be you still.
3. "My Son, this is how you must stand if you want to walk with me. You must be equally ready for suffering and for joy. You must be as willing to be poor and needy as to be full and rich."

4. Lord, I will gladly bear for your sake whatever you send. Without choosing, I will accept from your hand both good and bad, sweet and bitter, joy and sorrow, and I will give thanks for everything that happens. Only keep me from all sin, and I will fear neither death nor hell. Just do not cast me away forever or blot me from the book of life. Then no trouble that comes upon me will do me harm.

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: On bearing earthly suffering patiently, following Christ's example

"My Son, I came down from heaven for your salvation. I took on your sufferings not out of necessity but drawn by love—so that you might learn patience and bear the miseries of this life without complaint. From the hour of my birth until my death on the cross, I never stopped bearing sorrow. I lacked many material things. I often heard harsh accusations against me. I gently bore opposition and hard words. I received ingratitude for kindness, blasphemy for miracles, and rebuke for my teaching."

2. Lord, because you were patient throughout your life—in this above all fulfilling your Father's command—it is right that I, a miserable sinner, should bear myself patiently according to your will. For as long as you see fit, I should carry the burden of this mortal life for the sake of my salvation. Though this present life seems heavy, it has already been made rich with merit through your grace. Through your example and the footsteps of your saints, it has become easier and brighter for those who are weak. It is also far more full of comfort than it was under the old covenant, when the gate of heaven remained shut and even the way to heaven seemed darker, since so few sought the heavenly kingdom. And even those who were righteous and on the path to salvation could not enter the kingdom of heaven before your passion and the ransom of your holy death.

3. How deeply grateful I must be to you, for showing me and all your faithful people the good and true way to your eternal kingdom! Your way is our way, and through holy patience we walk toward you, who are our crown. If you had not gone before us and shown the way, who would bother to follow? If we had not your glorious example, how far backward would we have gone! We are still lukewarm, even after hearing of your many signs and teachings. What would become of us if we did not have such a light to guide us in following you?

chapters.title: Chapter XIX
paragraphs: On bearing injuries, and what true patience looks like

"What do you say, my Son? Stop complaining. Consider my suffering and that of my saints. You have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood. What you suffer is small compared to those who endured so much—who were so fiercely tempted, so severely troubled, so thoroughly tested and tried. You should call to mind the far worse sufferings of others, so that you can bear your own lighter ones more easily. And if they do not seem light to you, perhaps it is your impatience that makes them feel so heavy. But whether they are small or great, try to bear them all with patience.

2. "The more patiently you bear suffering, the more wisely you act and the more merit you gain. You will also find it easier if your mind and habits have been carefully trained for it. Do not say: 'I cannot take this from that person—this is not the kind of thing I should have to endure. He has done me serious harm and accused me of things I never even thought of. But from someone else I would suffer patiently—things that I can see I ought to bear.' This kind of thinking is foolish, because it ignores the virtue of patience itself and focuses on the person and the offense instead.

3. "The person who is only willing to suffer what seems reasonable to him, and only from people he chooses, is not truly patient. The truly patient person does not care who tests him—whether someone above him, an equal, or someone below; whether a good and holy person or a difficult and unworthy one. From every person and in every situation, whatever comes and however often it comes, he gratefully accepts it all from God's hand and counts it as pure gain. For with God, nothing suffered for his sake—however small—will go unrewarded.

4. "So be ready for the fight if you want the victory. Without struggle, you cannot win the crown of patience. If you refuse to suffer, you refuse to be crowned. But if you desire the crown, fight bravely and endure patiently. Without labor there is no rest, and without fighting there is no victory."

5. Make possible for me by grace, O Lord, what seems impossible to me by nature. You know how little I can bear and how quickly I collapse when trouble rises against me. Whatever trial or hardship may come to me, let it become something welcome and acceptable—for to suffer and be tested for your sake is deeply good for the soul.
(1) Hebrews xii. 4.

chapters.title: Chapter XX
paragraphs: On confessing our weakness and the miseries of this life

"I will confess my sin to you"; I will acknowledge my weakness before you, Lord. It is often a small thing that casts me down and makes me sad. I resolve to act bravely, but when even a minor temptation arrives, I am immediately in great difficulty. Sometimes the trigger for a serious temptation is amazingly trivial. When I think I am safe for a moment, I often find—when I am not even paying attention—that a small gust of wind has nearly knocked me over.

2. Look, then, O Lord, at my lowliness and my frailty, which you know completely. Be merciful to me, and "pull me out of the mire so that I do not sink." Do not let me stay cast down forever. What constantly throws me backward and leaves me confused before you is that I am so quick to fall and so weak in resisting my passions. Though their attack is not entirely my choice, it is violent and painful, and it exhausts me to live in this daily conflict. My weakness is plain to see: hateful thoughts rush in far more easily than they leave.

3. If only you, most mighty God of Israel, lover of all faithful souls, would look upon the labor and sorrow of your servant and strengthen him in all he attempts. Fill me with heavenly courage, so that the old self—this wretched flesh, not yet fully subject to the spirit—does not gain the upper hand. I must fight against it as long as I remain in this painful life. What a life this is, where troubles and miseries never end, where everything is full of traps and enemies! When one trial or temptation passes, another arrives—and while the first battle still rages, new ones come, more in number and completely unexpected.

4. How can anyone love this life, seeing that it holds so much bitterness and is subject to so many miseries and disasters? How can it even be called "life" when it produces so many forms of death and affliction? The world is often criticized as deceitful and empty, yet it is not easily given up, because the desires of the flesh hold too much power over it. Some things draw us to love the world, others to hate it. The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—these pull us toward the world. But the punishments and miseries that rightly follow these things produce hatred of the world and weariness of it.

5. But an evil desire conquers the mind that is attached to the world, and it considers it happiness to wallow in the weeds—because it does not taste or perceive the sweetness of God or the inner beauty of virtue. But those who fully despise the world and strive to live for God in holy discipline—these are not ignorant of the divine sweetness promised to all who truly deny themselves. They see clearly how badly the world goes astray, and in how many ways it is deceived.
(1) Psalm xxxii. 5. (2) Psalm lxix. 14. (3) Job xxx. 7.

chapters.title: Chapter XXI
paragraphs: On resting in God above all gifts and blessings

Above all things and in all things, my soul, you must always rest in the Lord, for he himself is the eternal rest of the saints. Grant me, most sweet and loving Jesus, to rest in you above every creature—above all health and beauty, above all glory and honor, above all power and rank, above all knowledge and skill, above all riches and arts, above all joy and gladness, above all fame and praise, above all sweetness and comfort, above all hope and promise, above all merit and desire, above all gifts and rewards that you can give or pour out, above all joy and celebration that the mind can receive or feel. In a word—above angels and archangels and the entire host of heaven, above everything visible and invisible, and above everything that you, my God, are not.

2. For you, O Lord my God, are the best of all things. You alone are the Most High, you alone the Almighty, you alone the All-Sufficient and the Fullness of all things. You alone are utterly delightful and utterly comforting. You alone are the most beautiful and most loving. You alone are the most exalted and most glorious above all things—in whom all things exist and have always existed and will always exist, complete and perfect. So whatever you give me apart from yourself, or whatever you reveal or promise about yourself, falls short and is not enough—as long as you are not seen and not fully possessed. For my heart cannot truly rest or be wholly content unless it rests in you, rising above every gift and every creature.

3. O my most beloved spouse, Jesus Christ, most holy lover of my soul, ruler of all creation—who will give me the wings of true freedom, so I can fly to you and find rest? When will I be fully open to receive you and to see how sweet you are, O Lord my God? When will I gather myself completely in you, so that because of your love I no longer feel myself at all—knowing only you, beyond every sense and measure, in a way unknown to others? But now I groan often, carrying my sorrows with grief. Many evils meet me in this valley of tears—constantly disturbing and saddening me, clouding my vision, blocking my way, distracting and entangling me, so that I cannot freely come to you or enjoy the sweet communion that is always close at hand for the blessed spirits. Let my deep sighing reach you, and my many sorrows here on earth.

4. O Jesus, light of eternal glory, comfort of the wandering soul—before you my mouth has no words, and my silence speaks to you. How long will my Lord delay in coming to me? Let him come to his poor and humble one and make me glad. Let him stretch out his hand and rescue his faithful one from every trap. Come, come—for without you, no day or hour will be joyful. You are my joy, and without you my table is empty. I am miserable—in a way imprisoned and weighed down with chains—until you refresh me with the light of your presence, set me free, and show me your loving face.

5. Let others seek whatever they wish instead of you. But nothing else pleases me or ever will please me—only you, my God, my hope, my eternal salvation. I will not keep silent. I will not stop asking until your grace returns and you speak to me within.
6. "Here I am! I come to you, for you called me. Your tears and the longing of your soul, your humility and the sorrow of your heart—these have moved me and brought me to you."

7. And I said: Lord, I have called upon you, and I have longed to be with you. I was ready to give up everything for your sake. For you first moved me to seek you. So blessed be you, O Lord, for doing this good work in your servant, according to your great mercy. What can your servant say in your presence except to humble himself deeply before you, always remembering his own sin and worthlessness? For there is no one like you in all the wonders of heaven and earth. Your works are excellent, your judgments true, and by your providence all things are governed. So praise and glory be to you, O wisdom of the Father. Let my lips, my soul, and all created things praise and bless you together.

chapters.title: Chapter XXII
paragraphs: On remembering God's many gifts

Open my heart to your law, O Lord, and teach me to walk in the way of your commandments. Help me to understand your will, and to remember your blessings—both the ones given to everyone and the ones given especially to me—with deep reverence and careful reflection, so that I may be able to thank you properly. Yet I know and confess that I cannot give you fitting praise even for the least of your mercies. I am less than the smallest of all the good things you have given me. When I consider your majesty, my spirit falters before its greatness.

2. Everything we have in soul and body—everything we possess, outward or inward, natural or supernatural—comes from you as a good gift, and proves you to be a good, gentle, and generous Giver. Whether one person receives more and another less, all gifts are yours. Without you, not even the smallest thing can be had. The person who has received much cannot boast of his own merit, nor lift himself above others, nor look down on those with less. The one who credits himself least and gives thanks most humbly is the greater and better person. And the one who considers himself the most unworthy is the most fit to receive even greater gifts.

3. The person who has received fewer gifts should not be discouraged or resentful or envious of those who have more. Instead, he should look to you and greatly praise your goodness, for you pour out your gifts so richly, freely, and generously, without favoritism. All things come from you, and in all things you are to be praised. You know what is best to give each person, and why one has less and another more—that is not for us to understand but for you alone, since you know what each person truly deserves.

4. Therefore, O Lord God, I consider it a great blessing not to have many things that would earn me outward praise and human admiration. For the person who reflects on his own poverty and unworthiness should not be sad, troubled, or discouraged by it, but rather comforted and cheerful—because you, Lord, have chosen the poor and humble, those who are poor in this world's eyes, to be your friends and companions. Your apostles are witness to this—those you made leaders in every land. Yet they lived in this world blamelessly, so humble and gentle, without any malice or deceit, that they actually rejoiced to suffer insults for your name. They eagerly embraced what the world despised.

5. So nothing should bring greater joy to someone who loves you and knows your gifts than your will being done in him—the good pleasure of your eternal plan. He should be so content and comforted by this that he would be as willing to be the least as anyone else would want to be the greatest. He should be as peaceful and satisfied in the lowest place as in the highest, as gladly overlooked and unknown as honored and celebrated above others. For your will and the love of your honor should come before everything else, and should please and comfort him more than any gift he has received or could ever receive.
(1) Acts v. 41.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIII
paragraphs: On four things that bring great peace
"My Son, now I will teach you the way of peace and true freedom."
2. Do it, my Lord, as you say—I love to hear this.

3. "Try, my Son, to do another's will rather than your own. Always choose to have less rather than more. Always seek the lowest place and be subject to everyone. Always wish and pray that God's will be completely fulfilled in you. The person who does this enters into the land of peace and rest."

4. My Lord, this short teaching of yours contains great perfection. It is brief in words but rich in meaning and abundant in fruit. If I could fully keep it, inner turmoil would not arise so easily. For every time I feel disturbed and weighed down, I realize I have strayed from this teaching. But you, who are all-powerful and who always love the soul's progress, grant me more grace so that I can live out your instruction and work out my salvation.
A PRAYER AGAINST EVIL THOUGHTS
