5. O Lord my God, do not be far from me. My God, hurry to help me, for many thoughts and great fears have risen against me, attacking my soul. How can I pass through them without being hurt? How can I break through them?
6. "I," he says, "will go before you and make the crooked paths straight. I will open the prison doors and reveal the hidden places to you."

7. Do as you say, Lord, and let all evil thoughts flee before your face. This is my hope and my only comfort: to run to you in every trouble, to trust in you, to call on you from the depths of my heart, and to wait patiently for your kindness.
A PRAYER FOR ENLIGHTENMENT OF THE MIND

8. Shine upon me, blessed Jesus, with the brightness of your inner light, and drive out all darkness from the dwelling place of my heart. Restrain my wandering thoughts and crush the temptations that try to harm me. Fight powerfully for me, and drive away the savage beasts—by which I mean alluring desires—so that peace may reign within your walls and abundant praise within your courts, that is, within my clean conscience. Command the winds and the storms. Say to the sea, "Be still." Say to the stormy wind, "Be quiet"—and there will be a great calm.

9. Send out your light and your truth, that they may shine upon the earth, for I am formless and empty ground until you give me light. Pour your grace from above. Water my heart with heavenly dew. Send the rains of devotion to water the face of the earth and make it bring forth good and perfect fruit. Lift up my mind, weighed down by the burden of sin, and raise all my desire toward heavenly things—so that, having tasted the sweetness of that higher happiness, I may take no pleasure in thinking about earthly things.

10. Draw me out and rescue me from every passing comfort of created things, for nothing created can fully satisfy my desire or give me true comfort. Bind me to yourself with an unbreakable bond of love, for you alone are enough for the one who loves you—and without you, all things are empty toys.
(1) Psalm lxxi. 12. (2) Isaiah xlv. 2. (3) Psalm cxxii. 7. (4) Psalm xliii. 3.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIV
paragraphs: On avoiding curious inquiry into other people's lives

"My Son, do not be nosy or trouble yourself with pointless concerns. 'What is that to you? Follow me.' What does it matter to you whether someone is this or that, or says or does this or that? You do not need to answer for others—you must answer for yourself. So why do you get tangled up in these things? I know everyone; I see everything done under the sun. I know how things stand with each person—what he thinks, what he wants, and where his thoughts are leading. So commit everything to me. Watch over yourself in godly peace, and let the restless be restless as they choose. Whatever anyone does or says will come back to him, for no one can deceive me.

2. "Do not trouble yourself over the shadow of a famous name, or over having many friends, or over people's affection for you. These things breed distraction and heavy sorrow. My word would speak freely to you, and I would reveal secrets to you, if only you watched eagerly for my coming and opened the gates of your heart to me. Be sober and watchful in prayer, and humble yourself in all things."
(1) John xxi. 22. (2) 1 Peter iv. 7.

chapters.title: Chapter XXV
paragraphs: On where firm peace and true growth are found

"My Son, I have said: 'Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you.' Everyone desires peace, but not everyone pursues what true peace requires. My peace is with the humble and gentle of heart. Your peace will be found in great patience. If you listen to me and follow my voice, you will enjoy deep peace."
2. What should I do then, Lord?

3. "In everything, watch what you are doing and saying. Direct your whole purpose toward this: to please me alone, and to desire or seek nothing apart from me. Also, do not judge rashly about the words or deeds of others, and do not meddle in matters that are not your concern. If you do this, you will be disturbed little or rarely. But never to feel any anxiety or suffer any pain of heart or body—that does not belong to this life, but to the state of eternal rest. So do not think you have found true peace just because you feel no grief, or that everything is well just because you have no opposition, or that things are perfect just because everything goes your way. And do not consider yourself great or specially loved simply because you experience intense spiritual sweetness. These are not the marks by which a true lover of virtue is known, and true progress does not depend on them."
4. On what then, Lord?

5. "On offering yourself wholeheartedly to the divine will. On not seeking your own interests, whether great or small, whether in time or in eternity. On remaining equally thankful in prosperity and adversity, weighing everything in the same balance. If you are so courageous and long-suffering in hope that when inner comfort is taken from you, you prepare your heart for even greater endurance—and if you do not justify yourself, as though you should not have to suffer such hard things, but instead justify me in all that I ordain and bless my holy name—then you are walking in the true and right way of peace. You can have sure hope that you will see my face again with joy. For if you come to a complete disregard for yourself, know that you will enjoy as much peace as is possible for someone still on the journey."
(1) John xiv. 27.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVI
paragraphs: On the freedom of a spirit lifted above earthly things, which humble prayer deserves more than much reading

Lord, this is the work of a perfect person: never to let the mind wander from heavenly things, and to pass through many responsibilities as though without a care—not from indifference, but with the freedom of a mind that clings to no creature with disordered affection.

2. I beg you, my most merciful Lord God, protect me from the cares of this life, so that I am not too entangled by them. Guard me from the many demands of the body, so that I am not captured by pleasure. Shield me from all obstacles of the spirit, so that I am not broken and crushed by worry. I do not mean the things that worldly vanity eagerly chases after, but those miseries that weigh down and hold back the soul of your servant under the universal curse of our mortal condition—keeping it from entering into freedom of spirit as often as it would.

3. O my God, sweetness beyond words, turn all my earthly consolation into bitterness—every comfort that draws me away from the love of eternal things and wickedly lures me toward itself by dangling present pleasure before me. Do not let flesh and blood overpower me, O my God. Do not let the world and its brief glory deceive me. Do not let the devil and his cunning undermine me. Give me courage to resist, patience to endure, and steadfastness to persevere. Instead of all the world's consolations, give me the sweet anointing of your Spirit, and instead of earthly love, pour into me the love of your name.

4. Food, drink, clothing, and all the other things the body needs are a burden to the devout spirit. Let me use them with moderation and not become overly attached to them. It is not right to reject them entirely, since the body must be cared for, but to seek luxuries and things that merely give pleasure is forbidden by the holy law—otherwise the flesh would rebel against the spirit. In all these things, I ask you: let your hand guide and teach me, so that I never go too far.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVII
paragraphs: On how self-love is the greatest obstacle to the highest good

"My Son, you must give everything for everything, and keep nothing for yourself. Understand that love of self does you more harm than anything else in the world. Everything clings to you more or less, depending on your loves and desires. If your love is pure, sincere, and well-ordered, nothing will hold you captive. Do not covet what you may not have. Do not hold on to what hinders you and robs you of inner freedom. It is strange that you do not commit yourself to me from the very bottom of your heart, along with everything you could ever want or have.

2. "Why are you consumed with pointless sorrow? Why are you exhausted by unnecessary worries? Rest in my good pleasure, and you will suffer no real loss. If you chase after this or that, wanting to be here or there for your own convenience and pleasure, you will never be at rest or free from anxiety. In everything, something will be found lacking, and everywhere someone will oppose you.

3. "What helps you is not gaining or accumulating this or that, but despising it and cutting it out at the root. This applies not just to money and possessions, but also to the craving for honor and empty praise—all of which pass away with the world. The place matters little if the spirit of devotion is missing. And any peace sought from outside will not last if your heart lacks a true foundation—that is, if it does not rest in me. You may change your location, but you cannot improve yourself that way. When the opportunity arises, you will find exactly what you fled from—and more."
A PRAYER FOR CLEANSING OF THE HEART AND HEAVENLY WISDOM

4. Strengthen me, O God, by the grace of your Holy Spirit. Give me the power to be strengthened in the inner person and to free my heart from every fruitless worry and concern. Do not let me be pulled away by various desires for anything—whether small or great—but help me see everything as passing away, and myself as passing with it. For there is nothing lasting under the sun; all is vanity and a chasing after wind. How wise is the person who sees things this way!

5. Give me, O Lord, heavenly wisdom, so that I may learn to seek you above all things and to find you, to savor you above all things and to love you, and to understand everything else as it truly is, according to your wise ordering. Grant me the sense to avoid those who flatter me, and the patience to bear with those who oppose me. This is great wisdom: not to be swayed by every gust of words, nor to listen to the wicked, flattering siren's call. This is how we walk safely on the path we have begun.
(1) Ecclesiastes ii. 11.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVIII
paragraphs: Against those who speak ill of us

"My Son, do not take it to heart if people think badly of you and say things you do not want to hear. You should think worse of yourself and believe that no one is weaker than you. If you live an inner life, you will not give much weight to passing words. It is wise to keep silent in difficult times and to turn inward to me, rather than being troubled by human opinions.

2. "Do not let your peace depend on what people say. Whether they judge you well or badly, you are still the same person. Where is true peace and true glory? Is it not in me? The person who does not try to please others and is not afraid of displeasing them will enjoy great peace. All restlessness of heart and distraction of the senses comes from disordered affection and groundless fear."

chapters.title: Chapter XXIX
paragraphs: On calling upon God and blessing him when trouble comes

Blessed be your name, O Lord, forever—you who have willed this trial and trouble to come upon me. I cannot escape it, so I must flee to you for help, that you may turn it to my good. Lord, I am in distress, and it is not well within my heart. I am deeply troubled by the suffering that weighs on me. Dear Father, what can I say? I am caught in a trap. Save me from this hour—yet for this very reason I came to this hour, so that you might be glorified when I am deeply humbled and then delivered by you. May it please you to rescue me, for what can I do, poor as I am? Where can I go without you? Give me patience once more. Help me, O Lord my God, and I will not be afraid, no matter how heavy the burden.

2. And now, in the midst of all this, what can I say? Lord, your will be done. I have fully deserved this trouble and pressure. So I must bear it—if only with patience—until the storm passes and comfort returns. Yet your almighty arm is able to take even this trial from me, and to soften its force so that I am not completely overwhelmed—just as you have helped me many times before, O God, my merciful God. And as difficult as this deliverance is for me, it is easy for you, O right hand of the Most High.
(1) John xii. 27. (2) Psalm xl. 16.

chapters.title: Chapter XXX
paragraphs: On seeking God's help and trusting in his grace
"My Son, I the Lord am a stronghold in the day of trouble. Come to me when things are not going well.

"What most hinders heavenly comfort is that you are too slow to turn to prayer. Before you earnestly seek me, you first look for many other sources of consolation and try to refresh yourself with outward things. So everything profits you little, until you learn that it is I who deliver those who trust in me. Apart from me, there is no strong help, no useful counsel, no lasting remedy. But now, recovering your courage after the storm, grow strong in the light of my mercy. For I am near, says the Lord, to restore all things—not just to their former state, but abundantly, one blessing upon another.

2. "Is anything too hard for me? Am I like someone who makes promises but does not keep them? Where is your faith? Stand firm and persevere. Be patient and strong. Comfort will come at the right time. Wait for me—wait! I will come and heal you. It is temptation that troubles you and groundless fear that terrifies you. What does worrying about future events bring you except sorrow upon sorrow? Each day has enough trouble of its own. It is pointless and useless to be anxious or excited about things that may never happen.

3. "But it is human nature to be deceived by such fantasies, and it is a sign of a weak mind to be so easily pulled away at the enemy's suggestion. He does not care whether he deceives you by truth or by lies, or whether he brings you down through love of the present or fear of the future. So do not let your heart be troubled, and do not be afraid. Trust in me, and put your confidence in my mercy. When you think you are far from me, I am often closer than ever. When you think nearly all is lost, that is often when the greatest opportunity for gain is at hand. Not everything is ruined when something goes against your wishes. Do not judge by present feelings, and do not let any grief overwhelm you as though all hope were gone.

4. "Do not think yourself completely abandoned, even if I send you some trial for a time, or withdraw some cherished comfort. This is the way to the kingdom of heaven. And it is certainly better for you and all my servants to be tested by difficulties than to have everything go your way. I know your hidden thoughts, and I know it is very necessary for your soul's health that sometimes you are left without spiritual pleasure, so that you do not become proud in prosperity and try to take credit for what you are not. What I have given, I can take away, and restore again whenever I choose.

5. "When I give it, it remains mine. When I take it back, I have not taken what belongs to you, for every good and perfect gift comes from me. If I send you grief or any trouble, do not be angry or let your heart grow heavy. I can quickly lift you up and turn every burden into joy. I am just and greatly to be praised when I deal with you this way.

6. "If you think rightly and look at things with truth, you should never be so sadly cast down by hardship, but rather should rejoice and give thanks. Indeed, you should count it your greatest joy that I afflict you with sorrows and do not spare you. 'As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you'—that is what I said to my beloved disciples. I did not send them to worldly pleasures, but to great struggles. Not to honors, but to contempt. Not to ease, but to hard work. Not to rest, but to bring forth much fruit through patience. Remember these words, my Son."
(1) Nahum i. 7. (2) Matthew vi. 34. (3) John xiv. 27; Psalm xiii. 5. (4) James i. 17. (5) John xv. 9.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXI
paragraphs: On letting go of every creature to find the Creator

O Lord, I still need more grace if I am to reach the place where no person or creature can hold me back. As long as anything keeps me bound, I cannot fly freely to you. The psalmist longed to fly this way when he cried, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! Then I would fly away and be at rest." What is more peaceful than the single eye? And what is freer than the person who desires nothing on earth? A person must rise above every creature, completely abandon himself, and with a mind lifted above all things stand and see that you, the Creator of all, have nothing among your creatures that resembles you. Unless a person is freed from all created things, he will not be able to reach freely after the things of God. This is why so few people give themselves to contemplation—because so few know how to separate themselves completely from what is passing and perishable.

2. For this, much grace is needed—grace that lifts the soul and raises it above itself. Unless a person is lifted up in spirit, freed from all creatures, and wholly united to God, whatever he knows and whatever he has matters very little. Whoever values anything as great besides the one incomprehensible, eternal Good will remain small and earthbound for a long time. Whatever is not God is nothing and should be counted as nothing. There is a vast difference between a devout person illuminated by wisdom and a scholar learned in books. The knowledge that flows down from divine fullness above is far nobler than what is laboriously acquired through human study.

3. Many people desire contemplation, but they do not make the effort to practice what it requires. A major obstacle is that too much importance is placed on outward signs and symbols, and too little on thorough self-denial. I do not know how it is, or by what spirit we are led, or what we who claim to be spiritual are really after—that we give so much effort and eager concern to temporary, worthless things, and hardly ever pause to examine our inner condition.

4. After only a brief moment of reflection, we rush back outdoors and fail to examine our actions carefully. We pay no attention to where our affections are fixed, and we do not weep over how impure everything within us has become. Because all humanity had corrupted itself on the earth, the great flood came. Since our deepest desires are so corrupt, it necessarily follows that our actions are corrupt too—revealing a lack of inner strength. Out of a pure heart comes the fruit of a good life.

5. We ask how much a person has accomplished, but we rarely consider how much virtue went into it. We ask if he is strong, rich, handsome, clever, a good writer, a good singer, a skilled worker. But how poor he may be in spirit, how patient and gentle, how devout and reflective—on these things many are silent. Nature looks at the outward appearance; grace looks at the heart. Nature is often deceived; grace trusts in God, so that it will not be led astray.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXII
paragraphs: On self-denial and letting go of all selfishness

"My Son, you cannot possess perfect freedom unless you completely deny yourself. All those are enslaved who cling to possessions, who love themselves, who are selfish, curious, and restless—those who always chase comfort and not the things of Jesus Christ, those who constantly plan and build things that will not last. For whatever does not come from God will perish. Hold fast this short and complete saying: 'Give up all things, and you will find all things. Let go of your desires, and you will find rest.' Reflect on this deeply, and when you have fully grasped it, you will understand everything."
2. O Lord, this is not the work of a single day, and it is no child's play. In this brief saying, all the perfection of the spiritual life is contained.

3. "My Son, you should not be turned aside or immediately discouraged because you have heard what the path of perfection requires. Instead, let it spur you toward higher goals, or at least make you long for them with all your heart. If only it were so—that you had come to the point where you were no longer a lover of yourself but were always ready to respond to my call, and to the one I have placed over you. Then you would please me greatly, and your whole life would pass in joy and peace. You still have much to give up, and unless you surrender it all to me completely, you will not gain what you are seeking. I advise you to buy from me gold refined in fire—that is, heavenly wisdom, which despises all worthless things. Set aside earthly wisdom and every craving for human approval or your own pleasure.

4. "I tell you: you must trade what people value for what they consider worthless. For true heavenly wisdom—which thinks nothing great of itself and does not seek to be praised on earth—appears to the world as something utterly small and insignificant, almost forgotten. Many honor it with their lips, but their hearts are far from it. It is the precious pearl, hidden from the many."
(1) Revelation iii. 18.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXIII
paragraphs: On the instability of the heart and keeping our aim fixed on God

"My Son, do not trust your feelings, for what you feel now will quickly change into something else. As long as you live, you are subject to change, whether you want it or not. One moment you are joyful, the next sad; now at peace, now anxious; now devout, now dry; now eager, now listless; now serious, now lighthearted. But the wise person—the one who is truly learned in the spirit—stands above all these shifting moods. He pays no attention to what he feels within himself or from which direction the wind blows. Instead, his whole mind is focused on reaching the right and desired end. In this way he remains one and the same, unshaken, with the single eye of his intention fixed steadfastly on me through all the ups and downs of life.

2. "The purer the eye of intention, the more steadily a person will navigate through life's storms. But in many people, that eye grows dim, because it quickly fastens on whatever pleasant thing comes along. It is rare to find someone completely free from the stain of self-interest. In the same way, the Jews of old came to Bethany, to the house of Martha and Mary, not to see Jesus, but to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. Therefore, the eye of intention must be cleansed, so that it is single and clear and—above all distractions—directed toward me."
(1) John xii. 9.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXIV
paragraphs: On how God is sweet above all things and in all things to those who love him

God is mine, and all things are mine! What more could I want? What happier thing could I desire? O delightful and sweet word—to the one who loves the Word, not the world or the things of the world. "My God, my all!" To the one who understands, that word is enough, and to repeat it again and again is a joy. When you are present, everything is delightful. When you are absent, everything is wearisome. You bring the heart to rest, give it deep peace and festive joy. You make it think rightly about everything and praise you in everything. Nothing can please for long without you. For anything to be pleasant and good, your grace must be present—your wisdom must give it its sweetness.

2. To the person who has tasted you, what could be unpleasant? And to the one who has not tasted you, what could bring real joy? The worldly wise and those who live for the flesh fall short of your wisdom, for in worldly wisdom there is only emptiness, and to be ruled by the flesh leads to death. But those who follow you by despising worldly things and disciplining the flesh are found to be truly wise. They are carried from emptiness to truth, from flesh to spirit. They taste that the Lord is good. Whatever good they find in created things, they credit entirely to the praise of the Creator. The enjoyment of the Creator and the enjoyment of the creature are vastly different—as different as the enjoyment of eternity and of time, of uncreated light and reflected light.

3. O everlasting Light, surpassing all created lights, send down your ray from on high to pierce the deepest places of my heart. Give purity, joy, clarity, and life to my spirit, so that with all its powers it may cling to you with a delight beyond all human understanding. When will that blessed, longed-for time come when you will satisfy me with your presence and be to me All in all? Until then, my joy will not be complete. Still—the old self lives in me. He is not yet fully crucified, not yet entirely dead. He still fights fiercely against the spirit, waging inner wars and refusing to let the soul's kingdom be at peace.

4. But you who rule the raging sea and still its waves when they rise up—rise up and help me. Scatter the people who delight in war. Destroy them by your power. Show your might, I beg you, and let your right hand be glorified, for I have no hope, no refuge except in you, O Lord my God.
(1) 1 John ii. 15. (2) Psalm lxviii. 30.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXV
paragraphs: On the certainty of temptation in this life

"My Son, you are never safe in this life. As long as you live, you will always need your spiritual armor. You dwell among enemies and are attacked from every side. If you do not use the shield of patience at all times, you will not remain unwounded for long. Above all, if you do not keep your heart fixed on me with a firm resolve to bear everything for my sake, you will not withstand the fury of the attack or reach the victory of the blessed. So you must fight bravely throughout your whole life and use a strong hand against everything that opposes you. To the one who overcomes, the hidden manna is given, but great misery is stored up for the lazy.

2. "If you seek rest in this life, how will you reach the eternal rest? Do not set your heart on much rest, but on much patience. Seek true peace not on earth but in heaven, not in people or any created thing, but in God alone. For the love of God, you must willingly accept everything—labor, sorrow, temptation, hardship, anxiety, need, sickness, injury, opposition, criticism, humiliation, shame, correction, and contempt. These things build virtue. These things test the disciple of Christ. These things shape the heavenly crown. I will give you an eternal reward for brief labor, and infinite glory for passing shame.

3. "Do you think you will always have spiritual consolation whenever you want it? My saints never had that. Instead, they faced many griefs, countless temptations, and deep desolation. Yet they bore it all patiently and trusted in God more than in themselves, knowing that 'the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that will be revealed in us.' Do you want to have immediately what others could barely attain after many tears and hard struggles? Wait for the Lord. Act like a man and be strong. Do not lose heart or turn away from me, but steadily devote your body and soul to the glory of God. I will reward you abundantly. I will be with you in trouble."
(1) Revelation ii. 17. (2) Romans viii. 17. (3) Psalm xci. 15.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVI
paragraphs: Against the empty judgments of others

"My Son, anchor your soul firmly in God and do not fear human judgment, as long as your conscience tells you that you are faithful and innocent. It is good and blessed to suffer this way. It will not weigh heavily on the heart that is humble and trusts in God more than in itself. Many people have many opinions, so you cannot put much stock in them. Besides, it is impossible to please everyone. Although Paul tried to please everyone in the Lord and became all things to all people, he still counted it a very small thing to be judged by any human court."

2. He worked tirelessly for the growth and salvation of others, yet he could not avoid being sometimes judged and looked down upon. So he committed everything to God, who knows all things, and defended himself against those who spoke evil or foolishly or falsely by patience and humility. Still, from time to time he answered them, so that his silence would not become a stumbling block for the weak.

3. "Who are you to be afraid of someone who will die? Today he exists; tomorrow he is gone. Fear God, and you will not shrink from human threats. What can anyone do to you with words or actions? He hurts himself more than you, and he will not escape God's judgment, whoever he may be. Keep God before your eyes and do not argue with bitter words. If for the moment you seem to give way and suffer embarrassment you did not deserve, do not be angry about it. Do not let impatience shrink your reward. Instead, look up to me in heaven. I am able to deliver you from all shame and hurt, and to repay each person according to his works."
(1) 1 Corinthians ix. 22. (2) 1 Corinthians iv. 3.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVII
paragraphs: On complete self-surrender for the sake of inner freedom

"My Son, let go of yourself and you will find me. Stand still, without choosing and without self-concern, and you will always gain. For more grace will be added to you as soon as you surrender yourself—and as long as you do not take yourself back again."
2. Lord, how often should I surrender myself, and in what areas should I let go?

3. "Always. Every hour. In small things and in great. I make no exceptions. I want you to be stripped bare in all things. How else can you be mine and I yours, unless you are free—inwardly and outwardly—from every self-willed desire? The sooner you do this, the better it will go for you. The more fully and sincerely you do it, the more you will please me and the more abundantly you will be rewarded.

4. "Some people surrender themselves, but with certain reservations. They do not fully trust in God and so they think they need to provide for themselves. Others offer everything at first, but when temptation presses them, they go back to their old ways and make no progress in virtue. These will not reach the true freedom of a pure heart or the grace of my sweet fellowship unless they first surrender completely and offer themselves daily as a sacrifice. Without this, fruitful union with me cannot exist and will not last.

5. "I have told you many times, and I tell you again: Give yourself up. Surrender yourself, and you will have great inner peace. Give everything for everything. Demand nothing. Ask for nothing in return. Stand simply and without hesitation in me, and you will possess me. You will have freedom of heart, and the darkness will not overwhelm you. Strive for this, pray for it, long for it—that you may be freed from all attachment to yourself. Follow Jesus naked, who was made naked for you. Die to yourself, and live eternally for me. Then all vain fantasies will vanish, all evil disturbances, and all unnecessary fears. Then excessive dread will leave you, and disordered love will die."

chapters.title: Chapter XXXVIII
paragraphs: On managing outward affairs well and turning to God in danger

"My Son, you must work hard at this: in every place and every outward activity, remain free within and in control of yourself. Let all things be under you, not you under them. Be the master and ruler of your actions, not a slave or hired hand. Be a free person—entering into the inheritance and liberty of the children of God, who stand above the present moment and look toward the eternal. With one eye they see temporal things, and with the other, heavenly things. Passing pleasures do not draw them to cling; rather, they bend temporal things to serve the good, as God ordained them to do—for the Master Craftsman left nothing in creation without purpose.

2. "And if in any situation you do not stop at outward appearances or judge things by what your physical senses tell you, but instead—like Moses—immediately enter the tabernacle to seek God's counsel, you will hear a divine answer and come out instructed about many things, present and future. Moses always turned to the tabernacle for the resolution of all doubts and questions, and he fled to prayer to be rescued from danger and the evil schemes of men. You too should flee to the secret chamber of your heart and earnestly beg for God's help. For we read that Joshua and the Israelites were deceived by the Gibeonites precisely because they 'did not consult the Lord'—they were too quick to listen to smooth words and were taken in by a show of false devotion."
(1) Joshua ix. 14.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXIX
paragraphs: On not being consumed by busyness
"My Son, always entrust your concerns to me. I will arrange everything rightly at the proper time. Wait for my ordering of things, and you will find it works to your benefit."
2. Lord, I freely commit everything to you, for my own planning accomplishes very little. If only I did not dwell so much on future events, but could offer myself to your will without hesitation!

3. "My Son, a person often strives passionately after something he desires, but once he gets it, he begins to feel differently about it—because his interest does not last but rushes from one thing to the next. So it is no small thing to resist self-will even in small matters."

4. True human progress lies in self-denial, and the person who denies himself is free and safe. But the old enemy, who opposes everything good, never stops tempting. Day and night he sets his wicked snares, hoping to trap the unwary. "Watch and pray," says the Lord, "so that you do not fall into temptation."
(1) Matthew xxvi. 41.

chapters.title: Chapter XL
paragraphs: On how we have no good in ourselves and nothing to boast about

Lord, what is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you care for him? What has man done to deserve your favor? Lord, what right do I have to complain if you abandon me? What claim can I make if you refuse to hear my prayer? Truly, this is what I must think and say: Lord, I am nothing. I have nothing good of my own. In everything, I fall short and tend toward nothing. Unless I am helped and inwardly supported by you, I become completely lukewarm and careless.

2. But you, O Lord, are always the same and endure forever—always good, righteous, and holy, doing everything well and rightly and wisely. But I, who am more ready to slide backward than to move forward, never stay in one place—changes sweep over me constantly. Yet things quickly improve when you choose to stretch out your hand and help me, for you alone can aid without any human assistance. You strengthen me so that my face is no longer troubled, and my heart turns to you and rests in you alone.

3. If only I knew how to cast off every human consolation—whether to cultivate devotion, or because I had no choice but to seek you, since no person could comfort me—then I could rightly trust in your grace and rejoice in the gift of fresh consolation.

4. I thank you, from whom all good things come, whenever things go well with me. But in your sight I am vanity and nothing—an inconstant and weak person. What do I have to boast about? Why do I want to be honored? Is it not for nothing at all? This too is completely empty. Truly, empty glory is a terrible plague—the worst of all vanities—because it draws us away from true glory and robs us of heavenly grace. While a person is busy pleasing himself, he displeases you. While he craves human praise, he is stripped of true virtue.

5. But true glory and holy joy lie in glorying in you, not in ourselves—in rejoicing in your name, not in our own strength—in taking no delight in any creature except for your sake. Let your name be praised, not mine. Let your work be celebrated, not mine. Let your holy name be blessed, but let me receive none of the praise that belongs to you. You are my glory. You are the joy of my heart. In you I will boast and be glad all day long. As for myself, I will boast only in my weaknesses.

6. Let the self-important seek glory from one another, but I will seek the glory that comes from God alone. Truly, all human glory, all worldly honor, all earthly triumph—compared to your eternal glory—is vanity and foolishness. O God, my Truth and my Mercy, blessed Trinity—to you alone be all praise, honor, power, and glory forever and ever. Amen.
(1) Psalm viii. 4. (2) 2 Corinthians xii. 5. (3) John v. 44.

chapters.title: Chapter XLI
paragraphs: On letting go of worldly honor

"My Son, do not be troubled if you see others honored and promoted while you are looked down upon and humbled. Lift your heart to me in heaven, and the contempt of people on earth will not make you sad."

2. Lord, we are blind and quickly led astray by vanity. When I look honestly at myself, no creature has ever truly wronged me, and so I have nothing to complain about before you. But because I have sinned against you many times and seriously, every creature has the right to take up arms against me. Shame and contempt are what I justly deserve; praise, honor, and glory belong to you. Unless I prepare myself for this—to be willing for every creature to despise and abandon me, and to be considered absolutely nothing—I cannot be filled with inner peace and strength, nor be spiritually enlightened, nor fully united to you.

chapters.title: Chapter XLII
paragraphs: On not placing our peace in other people

"My Son, if you stake your peace on any person because you think highly of him or enjoy his company, you will be unstable and trapped. But if you turn to the ever-living and abiding Truth, the loss or death of a friend will not make you desolate. Your love for any friend should be rooted in me, and for my sake everyone should be loved who seems good to you and is dear to you in this life. Without me, friendship has no strength or staying power, and no love is true or pure that I have not joined together. You should be so detached from the affections of loved ones that, as far as it depends on you, you would willingly live without any human company at all. The closer a person draws to God, the further he moves from all earthly comfort. And the deeper he descends into himself—the smaller he appears in his own eyes—the higher he ascends toward God.

2. "But whoever takes credit for any good in himself blocks the grace of God from entering, because the grace of the Holy Spirit always seeks the humble heart. If you could make yourself utterly nothing, emptied of all self-love, then it would be my part to flood you with grace. When you fix your eyes on created things, the face of the Creator is hidden from you. Learn in all things to conquer yourself for the sake of your Creator, and then you will be able to reach divine knowledge. However small a thing may be, if it is loved and valued too much, it holds you back from the highest Good and corrupts you."

chapters.title: Chapter XLIII
paragraphs: Against empty and worldly knowledge

"My Son, do not be swayed by the polished and clever sayings of others. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of words but of power. Listen to my words—they kindle the heart and enlighten the mind; they bring sorrow for sin and offer rich consolation. Never read simply to appear more learned or wise. Instead, study how to overcome your sins, for this will benefit you far more than mastering difficult questions.

2. "When you have read and learned many things, you must always return to one foundational truth: I am the one who teaches knowledge to humanity, and I give clearer understanding to the humble than any human teacher can provide. The one to whom I speak will quickly become wise and will grow greatly in spirit. Woe to those who pursue endless curiosities from other people and care little about serving me. The time will come when Christ, the Master of masters and Lord of the angels, will appear to hear every person's account—to examine each conscience. Then he will search Jerusalem with a lamp, and the hidden things of darkness will be brought to light, and all arguments will fall silent.

3. "I am the one who instantly lifts up the humble mind to understand more of eternal truth than if someone had spent ten years studying in the universities. I teach without the noise of words, without the clash of opinions, without striving for status, without intellectual combat. I teach people to despise earthly things, to grow weary of the present, to seek heavenly things, to savor eternal things, to run from honors, to bear offenses, to place all hope in me, to want nothing outside of me, and above everything to love me with a burning heart.

4. "There was once a man who loved me from the bottom of his heart and who learned divine things and spoke with wonderful insight. He gained more by forsaking everything than by studying fine points. But to some I speak ordinary things, to others special things. To some I appear gently through signs and images; to others I reveal deep mysteries in brilliant light. The voice of books is one, but it does not teach everyone alike—because I am the inward Teacher of truth, the Searcher of hearts, the One who discerns thoughts and moves people to act, giving to each person as I see fit."
(1) 1 Corinthians iv. 20. (2) Psalm xciv. 10. (3) Zephaniah i. 12. (4) 1 Corinthians iv. 5.

chapters.title: Chapter XLIV
paragraphs: On not troubling ourselves about outward things

"My Son, in many things you must remain deliberately uninformed, and consider yourself as one dead to the world—as one to whom the whole world is crucified. Many things you must also pass by with a deaf ear, focusing instead on what leads to your peace. It is more profitable to turn away from what displeases you and leave each person to his own opinion than to get caught up in arguments. If you stand well with God and keep his judgment in mind, you will easily bear being seen as the loser."

2. O Lord, what have we come to? We mourn over a small financial loss and run after a trivial gain, but spiritual loss is forgotten and rarely recovered. What matters little or nothing gets our full attention, while what is truly necessary is carelessly overlooked—because the whole person slides toward outward things, and unless he quickly recovers himself, he willingly stays stuck there.

chapters.title: Chapter XLV
paragraphs: On not believing everyone, and on how easily we fail in our words

Lord, be my help in trouble, for human help is worthless. How often I have failed to find faithfulness where I was sure I had it! How many times I have found it where I least expected! Trust in people is empty, but the salvation of the righteous comes from you, O God. Blessed be you, O Lord my God, in everything that happens to us. We are weak and unstable, easily deceived and quickly changed.

2. Who can guard himself so carefully that he never falls into some difficulty? But the one who trusts in you, O Lord, and seeks you with an honest heart does not slip so easily. And if he does fall into trouble, however entangled he may be, he will quickly be rescued or comforted by you—because you never abandon the one who trusts in you to the end. A friend who remains faithful through all his friend's hardships is rare indeed. You, O Lord, you alone are perfectly faithful in all things, and there is no one else like you.

3. How truly wise was that holy soul who said: "My mind is firmly fixed, and it is grounded in Christ." If it were so with me, the fear of others would not trouble me so easily, and stinging words would not move me. Who can foresee everything? Who can guard against every future trouble? If even things we anticipate still hurt us, how much more damage can unexpected ones do? But why have I not prepared myself better? Why have I trusted others so readily? We are only human—nothing more than fragile, fallible creatures, even if many consider us angels. Whom shall I trust, O Lord? Whom, if not you? You are the truth—you do not deceive and cannot be deceived. On the other hand, "every person is a liar"—weak, unstable, and unreliable, especially in his words. So we should hardly ever take at face value what sounds right on the surface.

4. With what wisdom you warned us to beware of people, and that a person's enemies may be those of his own household, and that we should not believe anyone who says "Look, here!" or "Look, there!" I have been taught by painful experience—may it make me more careful and not more foolish. "Be cautious," someone says, "keep to yourself what I tell you." And while I stay silent, believing it is safe with me, he himself cannot keep quiet and immediately betrays both me and himself, and goes his way. Protect me, O Lord, from such careless and reckless people. Do not let me fall into their hands, and do not let me behave that way myself. Put a true and steady word on my lips, and keep a deceitful tongue far from me. What I would not want to suffer, I must be careful never to do.

5. How good and how peaceful it is to stay silent about other people—not to believe every report carelessly or pass it along further! How good to open yourself up to few, to always seek God as the witness of your heart, to refuse to be carried by every wind of words, and to desire that all things inward and outward be done according to God's will! How safe it is, for the preservation of heavenly grace, to avoid human applause and not to chase after the things that win admiration abroad, but instead to pursue earnestly whatever leads to real change of life and spiritual fervor! How many people have been harmed by having their virtue made public and praised too quickly! How truly valuable is grace kept quietly in silence—in this fragile life that, as we are told, is nothing but temptation and struggle.
(1) Psalm lx. 11. (2) St. Agatha. (3) Psalm cxvi. 11; Romans iii. 4. (4) Matthew x. 17, 36. (5) Matthew xxiv. 23.

chapters.title: Chapter XLVI
paragraphs: On trusting God when harsh words are spoken against us

"My Son, stand firm and trust in me. For what are words but words? They fly through the air but they bruise no stone. If you are guilty, consider how gladly you should change. If you know nothing against yourself, consider that you can gladly bear this for God's sake. It is a small enough thing to endure hard words sometimes, since you are not yet strong enough to endure hard blows. Why do such trivial things cut so deep? Because you are still ruled by the flesh and care too much about what others think. You are unwilling to be corrected for your faults because you fear being looked down on, and you hide behind flimsy excuses.

2. "But look more honestly at yourself, and you will see that the world is still alive in you, along with a foolish desire to please people. When you run from being humbled and embarrassed for your faults, it is clear that you are neither truly humble nor truly dead to the world, and that the world is not crucified to you. But listen to my word, and you will not care about ten thousand words from others. Even if everything that the worst malice could invent were said against you, what would it really do to you if you simply let it go and counted it as nothing? Could it pull out a single hair from your head?

3. "But the person who has no inner strength and does not keep God before his eyes is easily shaken by a word of criticism. The one who trusts in me and does not cling to his own judgment will be free from the fear of others. For I am the Judge and the One who sees all secrets. I know how things happened. I know both the one who inflicted the injury and the one who suffered it. That word came from me; by my permission this happened—so that the thoughts of many hearts might be revealed. I will judge both the guilty and the innocent, but I have chosen to test them both first through a hidden trial.

4. "Human testimony often deceives. My judgment is true—it will stand and will not be overturned. It usually remains hidden, and only to a few in certain cases is it made known. Yet it never errs, and cannot err, even though it may not seem right to foolish eyes. Therefore, people must turn to me in every judgment and not lean on their own opinion. For no evil will happen to the righteous, whatever God may send. Even if some unjust accusation is brought, he will not care much. And neither will he celebrate excessively if others clearly vindicate him. For he knows that I am the one who searches hearts and minds, who judges not by outward appearance. For often what I find blameworthy is what human judgment considers praiseworthy."

5. O Lord God, just, strong, and patient Judge, you who know the frailty and sinfulness of humanity—be my strength and my whole confidence, for my own conscience is not enough. You know what I do not know, and so under every rebuke I should humble myself and bear it gently. Mercifully forgive me for all the times I have not done this, and grant me the grace of greater endurance next time. For your abundant mercy in granting forgiveness is better for me than any righteousness I might claim in my own defense against the conscience that lies in wait against me. Though I know nothing against myself, I am not thereby justified—for without your mercy, no living person could be found righteous in your sight.
(1) Luke ii. 35. (2) Proverbs xii. 21. (3) Psalm vii. 9. (4) 1 Corinthians iv. 4. (5) Psalm cxliii. 2.

chapters.title: Chapter XLVII
paragraphs: On enduring every hardship for the sake of eternal life

"My Son, do not let the work you have undertaken for me break you down, and do not let troubles cast you into despair. Let my promise strengthen and comfort you in every situation. I am more than able to reward you beyond all limits. You will not labor here for long, and you will not always be weighed down with sorrows. Wait a little while, and you will see a swift end to your troubles. An hour is coming when all work and turmoil will cease. Everything that passes with time is brief and small.

2. "Do your work faithfully. Labor in my vineyard with dedication; I will be your reward. Write, read, sing, weep, be silent, pray, endure hardship bravely—eternal life is worth all these struggles, and greater ones too. Peace will come on a day known to the Lord—a day that is neither day nor night, but eternal light, infinite brightness, unshakeable peace, and undisturbed rest. Then you will no longer cry, 'Who will deliver me from this body of death?' or 'How long must I endure this exile?' For death will be completely destroyed, and there will be salvation that can never fail—no more anxiety, only happy delight and noble, sweet companionship.

3. "If you could see the unfading crowns of the saints in heaven, and the great glory they now enjoy—they who once were considered worthless and unfit for life by this world—you would immediately humble yourself to the ground. You would rather be subject to everyone than have authority over even one. You would not long for comfortable days in this life, but would actually rejoice in suffering for God's sake and count it as gain to be regarded as nothing among others.

4. "If these truths were sweet to you and moved you to the depths of your heart, how could you dare even once to complain? Are not all hardships worth enduring for the sake of eternal life? It is no small thing to gain or lose the kingdom of God. Lift up your face to heaven. Look—I and all my saints are with me. They had a hard struggle in this world, but now they rejoice, now they are comforted, now they are safe, now they are at peace, and they will remain with me forever in my Father's kingdom."
(1) Zechariah xiv. 7. (2) Romans vii. 24. (3) Psalm cxx.

chapters.title: Chapter XLVIII
paragraphs: On the day of eternity and the hardships of this life

O most blessed dwelling of the city above! O brightest day of eternity, which no night can darken, but which the Supreme Truth always illumines! A day of unceasing joy, of perfect security, that never changes into its opposite. If only this day would dawn, and all these temporal things would come to an end! It shines indeed upon the saints, glowing with unending brightness—but upon us who are still pilgrims on earth, it shines only from afar, as through a glass.

2. The citizens of heaven know how glorious that day is. The exiled children of Eve groan, because this present life is bitter and wearisome. The days of this life are few and evil, full of sorrows and difficulties. Here a person is stained by many sins, trapped by many passions, chained by many fears, exhausted by many cares, distracted by many curiosities, entangled in many vanities, surrounded by many errors, worn out by many labors, burdened by temptations, weakened by pleasures, and tormented by poverty.

3. When will there be an end to these evils? When will I be delivered from the miserable slavery of my sins? When will I remember only you, O Lord? When will I rejoice fully in you? When will I have true freedom, with nothing burdening my mind or body? When will there be solid peace—peace unshakeable and secure, peace within and without, peace firm on every side? Blessed Jesus, when will I stand before you and gaze on you? When will I behold the glory of your kingdom? When will you be to me all in all? When will I be with you in the kingdom you prepared from the foundation of the world for those who love you? I am left here—a poor exile in a hostile land, where there are daily wars and terrible misfortunes.

4. Comfort me in my exile. Ease my sorrow, for all my longing reaches toward you. Everything this world offers for consolation is a burden to me. I yearn to be close to you, but I cannot reach you. I long to cling to heavenly things, but earthly concerns and unconquered passions drag me down. In my mind I want to be above all things, but in my body I am forced to be beneath them. And so, wretched as I am, I fight against myself and become a burden to myself—the spirit striving to rise while the flesh pulls downward.

5. How I suffer inwardly! While I try to think about heavenly things, a crowd of earthly thoughts rushes in during prayer. My God, do not be far from me. Do not turn away from your servant in anger. Flash your lightning and scatter them. Send out your arrows, and let every illusion of the enemy be destroyed. Gather my scattered senses back to you. Make me forget all worldly things. Help me to quickly cast aside and despise sinful imaginings. Come to my aid, eternal Truth, so that no emptiness can move me. Come to me, heavenly Sweetness, and let all impurity flee before your face. Forgive me also, and deal gently with me in your mercy, whenever in prayer I think about anything besides you. For I confess that I am constantly distracted. Often where my body stands or sits, there I myself am not—rather, I am wherever my thoughts carry me. Where my thought is, there I am. And my thoughts are usually where the thing I love is. Whatever naturally delights me or pleases me through habit—that is what comes most readily to mind.

6. That is why you, who are the Truth, have plainly said: "Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." If I love heaven, I gladly think about heavenly things. If I love the world, I rejoice in its pleasures and grieve at its troubles. If I love the flesh, I constantly imagine fleshly things. If I love the spirit, I delight in meditating on spiritual things. Whatever I love, those are the topics I readily discuss, listen to, and carry home with me in my mind. Blessed is the person who, for your sake, O Lord, is willing to part from every creature—who does violence to his bodily nature and crucifies the desires of the flesh by the fervor of the spirit. Then, with a clear conscience, he can offer you a pure prayer and become worthy to join the angelic choirs, having shut out from himself—both outwardly and inwardly—all worldly things.
(1) Psalm lxxi. 12. (2) Matthew vi. 21.

chapters.title: Chapter XLIX
paragraphs: On the desire for eternal life and the great blessings promised to those who persevere

"My Son, when you feel the desire for eternal happiness being poured into you from above, and you long to leave the tent of this body so that you may behold my glory without any shadow of change—open your heart wide and receive this holy inspiration with all your desire. Give heartfelt thanks to the Supreme Goodness, who deals with you so graciously, visits you so lovingly, stirs you so fervently, and lifts you so powerfully—lest you sink back under your own weight to earthly things. You do not receive this gift by your own meditation or effort, but solely by the gracious favor of Supreme Grace and the divine gaze—so that you may grow in virtue and humility, prepare yourself for future struggles, cling to me with all the love of your heart, and strive to serve me with fervent will.

2. "My Son, the fire often burns, but the flame does not rise without smoke. In the same way, the desires of some people burn toward heavenly things, yet they are not free from the pull of bodily desire. So their prayer, however earnest it seems, is not offered with a purely simple desire for God's glory. Your own desires are often like this too, even when you imagine them to be perfectly sincere. For whatever is tainted with self-interest is not pure and perfect.

3. "Do not seek what is pleasant and advantageous for yourself, but what is acceptable and honorable to me. If you judge rightly, you must follow my will rather than your own desire—indeed, rather than anything that can be desired. I know your longing, and I have heard your many groans. Already you yearn for the glorious freedom of the children of God. Already your heart is drawn to the eternal home and the heavenly country full of joy. But the hour has not yet come. There is still another season—a time of warfare, a time of labor and testing. You long to be filled with the highest Good, but you cannot have it yet. I AM that Good. Wait for me, until the kingdom of God comes.

4. "You must still be tested on earth and exercised in many things. Comfort will be given to you from time to time, but complete satisfaction will not be granted. Take courage, then, and be brave both in doing and in enduring things that go against your nature. You must put on the new self and be changed into a different person. You must often do what you would rather not, and leave undone what you would like to do. What others want will succeed; what you want will not. Others will be heard when they speak; what you say will receive no attention. Others will ask and receive; you will ask and not obtain. Others will be praised and promoted; about you, nothing will be said. Others will be given this or that responsibility; you will be judged useless.

5. "This will naturally make you sad, and it is a great thing if you bear it in silence. In these and many similar ways, the faithful servant of the Lord is tested—to see how far he can deny himself and bring himself into submission. There is hardly anything you need to master more than accepting things that go against your will—especially when you are told to do something that seems pointless or unhelpful. And because you dare not resist a higher authority, it feels hard to shape your course according to another's direction and let go of your own opinion.

6. "But consider, my Son, the fruit of these labors, the swift end, and the immense reward—and you will find not pain in bearing them but rather the strongest comfort for your patience. In exchange for this small desire that you have willingly given up, you will always have your will in heaven. There you will find everything you ever wanted, everything you could ever long for. There all good things will be within your reach, without any fear of losing them. There your will, always one with mine, will desire nothing outside of me. There no one will resist you, no one will complain about you, no one will hinder you. Everything you desire will be present at once, refreshing and satisfying your heart to the brim. There I will give you glory for the scorn you suffered here, a garment of praise for sorrow, and for the lowest place, a throne in the kingdom forever. There the fruit of obedience will be seen, the labor of repentance will bring joy, and humble submission will be crowned in glory.

7. "So bow humbly now under the hands of everyone, and do not worry about who said this or who ordered that. Instead, make it your special care that whether your superior, your equal, or someone below you asks anything of you—or even hints at a wish—take it all in good spirit and try wholeheartedly to fulfill it. Let one person seek this and another that. Let this one boast in this and that one in that, and be praised a thousand times over. But you—rejoice only in being overlooked, and in my good pleasure and glory alone. This is what you are to long for: that whether through life or through death, God may always be honored in you."
(1) Philippians i. 20.

chapters.title: Chapter L
paragraphs: On how a desolate person should place himself in God's hands

O Lord, Holy Father, may you be blessed now and forever, because as you will, so it is done—and what you do is good. Let your servant rejoice in you, not in himself or in anyone else, for you alone are true joy. You are my hope and my crown, my gladness and my honor, O Lord. What does your servant have that he did not receive from you—without any merit of his own? Everything is yours: what you have given and what you have made. I am poor and in misery from my youth, and my soul is sometimes sorrowful to the point of tears. Sometimes it is disturbed within, because of the sufferings that press in upon it.

2. I long for the joy of peace. I beg for the peace of your children, for those who are fed by you in the light of your comfort. If you give peace, if you pour holy joy into me, the soul of your servant will be full of song and devoted in your praise. But if you withdraw—as you so often do—he will not be able to run in the way of your commandments. Instead, he will beat his chest and bow his knees, because things are not as they were yesterday and the day before, when your lamp shone upon his head, and he walked safely under the shadow of your wings, sheltered from temptation.

3. O righteous Father, worthy of all praise, the hour has come for your servant to be tested. Beloved Father, it is fitting that in this hour your servant suffer something for your sake. O Father, eternally to be adored—the hour has arrived that you foreknew from all eternity, when for a little while your servant should outwardly be brought low, yet always live inwardly with you. For a little while, let him be overlooked, humbled, and failing in the eyes of others. Let him be worn down by suffering and weakness, so that he may rise again with you in the dawn of new light and be glorified in heaven. Holy Father, you have ordained this and willed it so, and what has happened is what you yourself commanded.

4. For this is your way of showing love to your friends—that they should suffer and be troubled in this world for your sake, however often and by whoever you allow it. Nothing happens on earth without your counsel and permission, and without good reason. It is good for me, Lord, that I have been in trouble, so that I may learn your ways and cast away all pride and self-importance from my heart. It is profitable for me that shame has covered my face, so that I seek you for comfort rather than turning to people. I have also learned from this to stand in awe of your unsearchable judgment, which afflicts both the righteous and the wicked—but never without fairness and justice.

5. Thank you for not sparing my sins, but striking me with loving blows, sending troubles upon me both outward and inward. There is nothing under heaven that can comfort me except you alone, O Lord my God, the heavenly Physician of souls, who wounds and heals, who brings down to the grave and raises up again. Your discipline is upon me, and your very rod will teach me.

6. Here I am, beloved Father—in your hands. I bow beneath the rod of your correction. Strike my back and my neck, that I may bend my crookedness to your will. Make me a humble and lowly disciple, as you have always been kind to do, so that I may walk according to your every direction. I entrust myself and everything I have to your correction. It is better to be punished here than in the life to come. You know all things, and nothing in the human conscience is hidden from you. Before things happen, you know they will happen. You do not need anyone to teach you or tell you what is taking place on earth. You know what is best for my growth, and how greatly trouble serves to scrub away the rust of sin. Do with me as your good pleasure directs, and do not reject my sinful life—known to no one so fully as to you alone.

7. Grant me, Lord, to know what ought to be known, to love what ought to be loved, to praise what pleases you most, to value what is precious in your eyes, and to reject what is worthless before you. Do not let me judge by outward appearances or pronounce judgment based on the opinions of the ignorant. Instead, help me to discern with true judgment between visible and spiritual things, and above all, to be always seeking after the will of your good pleasure.

8. Human senses are often deceived in their judgments, and the lovers of this world are deceived because they love only visible things. Is a person any better because others consider him great? The deceiver deceives the deceiver, the vain person flatters the vain, the blind leads the blind, the weak props up the weak—and in praising one another, they actually bring shame upon each other. For as humble St. Francis said, "What each one is in your eyes, O God—that much he is, and no more."
(1) Psalm lxxxviii. 15. (2) Job xxix. 3. (3) Psalm xvii. 8. (4) Psalm cxix. 71. (5) Job xiii. 2.

chapters.title: Chapter LI
paragraphs: On turning to humble tasks when we cannot manage lofty ones

"My Son, you are not always able to sustain a burning desire for virtue or to remain at the heights of contemplation. Because of our fallen nature, you must sometimes come down to lower things and carry the burden of this mortal life, however unwillingly and wearily. As long as you wear a mortal body, you will feel weariness and heaviness of heart. You should groan often under the weight of the flesh, because you cannot devote yourself to spiritual studies and divine contemplation without interruption.

2. "At such times, it is good to turn to humble, practical tasks and to refresh yourself with good deeds. Wait with sure confidence for my coming and my heavenly visit. Bear your exile and dryness of spirit with patience until I visit you again and set you free from all anxiety. I will make you forget your labors and enjoy deep peace. I will spread before you the green pastures of Scripture, so that with an enlarged heart you may begin to run in the way of my commandments. And you will say: 'The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that will be revealed in us.'"
(1) Romans viii. 18.

chapters.title: Chapter LII
paragraphs: On recognizing that we deserve punishment, not comfort

O Lord, I am not worthy of your comfort or any spiritual visit, and so you deal justly with me when you leave me poor and desolate. Even if I could pour out tears like the sea, I would still not be worthy of your consolation. I deserve nothing except to be disciplined and punished, because I have offended you grievously and many times, and have sinned greatly in many ways. Taking an honest account, I do not deserve even the smallest of your comforts. But you, gracious and merciful God—who do not want your creation to be destroyed—choose to show the riches of your mercy to the vessels of mercy, and comfort your servant far beyond anything he deserves, beyond all human measure. For your consolations are nothing like the empty talk of human beings.

2. What have I done, O Lord, to deserve any heavenly comfort? I cannot remember doing anything good. I have always been inclined to sin and slow to change. This is the truth, and I cannot deny it. If I said otherwise, you would stand against me, and no one could defend me. What have I earned by my sins except hell and eternal fire? I confess in all honesty that I deserve every form of scorn and contempt, and it is not fitting that I be counted among your faithful servants. Though I would rather not hear this, I will—for the sake of truth—accuse myself of my sins, so that I may more readily receive your mercy.

3. What can I say, guilty and full of shame as I am? I have nothing to say except this one word: "I have sinned, Lord; I have sinned. Have mercy on me. Forgive me." Let me grieve for a little while before I go where I will not return—to the land of darkness and the shadow of death. What do you require most from a guilty and miserable sinner? That he be truly sorry and humble himself for his sins. In genuine sorrow and humility of heart, the hope of forgiveness is born, a troubled conscience is reconciled, lost grace is restored, a person is saved from future wrath, and God and the repentant soul rush to meet each other with a holy kiss.

4. The humble sorrow of sinners is an acceptable sacrifice to you, O Lord, giving off a fragrance far sweeter in your sight than incense. This is also that precious ointment you desired to have poured on your sacred feet. For a broken and contrite heart you have never despised. There is the place of refuge from the face of the enemy's wrath. There, whatever evil has been accumulated elsewhere is washed clean and made right.
(1) Romans ix. 23. (2) Job x. 20, 21. (3) Luke xv. 20. (4) Psalm li. 17.

chapters.title: Chapter LIII
paragraphs: On how God's grace does not mix with worldly attachment

"My Son, my grace is precious. It does not allow itself to be mixed with outward things or earthly comforts. You must therefore cast away everything that blocks grace, if you long to receive its inpouring. Find a quiet place for yourself. Love being alone with yourself. Seek no one's conversation, but rather pour out devout prayer to God, that you may keep a contrite mind and a pure conscience. Count the whole world as nothing. Seek to be alone with God before all outward things. For you cannot be alone with me and at the same time be delighted with passing pleasures. You should distance yourself from acquaintances and dear friends, and keep your mind free from all worldly comfort. As the blessed apostle Peter urged, Christ's faithful ones should live in this world as strangers and pilgrims.

2. "What great confidence the dying person will have if no attachment to anything in the world holds him back! But to have a heart so detached from everything—a spiritually sick soul does not yet understand this, and the person ruled by the flesh does not know the freedom of the spiritual person. Yet if he truly desires to be spiritual, he must let go of both those who are far away and those who are near, and must be on guard against no one more than himself. If you fully conquer yourself, everything else will be easy to overcome. Perfect victory is the triumph over yourself. Whoever keeps himself in check—so that bodily desires obey reason, and reason in all things obeys me—is truly the conqueror of himself and the master of the world.

3. "If you desire to climb to this height, you must begin bravely and lay the axe to the root—to pull up and destroy the hidden, disordered love of yourself and of all selfish, earthly goods. From this single fault—that a person loves himself too much—flows almost everything that needs to be completely overcome. When that evil is conquered and brought under control, great peace and lasting calm will follow. But because few people strive earnestly to die completely to themselves and do not wholeheartedly go beyond themselves, they remain trapped within themselves and cannot be raised in spirit above themselves. Whoever desires to walk freely with me must put to death all his evil and disordered desires, and must cling to no creature with selfish love."
(1) 1 Peter ii. 11.

chapters.title: Chapter LIV
paragraphs: On the different movements of nature and grace

"My Son, pay careful attention to the movements of nature and of grace, because they operate in very different and subtle ways, and can hardly be distinguished except by someone who is spiritual and inwardly enlightened. Everyone claims to seek good, and everyone makes a show of goodness in what they say and do. And so, under the appearance of good, many are deceived.

2. "Nature is deceitful. It lures, traps, and deceives many people, and its goal is always self-interest. But grace walks in simplicity, turns away from every appearance of evil, makes no false pretenses, and does everything purely for the sake of God, in whom it ultimately rests.

3. "Nature is very unwilling to die, to be pressed down, to be overcome, to submit, or to bear the yoke readily. But grace practices self-denial, resists physical indulgence, seeks to be brought under control, longs to be conquered, and does not want to use its own freedom. It loves to be held by discipline, does not desire authority over anyone, and always wants to live and remain under God. For God's sake, it is ready to submit humbly to every human authority.
4. "Nature works for its own advantage and considers what profit it can gain from others. But grace considers not what is useful and convenient for itself, but what may benefit the many.
5. "Nature gladly receives honor and attention. But grace faithfully gives all honor and glory to God.
6. "Nature fears shame and contempt. But grace rejoices in suffering disgrace for the name of Jesus.
7. "Nature loves ease and physical rest. Grace cannot be idle but gladly embraces work.

8. "Nature seeks to own rare and attractive things, and dislikes what is rough and cheap. Grace is delighted with simple and humble things, does not reject what is rough, and is not unwilling to wear old clothing.

9. "Nature looks at temporal things, rejoices in earthly gains, is saddened by loss, and is irritated by any small slight. But grace reaches after eternal things, does not cling to what is temporary, is not disturbed by losses, and is not embittered by harsh words—because it has placed its treasure and joy in heaven, where nothing perishes.

10. "Nature is greedy and would rather receive than give. It loves things that are personal and private. But grace is kind and generous, avoids selfishness, is content with little, and believes it is more blessed to give than to receive.

11. "Nature draws you toward created things, toward your own body, toward vanities and distractions. But grace draws you to God and to virtues. It renounces created things, flees the world, hates bodily desires, restrains wandering, and is ashamed to be seen in public.
12. "Nature is glad to have some outward pleasure in which the senses can delight. But grace seeks to be comforted in God alone, and to find its delight in the highest Good above all visible things.

13. "Nature does everything for its own gain and profit, can do nothing as a free gift, and hopes to get something equally good or better in return, or some praise or favor for its efforts. It loves to have its deeds and gifts highly valued. But grace seeks nothing temporal and asks for no reward other than God alone. It does not desire more of temporal necessities than what may serve to gain eternal life.

14. "Nature rejoices in many friends and relatives. It boasts of noble position and birth. It smiles at the powerful, flatters the rich, and applauds those who are like itself. But grace loves even its enemies and is not proud of having many friends. It places no value on high position or noble birth unless greater virtue comes with it. It favors the poor over the rich, sympathizes more with the innocent than the powerful, and rejoices with the truthful, not with the liar. It always encourages the good to strive for better gifts of grace and to become like the Son of God through holiness.
15. "Nature quickly complains about poverty and trouble. Grace bears hardship with steadfastness.

16. "Nature sees everything in terms of self. It argues and fights for its own cause. But grace brings everything back to God, from whom all things came in the beginning. It claims no good for itself and does not arrogantly presume. It is not quarrelsome and does not prefer its own opinion above others, but in every sense and understanding submits itself to the Eternal Wisdom and the Divine Judgment.

17. "Nature is eager to know secrets and hear the latest news. It loves to appear in public and to experience many things through the senses. It desires to be recognized and to do things that win praise and admiration. But grace does not care about gathering novelties or curiosities, because all this springs from the old corruption—since there is nothing new or lasting on earth. So grace teaches us to restrain the senses, to avoid vanity and showing off, to hide humbly whatever deserves praise and real admiration, and in everything and in all knowledge to seek what is genuinely useful and what brings praise and honor to God. It does not desire praise for itself, but longs that God be blessed in all his gifts, which he bestows out of pure love."

18. This grace is a supernatural light, a special gift of God, the distinguishing mark of the chosen, and the pledge of eternal salvation. It lifts a person from earthly things to love heavenly things, and it transforms the worldly person into a spiritual one. Therefore, the more thoroughly nature is pressed down and overcome, the more abundantly grace is given, and the inner person is daily renewed through fresh visits, formed ever more closely after the image of God.

chapters.title: Chapter LV
paragraphs: On the corruption of nature and the power of divine grace

O Lord my God, you created me in your own image and likeness. Grant me this grace, which you have shown to be so great and so necessary for salvation, that I may conquer my sinful nature, which drags me toward sin and destruction. I feel in my body the law of sin, contradicting the law of my mind and taking me captive to obey my lower impulses in many things. I cannot resist my passions unless your most holy grace is fervently poured into my heart.

2. I need your grace—and a great measure of it—to overcome this nature that has always been inclined toward evil from my youth. Through the fall of Adam and the corruption of sin, the stain of punishment descended on all humanity. So nature itself, which you made good and upright, now serves as the vehicle for the vice and weakness of our corrupted condition. The small power that remains is like a single spark buried in ashes. This is natural reason itself, surrounded by thick clouds, still able to distinguish good from evil and true from false—yet powerless to fulfill all it approves, no longer possessing the full light of truth or the health of its desires.

3. This is why, O my God, I delight in your law in my inner being. I know your commandment is holy, just, and good. I recognize that all evil and sin should be avoided. Yet in my flesh I serve the law of sin, obeying my impulses rather than my reason. The desire to do good is present in me, but how to carry it out, I cannot find. I make many good resolutions, but because grace is not there to help my weakness, I fall back at the first resistance and give up. I see the way of perfection clearly. I know exactly what I should do. But crushed under the weight of my own corruption, I cannot rise to what is higher.
