4. How utterly necessary your grace is to me, O Lord—for a good beginning, for progress, and for reaching the goal. Without it I can do nothing, but through your grace which strengthens me, I can do all things. Truly heavenly grace! Without it, our merits count for nothing, and no natural gifts have any value. Arts, riches, beauty, strength, intelligence, eloquence—none of these matter before you, Lord, without your grace. For the gifts of nature belong to good and evil alike, but the unique gift of the chosen is grace—that is, love—and those who bear its mark are counted worthy of eternal life. This grace is so mighty that without it, neither the gift of prophecy, nor the working of miracles, nor any depth of thought has any value at all. Neither faith, nor hope, nor any other virtue is accepted by you without love and grace.

5. O most blessed grace, you who make the poor in spirit rich in virtues, and the one who is rich in many things humble in heart—come, descend upon me, fill me early with your consolation, or my soul may faint from weariness and dryness. I beg you, Lord, let me find grace in your sight, for your grace is enough for me, even when I cannot obtain the things that nature craves. If I am tempted and afflicted by many trials, I will fear no evil, as long as your grace is with me. This alone is my strength, my counsel, and my help. It is more powerful than all enemies and wiser than all the wise in the world.

6. Grace is the teacher of truth, the instructor of discipline, the light of the heart, the comfort of anxiety, the banisher of sorrow, the deliverer from fear, the nourisher of devotion, the one who draws forth tears. Without it, what am I but a dry tree, a useless branch, fit only to be thrown away? "Let your grace, therefore, O Lord, always go before me and follow me, and make me always devoted to good works, through Jesus Christ, your Son. Amen."
(1) Romans vii. 12, 22. 25. (2) Romans vii. 18. (3) Philippians iv. 13. (4) 2 Corinthians xii. 9.

chapters.title: Chapter LVI
paragraphs: On denying ourselves and imitating Christ through the cross

"My Son, as far as you are able to go out of yourself, so far you will be able to enter into me. Just as desiring nothing outward creates inner peace, so letting go of yourself inwardly unites you to God. I want you to learn perfect self-denial, living in my will without argument or complaint. Follow me: I am the way, the truth, and the life. Without the way, you cannot walk. Without the truth, you cannot know. Without the life, you cannot live. I am the way you must follow, the truth you must believe, the life you must hope for. I am the way that never changes, the truth that never fails, the life that never ends. I am the perfectly straight way, the supreme truth, the true life, the blessed life, the uncreated life. If you remain in my way, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free, and you will take hold of eternal life."

2. "If you want to enter into life, keep the commandments. If you want to know the truth, believe in me. If you want to be perfect, sell everything you have. If you want to be my disciple, deny yourself. If you want to possess the blessed life, despise the life you have now. If you want to be exalted in heaven, humble yourself in the world. If you want to reign with me, carry the cross with me. For only the servants of the cross find the way of blessedness and true light."

3. O Lord Jesus, because your life was narrow and despised by the world, grant me the grace to imitate you in despising the world. For the servant is not greater than his master, nor the student above his teacher. Let your servant be trained in your life, because there lies my salvation and true holiness. Whatever I read or hear beyond it does not refresh me or give me real delight.

4. "My Son, because you know these things and have read them all, you will be blessed if you do them. The one who has my commandments and keeps them—he is the one who loves me. And I will love him and will reveal myself to him, and will make him sit with me in my Father's kingdom."

5. O Lord Jesus, as you have said and promised, let it be so for me. I have received the cross from your hand. I have carried it, and I will carry it to the very end, just as you have laid it upon me. Truly, the life of a devoted servant is a cross—but it leads to paradise. I have begun; I must not turn back or abandon it.

6. Come, my brothers—let us go forward together. Jesus will be with us. For the sake of Jesus we took up this cross; for his sake let us persevere in it. He will be our helper, he who was our captain and went before us. Look—our King enters before us, and he will fight for us. Let us follow bravely. Let no one be afraid. Let us be ready to die courageously in battle, and let us not disgrace our honor by fleeing from the cross.
(1) John xiv. 6. (2) John viii. 32. (3) Matthew xix. 17, 21. (4) Matthew x. 24. (5) John xiv. 21. (6) 1 Mac. ix. 10.

chapters.title: Chapter LVII
paragraphs: On not being too discouraged when you fall into faults

"My Son, patience and humility in hard times are more pleasing to me than much comfort and devotion in good times. Why does a small criticism make you so sad? Even if it had been a far worse insult, you still should not be shaken. But let it pass. It is not the first, it is not new, and if you live long it will not be the last. You are brave enough when nothing goes wrong. You can give good advice and strengthen others with your words. But when trouble suddenly knocks at your own door, your advice and strength collapse. Consider your great fragility, which you experience so often in small matters. Yet these things happen for the good of your soul.

2. "Put these setbacks out of your heart as best you can. If trouble has touched you, do not let it throw you down or entangle you for long. At the very least, bear it patiently, even if you cannot bear it joyfully. Even if you are very reluctant to hear criticism and feel anger rising, hold yourself in check. Do not let any rash word escape your lips that could cause harm to others. The storm that was raised will soon be calmed, and your inner pain will be sweetened by returning grace. 'I still live,' says the Lord, 'ready to help you and to give you even more comfort than before, if you trust in me and call on me devoutly.'

3. "Be calmer in spirit and brace yourself for greater endurance. All is not lost even when you find yourself frequently afflicted or severely tempted. You are a human being, not God. You are flesh, not an angel. How could you always remain at the same level of virtue, when even an angel fell from heaven and the first man fell in paradise? I am the one who lifts up the mourner and sets him free. Those who acknowledge their own weakness, I raise up to share my own nature."

4. O Lord, blessed be your word—sweeter to my mouth than honey from the comb. What would I do in my great troubles and anxieties if you did not comfort me with your holy words? As long as I reach the haven of salvation at last, what does it matter what I suffer or how much? Give me a good end. Give me a peaceful passage out of this world. Remember me, O my God, and lead me by the right way into your kingdom. Amen.

chapters.title: Chapter LVIII
paragraphs: On deeper mysteries and God's hidden judgments, which we must not try to penetrate

"My Son, beware of arguing about deep matters and God's hidden judgments—why this person is left in darkness and that one is given such great favor, why one is so heavily afflicted and another so highly exalted. These things are beyond all human ability to judge, and no reasoning or debate can search out the divine judgments. When the enemy puts these questions in your mind, or when curious people raise them, answer with the prophet's words: 'You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is true,' and with this: 'The judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether.' My judgments are to be respected with awe, not debated—because they are beyond human understanding.

2. "Do not investigate or argue about which saint is holier than another, or who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Such questions often breed useless conflicts and quarrels. They feed pride and empty boasting, which in turn produce envy and division, as one person arrogantly champions one saint and another promotes a different one. Wanting to know and research such things produces no good fruit; it actually displeases the saints. For I am not the God of confusion but of peace—and that peace consists more in true humility than in self-promotion.

3. "Some are drawn by enthusiasm to feel greater devotion toward certain saints, but this is more human feeling than divine inspiration. I am the one who made all the saints. I gave them grace. I brought them to glory. I know each one's merits. I blessed them before they came to me. I knew my beloved ones from all eternity. I chose them out of the world—they did not choose me. I called them by my grace, drew them by my mercy, led them through many trials. I poured powerful consolation upon them. I gave them perseverance. I crowned their patience.

4. "I know the first and the last. I embrace all of them with immeasurable love. I am to be praised in all my saints. I am to be blessed above all things and honored in every one whom I have so gloriously lifted up and chosen—without any prior merit of their own. So whoever despises even the least of my people does not honor the great, because I made both the small and the great. And whoever speaks against any of my saints speaks against me and against everyone else in the kingdom of heaven."
They are all one through the bond of love. They think the same, will the same, and are united in love for one another.

5. "But what is far better—they love me above themselves and above their own achievements. Caught up beyond themselves and drawn past self-love, they move entirely into the love of me and rest in me with perfect delight. Nothing can turn them away or drag them down, because they are full of eternal truth and burn with the fire of unquenchable love. So let all worldly and self-centered people keep quiet about the state of the saints, for they know nothing except how to love their own personal pleasure. They add and subtract according to their own preferences, not according to the eternal truth.

6. "In many people this is simply ignorance—especially in those who, being spiritually dim, rarely learn to love anyone with a truly spiritual love. They are still strongly pulled by natural affection and human friendship toward this person or that. And just as they judge their own earthly relationships, they project the same onto heavenly things. But there is an immeasurable difference between what they imperfectly imagine and what enlightened souls see through supernatural revelation.

7. "Be careful, then, my Son, not to meddle curiously with things that exceed your understanding. Instead, make this your business and goal: to be found, even as the least, in the kingdom of God. Even if someone knew which saint was holier or which was held greatest in heaven—what good would that knowledge do him, unless it moved him to humble himself before me and rise up to give greater praise to my name? The person who considers how great his own sins are, how small his virtues, and how far he is from the perfection of the saints—that person does far more that is pleasing in God's sight than the one who debates about the saints' greatness or ranking.

8. "The saints are perfectly content. If only people would learn to be content too and stop their idle talk! The saints do not boast of their own merits, since they claim no goodness for themselves but attribute everything to me. They are filled with such great love of God and such overflowing joy that nothing is lacking in their glory or happiness. The higher the saints are exalted in glory, the humbler they are within themselves, and the nearer and dearer they are to me. That is why Scripture says they cast their crowns before God, and fell on their faces before the Lamb, and worshipped him who lives forever and ever.

9. "Many ask who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven, when they do not even know whether they will be worthy to be counted among the least. It is a great thing to be even the least in heaven, where all are great, because all shall be called—and shall truly be—children of God. 'A little one shall become a thousand, but a sinner a hundred years old shall be cursed.' When the disciples asked who should be greatest in the kingdom of heaven, they received this answer: 'Unless you are converted and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.'"

10. Woe to those who refuse to humble themselves willingly like little children, for the low gate of the kingdom of heaven will not let them through. Woe also to the rich, who have their comfort here—because while the poor enter the kingdom of God, they will stand outside in lamentation. Rejoice, you who are humble! Be glad, you who are poor! For yours is the kingdom of God—if only you walk in the truth.
(1) Psalm cxix. 137. (2) Psalm xix. 9. (3) 1 Corinthians xiv. 33. (4) Psalm xxi. 3. (5) John xv. 19. (6) Wisd. vi. 8. (7) Revelation iv. 10; v. 14. (8) Matthew xviii. 3. (9) Luke vi. 24.

chapters.title: Chapter LIX
paragraphs: On fixing all hope and trust in God alone

O Lord, what is my confidence in this life? What is my greatest comfort among all the things I see on earth? Is it not you, O Lord my God, whose mercies are without number? Where has it ever gone well with me without you? When could things go badly while you were near? I would rather be poor with you than rich without you. I would rather wander the earth as a pilgrim at your side than possess heaven without you. Where you are, there is heaven. Where you are not, there is death and hell. You are everything I long for, and so I must groan, cry out, and earnestly pray to reach you. I can fully rely on no one to give me help in time of need except you alone, O my God. You are my hope, my trust, my Comforter, and the most faithful one in all things.

2. Everyone else looks out for themselves. You alone work for my salvation and my good, turning all things to my benefit. Even when you expose me to trials and difficulties, you arrange everything for my advantage—for you are accustomed to testing your beloved ones in a thousand ways. And in this testing, you deserve to be loved and praised no less than if you were filling me with heavenly consolation.

3. In you, then, O Lord God, I place all my hope and my refuge. On you I lay all my trouble and anguish, because everything I see apart from you is weak and unstable. Many friends will not help. Strong supporters cannot save. Wise counselors cannot give a useful answer. Scholarly books cannot comfort. No precious thing can buy my freedom. No hidden, beautiful place can offer shelter—unless you yourself assist, help, strengthen, comfort, teach, and protect me.

4. For all things that seem to promise peace and happiness are nothing when you are absent, and in reality they bring no happiness at all. You are the goal of all that is good, the fullness of life, and the soul of all eloquence. To hope in you above all things is the strongest comfort your servants can have. My eyes look to you. In you is my trust, O God, Father of mercies.

5. Bless and sanctify my soul with heavenly blessing, that it may become your holy dwelling and the seat of your eternal glory. Let nothing be found in the temple of your presence that offends your eyes. According to the greatness of your goodness and the abundance of your mercies, look upon me and hear the prayer of your poor servant, far exiled from you in the land of the shadow of death. Protect and keep the soul of your least servant through all the dangers of this perishable life. By your accompanying grace, lead it along the way of peace to its home of everlasting light. Amen.
(1) Philippians ii. 21 (2) Psalm cxli. 8.
OF THE SACRAMENT OF THE ALTAR
A devout exhortation to the Holy Communion
The Voice of Christ

"Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest," says the Lord. "The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I give for the life of the world. Take, eat: this is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. The words I speak to you are spirit and life."
(1) Matthew xi. 28 (2) John vi. 51. (3) Matthew xxvi. 26; Luke xxii. 19. (4) John vi. 51, 63.

chapters.title: Chapter I
paragraphs: On receiving Christ with great reverence
The Voice of the Disciple

These are your words, O Christ, eternal Truth—though not spoken at one time or written in one place of Scripture. Because they are your words and true, I must receive them all with gratitude and faith. They are yours, and you spoke them. They are mine too, because you said them for my salvation. I gladly receive them from your mouth, that they may be more deeply planted in my heart. Words of such great grace stir me, for they are full of sweetness and love. But my own sins terrify me, and my impure conscience drives me back from receiving such great mysteries. The sweetness of your words draws me forward, but the weight of my many faults holds me down.

2. You command me to come to you with firm confidence, if I want to share in your life, and to receive the food of immortality if I desire eternal life and glory. "Come to me," you say, "all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." What a sweet and lovely word to the sinner's ear—that you, O Lord my God, invite the poor and needy to the communion of your most holy body and blood! But who am I, Lord, that I should presume to approach you? The highest heavens cannot contain you, and yet you say, "Come, all of you, to me."

3. What does this most gracious condescension mean? What is this most loving invitation? How dare I come, who know nothing good about myself that would give me the right? How can I bring you into my house, when I have sinned so often in your loving sight? Angels and archangels stand in awe of you. Saints and righteous people tremble before you—and yet you say, "Come to me!" If you, Lord, had not said it, who would believe it? And if you had not commanded it, who would dare to approach?

4. Noah, that righteous man, labored for a hundred years building the ark so that he and a few others might be saved. How, then, can I prepare myself in a single hour to receive with proper reverence the Maker of the universe? Moses, your great and special friend, built an ark of imperishable wood and covered it with the purest gold, to house the tablets of the law. And I, a perishable creature—shall I dare so casually to receive you, the Maker of the law and the Giver of life? Solomon, the wisest of Israel's kings, spent seven years building his magnificent temple to the praise of your name, celebrated its dedication for eight days, offered a thousand peace offerings, and solemnly carried the Ark of the Covenant to its prepared place with trumpets and great joy. And I, the unhappiest and poorest of people—how shall I bring you into my house, when I can hardly spend half an hour in devotion? If only it were even half an hour worthily spent!

5. O my God, how earnestly those holy men strove to please you! And how little and trivial is what I do—how short the time I spend when preparing for Communion! Rarely am I fully collected; almost never am I cleansed from all distraction. Surely, in the saving presence of your divine nature, no unworthy thought should intrude, and no creature should occupy my attention—for it is not an angel but the Lord of angels whom I am about to receive as my Guest.

6. Yet there is an enormous difference between the Ark of the Covenant with its relics, and your most pure Body with its infinite power—between those ancient sacrifices of the law, which were shadows of things to come, and the true sacrifice of your Body, which fulfills all the ancient sacrifices.

7. Why, then, do I not burn with greater longing for your adorable presence? Why do I not prepare myself with greater care to receive your holy gifts, when those ancient patriarchs, prophets, kings, and princes, with all the people, showed such deep devotion toward your divine worship?

8. The most devout King David danced with all his might before the Ark of God, remembering the blessings given to his ancestors. He made musical instruments of every kind, composed psalms and appointed them to be sung with joy, and often played the harp himself, inspired by the Holy Spirit. He taught the people of Israel to praise God with their whole hearts and with united voices, blessing and praising him every day. If such great devotion was shown before the Ark of the Testimony, how much more reverence and devotion ought to be shown now by me and all Christians at the celebration of the Sacrament, at the receiving of the most precious Body and Blood of Christ!

9. Many people travel far and wide to visit the shrines of departed saints, marvel at their deeds, admire their beautiful buildings. But here in the Sacrament of the Altar, you are present altogether—my God, the man Christ Jesus—where abundant fruit of eternal salvation is given to every person who receives you worthily and devoutly. What draws people to those pilgrimages is often curiosity and novelty, and they bring home very little spiritual fruit—especially when there is so much careless sightseeing and so little genuine repentance. But here in this Sacrament, no such superficiality draws us—only firm faith, devoted hope, and sincere love.

10. O God, invisible Creator of the world—how wonderfully you work in us! How sweetly and graciously you deal with your chosen ones, to whom you offer yourself in this Sacrament! For this surpasses all understanding, draws the hearts of the devoted, and sets their affections on fire. Even your most faithful followers, who order their whole lives toward spiritual growth, often receive from this most excellent Sacrament great grace of devotion and love of virtue.

11. O admirable and hidden grace of the Sacrament, known only to Christ's faithful ones, but beyond the experience of the faithless and those who serve sin! In this Sacrament spiritual grace is given, lost virtue is restored to the soul, and the beauty that was disfigured by sin returns. So great sometimes is this grace that from the fullness of devotion received, not only the mind but even the weak body feels new strength.

12. But we must deeply mourn our lukewarmness and negligence—that we are not drawn with greater love to become partakers of Christ, in whom all the hope and merit of those who will be saved consist. He himself is our holiness and our redemption. He is the comfort of pilgrims and the eternal delight of the saints. It is deeply sad that many pay so little attention to this life-giving mystery, which brings joy to heaven and preserves the whole world. How blind and hard the human heart must be, to pay so little regard to this priceless gift—and through daily familiarity, to let it slip into mere routine!

13. If this most holy Sacrament were celebrated in only one place and consecrated by only one priest in the whole world, imagine how eagerly people would flock to that place and that priest, just to witness the divine mysteries! But now many priests have been ordained and the Sacrament is celebrated in many places, so that God's grace and love for humanity might be seen more widely as Holy Communion is spread across the whole earth. Thank you, good Jesus, eternal Shepherd, for choosing to refresh us—poor exiles that we are—with your precious Body and Blood, and for inviting us to receive these holy mysteries with the words of your own mouth: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
(1) 1 Corinthians i. 30.

chapters.title: Chapter II
paragraphs: On the greatness and love of God shown to us in the Sacrament
The Voice of the Disciple

Trusting in your goodness and great mercy, O Lord, I come to you—the sick to the Healer, the hungry and thirsty to the Fountain of life, the pauper to the King of heaven, the servant to the Lord, the creature to the Creator, the lonely soul to my own gentle Comforter. But how is it that you come to me? Who am I that you should give yourself to me? How dare a sinner appear before you? And how is it that you choose to come to the sinner? You know your servant, and you know that he has nothing good in him that would earn this grace. So I confess my unworthiness, acknowledge your goodness, praise your tender mercy, and give you thanks for your immense love. You do this for your own sake, not for my merit—so that your goodness may be more clearly shown to me, your love more abundantly poured out upon me, and your humility more perfectly set before me. Since this is what pleases you, and since you have commanded it to be so, your condescension pleases me too. If only my sin does not stand in the way.

2. O most sweet and tender Jesus, what reverence and thanksgiving are owed to you forever for receiving your sacred Body and Blood—a gift whose dignity no one can express! But what should I think about as I approach you in Communion—you whom I cannot worthily honor, yet whom I long devoutly to receive? What could be a better or more wholesome meditation than utter humility before you and praise of your infinite goodness toward me? I praise you, my God, and exalt you forever. I despise myself and cast myself down before you into the depths of my unworthiness.

3. You are the Holy of Holies, and I am the worst of sinners. Yet you stoop down to me, who am not even worthy to look up at you. You come to me. You want to be with me. You invite me to your feast. You offer me heavenly food—the bread of angels—which is none other than yourself, the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world.

4. See where this love comes from! What extraordinary condescension shines forth here! How great the thanksgiving and praise owed to you for these gifts! How wise and beneficial was your plan when you established this Sacrament! How sweet and joyful the feast in which you gave yourself as food! How marvelous is your work, O Lord—how mighty your power, how far beyond words your truth! You spoke the word, and all things were made. And this too is accomplished because you have commanded it.

5. What a wonderful thing—worthy of faith and surpassing all human understanding—that you, O Lord my God, true God and true man, give yourself entirely to us in a little bread and wine, and become our inexhaustible food. You, the Lord of all, who need nothing, have chosen to dwell in us through your Sacrament. Keep my heart and body pure, so that with a joyful and clean conscience I may often receive—for my eternal health—your mysteries, which you consecrated and established both for your own honor and as an everlasting memorial.

6. Rejoice, O my soul, and give thanks to God for so great a gift and precious comfort, left for you in this valley of tears. For as often as you recall this mystery and receive the body of Christ, you celebrate the work of your redemption and share in all the merits of Christ. The love of Christ never grows less, and the greatness of his sacrifice is never exhausted. Therefore, by constantly renewing your spirit, you should prepare yourself for this gift and contemplate the great mystery of salvation with careful attention. It should seem as great, as new, and as joyful to you when you come to Communion as if, on that very day, Christ were descending for the first time into the Virgin's womb and becoming human—or hanging on the cross, suffering and dying for the salvation of the world.
(1) John vi. 51. (2) The words in brackets are only suitable for a priest.

chapters.title: Chapter III
paragraphs: On the value of receiving Communion often
The Voice of the Disciple

I come to you, O Lord, that I may be blessed by your gift and made joyful at your holy feast, which you, O God, in your goodness have prepared for the poor. In you is everything I can and should desire. You are my salvation and my redemption, my hope and my strength, my honor and my glory. So make the soul of your servant glad today, for to you, O Lord Jesus, I lift up my soul. I long now to receive you devoutly and reverently. I want to bring you into my house, so that like Zacchaeus I may be counted worthy of your blessing and numbered among the children of Abraham. My soul has a deep hunger for your body; my heart longs to be united with you.

2. Give me yourself, and it is enough. Apart from you, no comfort matters. Without you I cannot survive, and without your visit I have no strength to live. I must come to you often and receive you for the healing of my soul, or I may collapse along the way if I am deprived of heavenly food. For that is what you, most merciful Jesus, once did—preaching to the people and healing the sick, you said: "I will not send them away hungry, or they may faint on the way." Deal with me in the same way now, for you left yourself in the Sacrament for the comfort of the faithful. You are the sweet refreshment of the soul. Whoever eats you worthily will be a partaker and heir of eternal glory. It is absolutely necessary for me—who so often slide backward and sin, so quickly grow cold and faint—to renew, cleanse, and rekindle myself through frequent prayer, repentance, and receiving your sacred body and blood, lest by too long an absence I fall away from my holy resolutions.

3. The human heart is inclined toward evil from its youth, and without divine medicine, we slide continually toward the worse. Holy Communion draws us back from evil and strengthens us for good. If I am still so negligent and lukewarm when I do receive Communion, how much worse would I be if I did not take this medicine and seek this great help? This is the one principal comfort of a faithful soul while it is absent from you in a mortal body: that, remembering its God continually, it receives its Beloved with a devoted heart.

4. O wonderful condescension of your mercy toward us! That you, O Lord God, Creator and Giver of life to all spirits, should come to a soul so poor and weak, and satisfy its hunger with your full divinity and humanity! What a happy mind and blessed soul, to whom it is given to receive you devoutly—its Lord God—and in receiving you, to be filled with every spiritual joy! What a great Lord it welcomes! What a beloved Guest it brings in! What a delightful Companion it receives! What a faithful Friend it embraces! What a beautiful and noble Spouse—above every other beloved—it holds close! One to be loved above all things and all desires! O my sweetest Beloved, let heaven and earth and all their glory be silent in your presence, for whatever praise and beauty they possess comes from your gracious bounty. They can never match the loveliness of your name, whose wisdom is infinite.
(1) Psalm lxviii. 10. (2) Psalm lxxxvi. 4. (3) Matthew xv. 32. (4) Genesis viii. 21. (5) Psalm cxlvii. 5.

chapters.title: Chapter IV
paragraphs: On the many gifts given to those who receive Communion devoutly
The Voice of the Disciple

O Lord my God, go before your servant with the blessings of your sweetness, so that I may approach your glorious Sacrament worthily and devoutly. Awaken my heart toward you and free me from heavy drowsiness. Visit me with your salvation, so that my spirit may taste your sweetness, which lies hidden in abundance in this Sacrament as in a fountain. Open my eyes to behold this great mystery, and strengthen me to believe it with unwavering faith. For this is your work, not human power; your sacred institution, not a human invention. No one is capable in himself of receiving and understanding these things, which surpass even the wisdom of the angels. What, then, can I—an unworthy sinner, mere dust and ashes—hope to grasp of so deep a mystery?

2. O Lord, in the simplicity of my heart, with good and firm faith, and at your command, I approach you with hope and reverence. I truly believe that you are present here in the Sacrament—God and man. You want me to receive you and unite myself to you in love. So I beg your mercy and implore you for the special grace that I may be completely dissolved and overflow with love for you, and never again look for any other consolation. For this most high and glorious Sacrament is the health of soul and body, the cure for every spiritual sickness. Through it I am healed of my sins, my passions are reined in, temptations are conquered or weakened, more grace is poured in, growing virtue is strengthened, faith is made firm, hope is increased, and love is kindled and expanded.

3. For you have given many good things through this Sacrament and still give them continually to your chosen ones who receive Communion devoutly—O my God, Lifter of my soul, Healer of human weakness, and Giver of all inner comfort. You pour much consolation into them against every kind of trouble. Out of the depths of their own misery, you lift them to the hope of your protection, and with ever-new grace you inwardly refresh and enlighten them. Those who felt anxious and empty before Communion find themselves changed for the better afterward, refreshed with heavenly food and drink. You deal with your chosen ones in this way so that they may truly recognize and clearly prove that they have nothing of their own, and that all goodness and grace come from you—because, being in themselves cold, hard, and dry, through you they become fervent, eager, and devoted. Who comes humbly to the fountain of sweetness and carries away nothing of that sweetness? Who stands near a great fire and feels no warmth from it? You are an ever-full and overflowing fountain, a fire that burns continually and never goes out.

4. Even if I am not allowed to drink from the fullness of the fountain or to drink my fill, I will at least put my lips to the opening of the heavenly stream, so that I may receive even a small drop to quench my thirst and not dry up inside. Even if I cannot yet be entirely heavenly, ablaze like the Cherubim and Seraphim, I will still give myself to devotion and prepare my heart, that I may catch at least a small flame of the divine fire through the humble receiving of this life-giving Sacrament. Whatever is lacking in me, most merciful Jesus, most holy Savior, supply it from your kindness and grace—you who have called us all to yourself, saying: "Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest."

5. I labor in the sweat of my brow. I am tormented by sorrow of heart. I am weighed down by sin, disturbed by temptation, tangled and oppressed by many passions. There is no one to help me, no one to deliver and free me, except you, O Lord God, my Savior—to whom I commit myself and everything that is mine, that you may watch over me and lead me to eternal life.

Receive me for the praise and glory of your name—you who have prepared your Body and Blood to be my food and drink. Grant, O Lord God my Savior, that through coming often to your mysteries, the fire of my devotion may grow stronger.

chapters.title: Chapter V
paragraphs: On the dignity of this Sacrament and the office of the priest
The Voice of the Beloved

Even if you had the purity of angels and the holiness of John the Baptist, you would not be worthy to receive or minister this Sacrament. For it is not earned by human merit that a person should consecrate and celebrate the Body of Christ and take the bread of angels as food. It is a vast mystery and a great dignity given to priests, to whom is granted what is not given even to angels. Only priests who are properly ordained in the church have the power to consecrate and celebrate the Body of Christ. The priest is God's minister, using God's Word by God's command and institution. But God is the principal Author and invisible Worker—the one to whom all that he wills is subject, and all he commands is obedient.

2. In this most excellent Sacrament, then, you must trust God Almighty more than your own senses or any visible sign. Approach this sacred work with awe and reverence. Consider carefully what has been entrusted to you through the laying on of the bishop's hand. You have been made a priest and consecrated to celebrate. See to it that you carry out this duty before God faithfully and devoutly, at the proper time, and that you live without blame. You have not lightened your burden—you are now bound by a stricter discipline and held to a higher standard of holiness. A priest should be adorned with every virtue and serve as an example of good living. His way of life should not follow the popular ways of the world, but should be like that of the angels in heaven or of the most holy people on earth.

3. A priest who wears the sacred vestments stands in Christ's place, praying to God with all humility for himself and for all the people. He must always remember Christ's passion. He must carefully study Christ's footsteps and earnestly strive to follow them. He must bear patiently whatever suffering others inflict on him for God's sake. He must grieve for his own sins and for the sins of others, and he must never grow careless in prayer and holy worship until he obtains grace and mercy. When the priest celebrates, he honors God, gives joy to the angels, builds up the Church, helps the living, shares communion with the departed, and becomes a partaker of every good.

chapters.title: Chapter VI
paragraphs: A question about preparing for Communion
The Voice of the Disciple

When I consider your majesty, O Lord, and my own unworthiness, I tremble violently and am confused within myself. If I do not approach, I run from life. But if I come forward unworthily, I provoke your displeasure. What then shall I do, O my God, my helper and counselor in times of need?

2. Teach me the right way. Show me some brief practice suited to Holy Communion, for I need to know how to prepare my heart devoutly and reverently—so that I may receive your Sacrament for the good of my soul.

chapters.title: Chapter VII
paragraphs: On examining the conscience and resolving to change
The Voice of the Beloved

Above all things, the priest of God must approach this Sacrament with the deepest humility and reverent supplication, with full faith and a devout desire for God's honor—to celebrate, administer, and receive it. Examine your conscience carefully. With all your strength, through true sorrow and humble confession, cleanse and purify it, so that you carry no burden or unresolved guilt that would hinder your approach. Have displeasure toward all your sins in general, and feel special sorrow and grief over your daily failings. If you have time, confess to God in the secrecy of your heart all the miseries of your own passions.

2. Grieve deeply and be sorry that you are still so worldly and fleshly, so undisciplined in your desires, so unguarded in your outward senses, so often entangled in empty fantasies, so drawn to outward things, so neglectful of what is within. Be sorry that you are so quick to laugh and slow to weep, so inclined toward ease and bodily comfort, so dull when it comes to zeal and devotion. Be sorry that you are so curious about novelties and so reluctant to embrace what is humble and plain. Be sorry that you are so eager to acquire and so reluctant to give, so careless in speech and so unwilling to be silent, so disorderly in behavior and so thoughtless in actions. Be sorry that you are so eager for food and so deaf to the Word of God, so quick to seek rest and so slow to work, so alert for gossip and so drowsy during holy vigils. Be sorry that you are so impatient for the end of worship and so unfocused during it, so negligent in prayer and so lukewarm in celebration, so distracted and so rarely fully present. Be sorry that you are so easily angered and so ready to find fault with others, so prone to judging and so harsh in correcting, so happy in good times and so weak in bad times, so often making good resolutions and so rarely following through.

3. When you have confessed and mourned over these and your other failings, with sorrow and deep displeasure at your own weakness, make a firm resolution of constant improvement and progress in goodness. Then, with full surrender and your whole will, offer yourself on the altar of your heart as a perpetual sacrifice to the honor of my name. Faithfully entrust your body and soul to me, so that you may be counted worthy to approach and offer this sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving to God—and to receive the Sacrament of my Body and Blood for the health of your soul. For there is no offering more worthy, no satisfaction greater for destroying sin, than that a person offer himself to God purely and completely along with the offering of Christ's Body and Blood in Holy Communion. When a person has done what he can and has truly repented, then however often he comes to me for pardon and grace: "As I live," says the Lord, "I take no pleasure in the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live. All the sins he has committed will not be held against him."
(1) Ezekiel xviii. 22, 23.

chapters.title: Chapter VIII
paragraphs: On the offering of Christ on the cross and on surrendering yourself
The Voice of the Beloved

Just as I willingly offered myself to God the Father on the cross for your sins—with outstretched hands and naked body, so that nothing in me remained that was not given entirely as a sacrifice—so you also ought to offer yourself willingly to me every day as a pure and holy offering, with all your strength and affection, to the fullest extent of your heart. What more do I ask of you than that you give yourself entirely to me? Whatever you give besides yourself, I do not care about. I do not want your gift; I want you.

2. Just as it would not be enough for you to have everything except me, so whatever you give me will not please me if you do not give me yourself. Offer yourself to me and give yourself wholly to God—then your offering will be accepted. I offered my entire self to the Father for you. I gave my whole body and blood as food, so that I might be entirely yours and you might be entirely mine. But if you hold back, keeping yourself for yourself and not freely offering yourself to my will, your offering is not complete, and our union will not be perfect. A free offering of yourself into God's hands must come before all your works, if you want to gain freedom and grace. This is why so few are inwardly enlightened and truly free—because they do not know how to give up themselves completely. My word stands firm: unless a person gives up everything, he cannot be my disciple. So if you want to be my disciple, offer yourself to me with all your heart.
(1) Luke xiv. 33.

chapters.title: Chapter IX
paragraphs: On offering ourselves and all we have to God, and praying for everyone
The Voice of the Disciple

Lord, all that is in heaven and earth is yours. I desire to offer myself to you as a freewill offering and to remain yours forever. Lord, with an upright heart I willingly offer myself to you today—to be your servant forever, in humble submission and as a sacrifice of unending praise. Receive me with this holy Communion of your precious Body, which I celebrate before you today in the presence of the angels who invisibly surround us—that it may be for the salvation of me and all your people.

2. Lord, I place before you at this celebration all my sins and offenses that I have committed before you and your holy angels, from the day I was first able to sin until this very hour. May you consume and burn them all with the fire of your love. Wipe away every stain of my sin, cleanse my conscience from all guilt, restore me to your favor that I lost through sinning, fully forgive me, and mercifully welcome me with the kiss of peace.

3. What can I do about my sins except humbly confess them, grieve over them, and ceaselessly ask for your mercy? I beg you, be merciful to me and hear me, as I stand before you, O my God. All my sins deeply displease me. I will never commit them again. I grieve for them and will grieve as long as I live, firmly resolved to repent truly and make amends as far as I can. Forgive me, O God, forgive me my sins for the sake of your holy name. Save my soul, which you redeemed with your precious blood. I commit myself to your mercy. I place myself in your hands. Deal with me according to your loving-kindness, not according to my wickedness and sin.

4. I also offer to you all my goodness, though it is terribly small and imperfect—that you may improve and sanctify it, make it pleasing and acceptable in your sight, and continually draw it toward perfection. Bring me safely, lazy and useless creature that I am, to a good and blessed end.

5. I also offer to you the devout desires of all faithful people—the needs of parents, friends, brothers, sisters, and everyone dear to me, and of all who have done good to me or to others for your love, and of all who have asked for my prayers for themselves and their families. May all of them feel your grace helping them, your comfort enriching them, your protection shielding them from danger, your hand freeing them from pain. Delivered from every evil, may they joyfully give you abundant thanks.

6. I also offer prayers and sacramental intercessions for those who have hurt me in any way, who have made me sad, spoken evil about me, or caused me any loss or trouble. I pray also for all those whom I have ever saddened, disturbed, burdened, or scandalized by words or actions, knowingly or unknowingly—that you would equally forgive all of us our sins and offenses against one another. Take from our hearts, Lord, all suspicion, resentment, anger, and conflict, and everything that can wound love and weaken brotherly affection. Have mercy, have mercy, Lord, on those who ask for your mercy. Give grace to the needy. And make us the kind of people who are worthy to enjoy your grace and advance toward eternal life. Amen.
(1) 1 Chronicles xxix. 11. (2) 1 Chronicles xxix. 17.

chapters.title: Chapter X
paragraphs: On not neglecting Holy Communion lightly
The Voice of the Beloved

You must frequently turn to the Fountain of grace and divine mercy, the Fountain of goodness and all purity—so that you may be healed of your passions and vices, and grow stronger and more alert against all the temptations and tricks of the devil. The enemy knows what great benefit and powerful remedy lies in Holy Communion, so he tries by every means to draw back and hinder the faithful and devout, as much as he can.

2. When some people prepare for Holy Communion, they experience worse attacks from Satan. The evil spirit himself, as we read in Job, comes among the children of God to trouble them with his usual malice, or to make them overly fearful and anxious—hoping to weaken their devotion, or to destroy their faith through his attacks, so that they give up Communion altogether or come to it with lukewarm hearts. But his tricks and delusions must not be heeded, however wicked and terrible they may be. All his deception must be thrown back on his own head. The wretch should be despised and laughed at. Holy Communion must never be abandoned because of his insults and the inner turmoil he stirs up.

3. Often, too, excessive worry or some anxiety about confession gets in the way of devotion. Follow the advice of wise people and set aside anxiety and scruples, because these block God's grace and kill devotion. Do not neglect Holy Communion because of some small trouble or difficulty. Go quickly to confession, freely forgive all offenses against you, and if you have wronged anyone, humbly ask for pardon. God will freely forgive you.

4. What good does it do to put off confession for a long time or to delay Communion? Cleanse yourself immediately. Spit out the poison at once. Hurry to take the remedy, and you will feel better than if you had waited. If you put it off today for one reason, tomorrow something bigger may come along, and you may stay away from Communion for a long time and become less and less fit for it. Shake off your present heaviness and laziness as soon as you can. There is no benefit in prolonged anxiety, or in trudging along weighed down with a heavy heart, or in staying away from sacred things because of daily small obstacles. In fact, it is very harmful to delay Communion for a long time, because this usually brings on deep spiritual numbness. Sadly, some lukewarm and undisciplined people gladly make excuses to postpone repentance and wish to delay Communion so they won't have to keep a stricter watch over themselves.

5. How little love, how feeble devotion, those people have who so easily put off Holy Communion! How happy and how pleasing to God is the person who lives in such purity of conscience that he could be ready and willing to receive Communion any day, if it were allowed and could be done without drawing attention! If someone sometimes abstains out of humility or for some good reason, he is to be praised for his reverence. But if laziness has taken hold, he must rouse himself and do what he can. The Lord will honor his good intention, which God especially values.

6. When someone is prevented by a legitimate reason, he should still maintain a good will and a devout intention to receive Communion—and in this way, he will not lose the fruit of the Sacrament. For any devout person can, every day and every hour, draw near to Christ in spiritual communion—for the health of his soul and without any obstacle. Yet at set times and on appointed days, he should receive the Body and Blood of his Redeemer with loving reverence, seeking God's praise and honor rather than his own comfort. For as often as he devoutly recalls the mystery of Christ's incarnation and passion, and is set ablaze with love for him, he receives spiritual communion and is invisibly refreshed.

7. The person who only prepares himself when a feast day approaches or custom requires it will too often be unprepared. Blessed is the one who offers himself to God as a whole burnt offering every time he celebrates or receives Communion! Do not be too slow or too hurried in your celebration, but follow the good practice of those among whom you live. You should not cause weariness or annoyance to others, but follow the established custom according to the guidance of those who came before you—and serve the good of others rather than your own devotion or preference.

chapters.title: Chapter XI
paragraphs: On how the Body and Blood of Christ and the Holy Scriptures are most necessary to a faithful soul
The Voice of the Disciple

O most sweet Lord Jesus, how great is the happiness of the devout soul that feasts with you at your banquet, where there is no other food set before it than you yourself—its only Beloved, more desired than all the desires of the heart! To me it would be sweet indeed to pour out my tears in your presence from the very bottom of my heart, and with the devout Magdalene to wash your feet with my tears. But where is this devotion? Where the abundant flow of holy tears? Surely, in your presence and before the holy angels, my whole heart should burn and weep for joy. For I have you truly present in the Sacrament, though hidden under another form.

2. My eyes could not endure to behold you in your own divine brightness. The whole world could not stand before the splendor of your majestic glory. So you show consideration for my weakness by hiding yourself under the Sacrament. I truly possess and adore the one whom the angels adore in heaven. I see by faith, for now; they see face to face, without a veil. I must be content with the light of true faith and walk in it until the day of eternal brightness dawns and the shadows pass away. But when that which is perfect comes, the use of sacraments will cease, because the blessed in heavenly glory have no need of sacramental help. They rejoice endlessly in God's presence, beholding his glory face to face, and being transformed from glory to glory, they taste the Word of God made flesh—as he was in the beginning and remains forever.

3. When I think about these wonders, even spiritual comfort of any kind becomes wearisome to me. As long as I do not see my Lord openly in his own glory, I count as nothing everything I see and hear in this world. You are my witness, O God, that nothing can comfort me and no creature can give me rest except you, my God, whom I long to contemplate forever. But this is not possible as long as I remain in this mortal body. So I must set myself to great patience and submit myself to you in every desire. For even your saints, Lord, who now rejoice with you in the kingdom of heaven, waited for the coming of your glory while they lived here—in faith and great patience. What they believed, I believe. What they hoped for, I hope for. Where they have arrived, I trust by your grace to arrive as well. Meanwhile, I will walk in faith, strengthened by the examples of the saints. I will also have holy books for comfort and as a mirror for my life. And above them all, your most holy Body and Blood will be my special remedy and refuge.

4. Two things feel absolutely essential to me in this life. Without them, this miserable existence would be unbearable. Detained in the prison of this body, I confess that I need two things: food and light. You have therefore given me—weak as I am—your sacred Body and Blood as refreshment for my soul and body, and you have set your Word as a lamp for my feet. Without these two I could not properly live, for the Word of God is the light of my soul, and your Sacrament is the bread of life. These may also be called two tables, placed on either side in the treasury of your holy Church. One table is the Sacred Altar, bearing the holy bread—the precious Body and Blood of Christ. The other is the table of the Divine Law, containing holy teaching, instructing in the true faith, and leading steadily onward even to the Holy of Holies.

5. Thank you, O Lord Jesus, Light of everlasting Light, for that table of holy teaching which you have provided through your servants the prophets and apostles and other teachers. Thank you, O Creator and Redeemer of all, for preparing a great feast to make your love known to the whole world. At this feast you have set before us not the symbolic lamb, but your own most holy Body and Blood—making all the faithful joyful with this holy banquet and giving them the cup of salvation to drink, in which are all the delights of paradise. The holy angels feast with us, but with an even sweeter joy.

6. How great and honorable is the office of the priest, to whom it is given to consecrate the Sacrament of the Lord of majesty with holy words, to bless it with his lips, to hold it in his hands, to receive it with his own mouth, and to give it to others! How clean those hands should be, how pure the lips, how holy the body, how spotless the heart of the priest, into whom the Author of all purity so often enters! From the mouth of a priest, nothing should come but what is holy, honest, and edifying, since he so often receives the Sacrament of Christ.

7. His eyes should be simple and pure, since they regularly look upon the Body of Christ. His hands should be clean and raised toward heaven, since they regularly hold the Creator of heaven and earth. To priests especially the law says: "Be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy."

8. Assist us with your grace, O Almighty God, that we who have taken on the priestly office may be able to serve you worthily and devoutly, in all purity and with a good conscience. And if we cannot live with the innocence we ought to have, grant us at least to grieve sincerely over the sins we have committed, and in the spirit of humility and with a firm resolve of good will, to serve you more earnestly in the future.
(1) Cant. ii. 17. (2) 2 Corinthians iii. 18. (3) Psalm cxix. 105. (4) Leviticus xix. 2.

chapters.title: Chapter XII
paragraphs: On preparing carefully before receiving Communion
The Voice of the Beloved

I am the Lover of purity and the Giver of holiness. I seek a pure heart, and there is the place of my rest. Prepare the large upper room, furnished and ready, and I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples. If you want me to come to you and remain with you, clear out the old leaven and cleanse the dwelling of your heart. Shut out the whole world and all the noise of sin. Sit like a sparrow alone on the rooftop, and think over your failings with bitterness of soul. For everyone who loves prepares the best and finest place for his beloved—and by this, the depth of his affection is revealed.

2. Yet understand that you cannot make sufficient preparation through any merit of your own, even if you spent an entire year preparing and thought of nothing else. Only through my tenderness and grace are you permitted to approach my table—as though a beggar were invited to a rich man's feast and had nothing to offer in return except humility and gratitude. So do what lies in your power, and do it carefully—not out of routine or obligation, but with reverence, love, and awe. Receive the Body of your beloved Lord God, who comes to you by his own choice. I am the one who called you. I commanded this to be done. I will supply what is lacking in you. Come and receive me.

3. When I give the grace of devotion, thank your God—not because you are worthy, but because I have shown you mercy. If you do not feel devotion but instead feel dry, keep praying. Do not stop groaning and knocking. Keep at it until you obtain at least some crumb or drop of saving grace. You need me; I do not need you. You do not come to make me holy—I come to make you holy and to make you better. You come so that you may be sanctified by me and united to me, so that you may receive fresh grace and be stirred to real change. Do not neglect this grace. Prepare your heart with all care, and welcome your Beloved.

4. You should not only prepare devoutly before Communion but also guard yourself carefully afterward. The watchfulness required after receiving the Sacrament is no less important than the devout preparation before it. Good watchfulness afterward becomes the best preparation for receiving even greater grace. Nothing makes a person more unfit for spiritual blessing than immediately running to outward distractions after Communion. Guard against excessive talking. Stay in a quiet place and hold communion with your God. You have him—and the whole world cannot take him from you. I am the one to whom you should give yourself entirely, so that from now on you may live not in yourself but in me, free from all anxiety.
(1) Mark xiv. 14, 15. (2) 1 Corinthians v. 7. (3) Psalm cii. 7.

chapters.title: Chapter XIII
paragraphs: On the devout soul's longing to be united with Christ in the Sacrament
The Voice of the Disciple

Who will grant me, O Lord, to find you alone and to open my whole heart to you, and to enjoy you as much as my soul longs for—so that no one else will notice me, and no creature will move me or draw my attention, but you alone will speak to me and I to you, as a beloved speaks to a beloved and a friend feasts with a friend? This is what I pray for and long for: to be wholly united to you and to withdraw my heart from all created things. Through Holy Communion and frequent celebration, may I learn more and more to savor heavenly and eternal things. Lord God, when will I be entirely united to you and lost in you, and completely forgetful of myself? "You in me, and I in you"—grant that we may remain together as one.

2. Truly you are my Beloved, the fairest among ten thousand, in whom my soul delights to dwell all the days of her life. You are my Peacemaker, in whom there is perfect peace and true rest. Apart from you, there is only labor, sorrow, and endless misery. You are a God who hides himself. Your counsel is not with the wicked, but your Word is with the humble and the simple. How sweet is your spirit, O Lord! To show your tenderness toward your children, you feed them with bread full of sweetness that comes down from heaven. Truly, there is no nation so great that has its gods coming near to it, as you, our God, are present to all your faithful ones—giving yourself for their daily comfort, to lift their hearts to heaven, as their food and their joy.

3. For what other nation is so honored as the Christian people? What creature under heaven is so beloved as the devout soul, into whom God enters to feed it with his glorious flesh? O unspeakable grace! O wonderful condescension! O immeasurable love, given especially to us! But what return can I make to the Lord for this grace, for such overwhelming love? There is nothing I can offer that is more fitting than to give my heart entirely to God, and to join it inwardly to him. Then all my inward being will rejoice, when my soul is perfectly united to God. Then he will say to me: "If you will be with me, I will be with you." And I will answer him: "Stay with me, Lord. I will gladly be with you. This is my whole desire—that my heart be united to you."
(1) John xv. 4. (2) Cant. v. 10. (3) Deuteronomy iv. 7.

chapters.title: Chapter XIV
paragraphs: On the passionate desire of certain devout people to receive the Body and Blood of Christ
The Voice of the Disciple

How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have stored up for those who fear you! When I think of certain devout people who come to your Sacrament with the deepest devotion and warmest feeling, I am often ashamed and embarrassed that I approach your altar and the table of Holy Communion so carelessly and coldly, that I remain so dry and without feeling, that I am not fully set ablaze with love in your presence, my God, nor as powerfully drawn and moved as many devout people have been. Out of their sheer hunger for Communion and tender love of heart, they could not hold back their tears. With both heart and body, they reached out inwardly to you, O God, O Fountain of Life, unable to ease or satisfy their hunger except by receiving your Body with every spiritual joy and eagerness.

2. What truly burning faith they had—itself a living proof of your sacred presence! They knew their Lord in the breaking of bread, because their hearts burned so intensely within them as Jesus walked with them on the road. Such love and devotion, such passionate longing, is usually far from me. Be merciful to me, O Jesus, good, sweet, and kind. Grant your poor, begging servant to feel sometimes in Holy Communion—even just a little—the warmth of your love, so that my faith may grow stronger, my hope in your goodness increase, and my love, once kindled by tasting the heavenly bread, may never grow cold.

3. Your mercy is powerful enough to give me the grace I long for and to visit me with overwhelming tenderness and the spirit of fervor, on the day of your good pleasure. Although I do not burn with the fierce desire of your most devoted followers, I do—by your grace—desire that very desire. I pray and long to be counted among all those who love you so fervently, and to be numbered in their holy company.
(1) Luke xxiv. 32.

chapters.title: Chapter XV
paragraphs: On gaining the grace of devotion through humility and self-denial
The Voice of the Beloved

You should seek the grace of devotion earnestly, ask for it with fervor, wait for it patiently and faithfully, receive it gratefully, guard it humbly, work with it diligently, and leave to God the time and manner of his heavenly visit until he comes. You should humble yourself especially when you feel little or no devotion inwardly, yet without becoming overly discouraged or grieving beyond measure. God often gives in a single moment what he has long withheld. He sometimes gives at the end of prayer what he delayed giving at the beginning.

2. If grace were always given immediately and were available on demand, it would be hard for weak human nature to handle. So the grace of devotion must be waited for with good hope and humble patience. When it is not given, or when it is mysteriously withdrawn, blame yourself and your sins. Sometimes a small thing blocks and hides grace—though if something can block so great a good, it should really be called great, not small. But if you remove this obstacle, whether small or great, and completely overcome it, you will receive what you asked for.

3. For as soon as you give yourself to God with your whole heart, seeking neither this nor that according to your own will and pleasure, but settling yourself entirely in him, you will find yourself united and at peace. Nothing will bring you such sweet delight as the good pleasure of the divine will. Whoever lifts up his will to God with a single heart, free from every disordered love or dislike of any created thing—that person is most fit for receiving grace and most worthy of the gift of devotion. For where the Lord finds empty vessels, there he pours out his blessing. The more completely a person forsakes what is worthless, the more he dies to himself. The more quickly grace comes, the more abundantly it enters, and the higher it lifts the free heart.

4. Then he will see, and overflow, and marvel, and his heart will be enlarged within him—because the Lord's hand is with him, and he has placed himself wholly in God's hand, forever. This is how the person will be blessed who seeks God with all his heart and does not receive his soul in vain. In receiving the Holy Eucharist, this person obtains the great grace of divine union—because he looks not to his own devotion and comfort, but above all devotion and comfort, to the glory and honor of God.
(1) 2 Kings iv. (2) Isaiah lx. 5.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI
paragraphs: On laying open our needs to Christ and asking for his grace
The Voice of the Disciple

O most sweet and loving Lord, whom I now desire to receive devoutly—you know my weakness and the trouble I endure, the evils and vices I am caught in, how often I am weighed down, tempted, disturbed, and stained. I come to you for healing. I ask you for comfort and support. I speak to you who know all things, to whom all my secrets are open, and who alone can perfectly comfort and help me. You know what good thing I need most, and how poor I am in virtues.

2. Here I stand, poor and naked before you, asking for grace and begging for mercy. Feed your hungry suppliant. Warm my coldness with the fire of your love. Enlighten my blindness with the brightness of your presence. Turn all earthly things into bitterness for me, all hardships and opposition into patience, all worthless created things into contempt and forgetfulness. Lift my heart to you in heaven, and do not let me wander over the earth. From this day forward and forever, be you alone sweet to me—for you alone are my food and drink, my love and joy, my sweetness and my whole good.

3. If only you would entirely set me ablaze by your presence, consume me and transform me into yourself—so that I might become one spirit with you, through the grace of inward union and the melting power of earnest love! Do not send me away hungry and dry, but deal mercifully with me, as you have so often dealt wonderfully with your saints. Would it be surprising if I were wholly set on fire by you, and in myself entirely fail—since you are the fire that always burns and never goes out, the love that purifies the heart and illuminates the mind?

chapters.title: Chapter XVII
paragraphs: On the fervent love and intense desire to receive Christ
The Voice of the Disciple

With the deepest devotion and burning love, with all the affection and fervor of my heart, I long to receive you, O Lord—just as many saints and devout people desired you when they received Communion. They were wholly pleasing to you by the holiness of their lives and dwelt in the most ardent devotion. O my God, eternal Love, my whole Good, my immeasurable Happiness—I desire to receive you with the most intense longing and fitting reverence that any saint ever had or could have.

2. Although I am unworthy of all those feelings of devotion, I still offer you the entire affection of my heart—as though I alone had all those burning, grateful desires. Indeed, whatever a devout mind can imagine and long for, all of this I offer and present to you with the deepest reverence and inward fervor. I wish to hold nothing back, but to offer myself and all that I have freely and entirely as a sacrifice to you. O Lord my God, my Creator and my Redeemer—with such affection, reverence, praise, and honor; with such gratitude, worthiness, and love; with such faith, hope, and purity do I desire to receive you today as your most blessed Mother, the glorious Virgin Mary, received and desired you, when she humbly and devoutly answered the angel who brought her the glad news of the Incarnation: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word."

3. And as your blessed forerunner, the greatest of saints, John the Baptist—full of joy in your presence—leaped in his mother's womb for joy in the Holy Spirit, and later, seeing Jesus walking among the people, humbled himself deeply and said with loving devotion: "The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice"—even so, I wish to be set ablaze with great and holy desires, and to present myself to you with my whole heart. On behalf of myself and everyone who has been commended to me in prayer, I offer and present to you the jubilation of all devout hearts, their burning desires, their spiritual ecstasies, and their heavenly visions, with all the virtues and praises celebrated and still to be celebrated by every creature in heaven and on earth—so that by all these you may be worthily praised and glorified forever.

4. Receive my prayers, O Lord my God, and my desire to give you infinite praise and boundless blessing—which, given the immensity of your unspeakable greatness, are most rightly owed to you. These I give you and desire to give you every day and every moment. With earnest requests and loving desire, I call upon all the heavenly spirits and all your faithful people to join me in rendering you thanks and praise.

5. Let all peoples, nations, and tongues praise you and magnify your holy and sweet name with the highest joy and burning devotion. And let all who reverently and devoutly celebrate your most high Sacrament and receive it with full confidence of faith be counted worthy to find grace and mercy with you. Let them pray for me, a sinner. And when they have reached the devotion and joyful union with you that they longed for, and depart from your holy heavenly table fully comforted and wonderfully refreshed—let them remember me, for I am poor and needy.
(1) Luke i. 38. (2) John iii. 29.

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: On not investigating the Sacrament with curiosity, but humbly imitating Christ and submitting our minds to holy faith
The Voice of the Beloved

You must guard against curious and useless probing into this most profound Sacrament, if you do not want to be plunged into a sea of doubt. "Whoever searches into majesty will be overwhelmed by its glory." God can do more than the human mind can grasp. A humble and reverent search after truth is permitted—one that is always ready to be taught and that tries to follow the sound teaching of the fathers.

2. Blessed is the simplicity that leaves behind the difficult paths of speculation and follows the plain, firm steps of God's commandments. Many people have lost their devotion by trying to explore things too deep for them. What is asked of you is faith and a sincere life—not a towering intellect or mastery of divine mysteries. If you cannot understand the things beneath you, how will you comprehend the things above? Submit yourself to God. Humble your reasoning before faith, and the light of knowledge will be given to you—as much as is profitable and necessary.

3. Some people are severely tempted about their faith and the Sacrament, but this should not be blamed on them. It comes from the enemy. Pay no attention to it. Do not argue with your own thoughts or respond to the doubts the devil throws at you. Instead, believe the words of God, believe his saints and prophets, and the wicked enemy will flee from you. Often it is actually beneficial for God's servant to endure such trials. The enemy does not bother tempting unbelievers and sinners, since he already has them securely in his grip. But he attacks and harasses the faithful and devout in every way he can.

4. Go forward, then, with simple and unwavering faith, and approach the Sacrament with humble reverence. Whatever you cannot understand, commit it without anxiety to Almighty God. God does not deceive you. The one who is deceived is the person who trusts too much in himself. God walks with the simple, reveals himself to the humble, gives understanding to the young, opens the minds of the pure, and hides his grace from the curious and the proud. Human reason is weak and can be misled. But true faith cannot be deceived.

5. All reasoning and natural investigation should follow faith, not go before it or try to break it. For faith and love hold the highest place here, and they work in hidden ways in this most holy and supremely excellent Sacrament. God, who is eternal, incomprehensible, and infinite in power, does great and unsearchable things in heaven and on earth—and his wonderful works are beyond all finding out. If God's works were the kind that human reason could easily grasp, they would no longer deserve to be called wonderful or beyond words.
